POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Sun, 15 Nov 2026 14:32:39 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 Estonia accuses Russia of attempted arson attack on defense firm https://www.politico.eu/article/estonia-accuses-russia-of-attempted-arson-attack-on-drone-maker/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sun, 15 Nov 2026 14:32:13 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9326907 Estonia has accused Russia’s military intelligence service of ordering an attempted arson attack on an Estonian drone maker, prompting Tallinn to threaten to close its border with Russia.

Intruders were found at Threod Systems in Viimsi, outside the Estonian capital, shortly after 3 a.m. on Saturday trying to break into the building with the aim of setting it on fire and causing an explosion, Prosecutor General Astrid Asi said Sunday.

Writing on X, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said: “This is part of Russia’s broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia. We will not be intimidated.”

He added that “Estonia is preparing for the possibility of closing its border with Russia to reduce the risks to our people and national security.”

Threod’s security staff stopped the attack before it could cause significant damage, authorities said. Eight suspects, all residents of neighboring Latvia, were detained. Five have been remanded in custody.

Estonia’s Internal Security Service, known as KAPO, said intelligence gathered by its officers showed the attack was commissioned by Russia’s GRU military intelligence agency. Threod makes long-range reconnaissance and attack drones.

“We will not be intimidated. Together with our allies, we will continue supporting Ukraine and standing firm against Russian aggression,” Estonia’s defense ministry said in a statement on X.

The latest attempt follows an August arson attack on Milrem Robotics, which supplies unmanned ground vehicles to Ukraine. Estonian authorities formally blamed Russian intelligence for that incident in September.

KAPO has warned that Russia is increasingly targeting European defense manufacturers to disrupt military production and deliveries to Ukraine. The investigation into Saturday’s attempted attack remains ongoing.

]]> en Romania slams ‘unacceptable’ drone strikes on Black Sea ships https://www.politico.eu/article/romanian-pm-condemns-unacceptable-drone-strikes-black-sea-ships/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sun, 15 Nov 2026 13:16:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9326718 Romanian Prime Minister Luca Niculescu on Sunday condemned drone strikes on three commercial ships near his country’s Black Sea coast, promising to work with NATO allies to strengthen security in the region following the latest attacks.

“These incidents are unacceptable and constitute a violation of international law,” Niculescu said in a post on X. He added that Russia’s war against Ukraine was causing the security situation in the Black Sea to deteriorate.

The ships were hit Saturday evening and overnight near Sulina, a Romanian port where the Danube River meets the Black Sea.

The Greek-flagged oil tanker Evia Petrol V was struck just after 9 p.m., followed 35 minutes later by a strike on another ship, the Marsol, according to a statement from Romania’s defense ministry published on its Facebook page.

“In both cases, the fires were extinguished by the ships’ crews. No casualties were reported,” the ministry said.

A third vessel, the Ali Najafov, also reported being struck overnight. It remains unclear who launched the drones.

Romania’s military detected aerial targets on radar and sent F-16 fighter jets into the air. Authorities also issued warnings to residents near the coast about possible drone threats.

The attacks came after another commercial ship, the Larissa 1, was reportedly hit by a drone near Romania’s coast on Friday.

Romanian Defense Minister Ștefan-Radu Oprea said Sunday he would raise the incidents with allied counterparts in Brussels. “We need the solidarity of our allies,” he said, calling for more surveillance aircraft and equipment to defend against drones.

Last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the EU will help finance some Black Sea security costs following recent attacks on commercial shipping.

In October, at least seven commercial vessels were struck by drones in the Black Sea close to NATO and EU members Romania and Bulgaria, leaving more than 20 sailors dead and dozens missing. 

]]> en Israel kills Hamas commander in Gaza strike https://www.politico.eu/article/israel-kills-hamas-commander-in-gaza-strike/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sun, 15 Nov 2026 09:43:15 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9326400 Israel said Sunday it had killed a senior Hamas commander in an overnight airstrike in southern Gaza, just two months after his predecessor was killed.

The Israel Defense Forces identified the commander as Samir Mahmoud Hassan Abu Younis, who led Hamas’ Rafah Brigade and reportedly had a leading role in planning the Oct. 7 2023 massacre in Israel.

“Abu Younis was appointed commander of the brigade approximately 2 months ago, following the elimination of his predecessor,” the IDF said in a statement posted on X on Sunday.

According to the Israeli military, Abu Younis previously served as deputy commander of the brigade and led its Tel al-Sultan Battalion.

The IDF accused him of directing attacks against Israeli civilians and soldiers, as well as working to rebuild Hamas’ military capabilities.

“The terrorist was eliminated in order to remove the threat he posed,” the military said.

Writing on Telegram, Hamas’s Al-Qassam Brigades said Abu Younis had been involved in “numerous high-profile operations” and was “one of the most important commanders involved in planning and overseeing the October 7th attack.”

Abu Younis succeeded Nael Abu Obeid, who was killed by Israel on Sept. 15, making him the latest in a series of Hamas commanders targeted by Israeli forces.

The killing comes amid a fragile ceasefire that took effect in Oct. 2025, ending major fighting but failing to stop Israeli strikes in Gaza. U.S. President Donald Trump’s broader peace plan remains stalled over disagreements about Hamas’ disarmament and Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has insisted that Hamas surrender its weapons before Israeli troops withdraw, rejecting a proposed phased approach that would see both steps take place in parallel.

]]> en Ukraine claims thousands of Russian casualties and a slowing Kremlin advance https://www.politico.eu/article/russian-army-is-slowing-down-as-ukrainian-forces-kill-thousands-of-kremlin-troops/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sun, 15 Nov 2026 03:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9322239 DNIPRO, Ukraine — Heavy Russian losses are one of the reasons for Moscow’s slowing advance in Ukraine this year, the commander of the country’s Air Assault Forces said.

“Even though the Russian offensive continues, the enemy is not demonstrating rapid operational successes that would allow it to advance quickly. They are slowing down,” Maj. Gen. Oleh Apostol told a group of journalists in a secure location on Tuesday.

“If they capture a single tree line in a month, that hardly constitutes an operational success upon which further gains can be built,” Apostol said.

Russian casualties are rising, according to the commander and to NATO officials.

“In the past few months, Russia has been losing more than 40,000 troops — killed or seriously wounded — every month. The United States in 14 years, in Vietnam, lost 56,000. Here in one month, Russia, dead or seriously wounded, 40,000. And in October, early reporting indicates this number may have climbed to over 50,000,” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said this week.

Neither Ukraine nor Russia publishes their exact military losses.

The Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies this summer estimated that Russian forces had suffered about 1.4 million casualties, including 400,000 to 450,000 fatalities, from the start of the full-scale invasion through June 2026. It estimated Ukrainian casualties at 525,000 to 625,000, including 125,000 to 150,000 fatalities, over the same period.

Despite rising casualties, the Russian military continues to press forward but is making few lasting gains, Apostol said. He estimated that Ukrainian forces had retaken more than 800 square kilometers from Russian forces this year as the result of two local counteroffensive operations.

Ukraine’s offensives have both a military and a political meaning as they show Kyiv is successfully resisting Russian pressure, Apostol said.

In his view, successes on the battlefield provide additional arguments for continuing military aid from Kyiv’s allies, while a lack of positive momentum could increase external pressure to negotiate.

“Ukrainian counter-offensive actions refute Russian claims regarding the impossibility of further resistance and strengthen Ukraine’s arguments in its engagement with international partners,” the general said.

Apostol said that many of Moscow’s claimed successes are propaganda efforts that do not mark real territorial gains and that lower-level commanders may mislead their superiors about the actual situation on the battlefield.

When it’s impossible to demonstrate real success, Russian forces use individual soldiers with flags to film proof of control over entire areas, Apostol said, adding that such soldiers are usually quickly killed by Ukrainian forces.

“A Russian flag at a given position does not necessarily mean that the location has actually been captured and is being held,” he said.

Claims and counter-claims

During the latest round of U.S.-led peace talks this week, Russia claimed it had occupied half of the territory in the Donbas that is currently under Ukrainian control, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

“So the Russians think and they share that they really occupied half of the territory of Donbas, which we control really,” he said, adding that Russian leader Vladimir Putin was being misinformed and that Kremlin negotiators were trying to use exaggerated territorial claims to influence the U.S.

“I think that Putin lives a little bit in different information,” Zelenskyy said. “It’s a different reality. And of course, he is sharing with America.”

Russia is claiming that it has taken 6,500 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory this year, while the Institute for the Study of War think tank estimates that the real total is a Russian net gain of only 73 square kilometers.

Putin is “trying once again to breathe life into the myth of inevitable Russian military victory in order to persuade the United States and other supporters of Ukraine to compel Kyiv to surrender,” ISW wrote.

Apostol underlined that Ukraine is being very careful in its operations to try and minimize troop losses because of its lack of manpower.

“You must attack where success is possible,” Apostol said, adding that Ukraine favors localized attacks instead of a massive counteroffensive. In many cases, the goal is to stabilize the frontline and not to take more territory. “Launching an offensive against a well-prepared enemy force that holds a numerical advantage may fail to yield the desired outcome,” he said.

Ukraine has a much smaller population than Russia and has had difficulties in recruiting new forces and preventing soldiers from deserting.

“If a person is treated like a dog, they might go AWOL,” Apostol said.

]]> en EU reiterates ‘grave concern’ over Gaza humanitarian crisis as winter approaches https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-reiterates-grave-concern-over-gaza-humanitarian-crisis-as-winter-approaches/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 14 Nov 2026 16:28:36 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9326097 Europe’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has called on Israel to protect civilians in Gaza as severe flooding batters the enclave, saying an airstrike on the Nasser Hospital on Thursday was “deeply alarming.”

“The severe flooding and winter conditions that have struck Gaza are further aggravating the living conditions of an already exhausted population, exacerbating unsafe conditions and human suffering,” Kallas said in a statement Saturday.

Kallas also called on Israel to comply with international law and allow the United Nations and humanitarian organizations unimpeded access and to reopen all border crossings into Gaza.

“After a year since the ceasefire was announced, military strikes continue and shortages of essential items, including suitable shelter, medicine and medical equipment, caused by the existing access restrictions persist, resulting in the absence of acceptable and dignified living conditions,” Kallas’ statement said. 

Israel denies breaching international law and blocking humanitarian aid. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defended the amount of aid allowed into Gaza. He said Israel was supporting winter preparedness in Gaza but wouldn’t allow terror group Hamas to exploit humanitarian supplies. 

Israel’s Foreign Affairs Minister Gideon Sa’ar severed ties with Kallas in June after a media report alleged she compared Israel to apartheid South Africa. Kallas has long backed a push from several member countries to pressure the European Commission to ban trade with territories illegally occupied by Israel.

Israel’s mission to the EU was reached for comment.

Israel launched the war in Gaza in response to Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023 attack that killed about 1,200 people and in which 250 people were taken hostage. Since then, more than 70,000 people have been killed in the Palestinian enclave.

]]> en Italy hits Meta with €805m fine over privacy law violation https://www.politico.eu/article/italy-hits-meta-with-e805m-fine-over-privacy-law-violation/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 14 Nov 2026 14:03:27 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9326010 Italian authorities fined Facebook’s parent company Meta €805 million for using photos and videos from Android phones without users’ specific consent, the Italian Data Protection Authority said in a statement Saturday. 

The fine concerned the “camera roll suggestions when browsing Facebook” feature, which suggests photos and videos from a phone’s gallery for users to add to posts.

The feature violates the Italian law implementing the EU’s ePrivacy directive, the authority said. It is by far the largest fine ever imposed by the Italian regulator.

The investigation, launched in 2025, established that access to a user’s camera roll is requested with a single permission for the entire app, which the authority said covers multiple features with different needs. The authorization request was preceded by a generic warning that didn’t allow users to understand that they were authorizing picture and video suggestions, the authority said. 

“If granted in full, this type of permission allows the app to read the device’s entire photo archive, usually permanently, without the user or the authorities being able to verify which information is actually being used,” the statement reads.

The authority also said it “rejected the objection of lack of jurisdiction raised by the company in favor of the Irish authority, because the ePrivacy regulation does not provide for the ‘one-stop-shop’ mechanism.”

Meta has 60 days to get consent separately and specifically for the feature, clearly explain what it does and how it can be disabled, the authority said. It also must be disabled by default, including for those who have already authorized it. 

Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. It has the right to appeal the decision.

]]> en Nearly €20m in cash found buried, hidden in Hungary corruption case https://www.politico.eu/article/nearly-e20m-in-cash-found-buried-hidden-in-hungary-corruption-case/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 14 Nov 2026 13:16:27 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9325980 Hungarian authorities have recovered nearly €20 million in cash buried in forests, hidden in warehouses and residential properties and stored in a high-value safe as part of a bribery investigation into a former minister. 

The money was found during searches on Thursday and Friday as part of a criminal investigation into former minister Miklós Seszták, who worked under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, relating to bribery allegations. ​Seszták, who is under pre-trial detention has denied wrongdoing.

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter ‌Magyar launched a wide anti-corruption campaign after ousting Orbán earlier this year.

The money — more than 5 billion forints, €2.6 million and €1.2 million — was found across locations in Budapest, Pest, Békés and Nógrád counties, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, an anti-corruption body, said in a statement.

“This officially marks the end for the Fidesz-KDNP mafia!” Magyar posted on Facebook, originally in Hungarian, in reference to Orbán’s government.

It took 12 Treasury staff eight hours to tally the cash using 5 counting machines, Finance Minister Kármán András said.

The announcement comes after Hungarian authorities detained Aron Orbán, the former prime minister’s brother, as part of an investigation into people smuggling. The former prime minister said on social media that the move, announced by Magyar on Monday, was part of a “political witch-hunt” to get him.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk reacted wryly to the latest announcement, referring to the arrest of Orbán’s brother and the cash discovery on X.

“Dear Victor, I’ve always been an admirer of your creativity, but now I must say I’m impressed as never before,” he wrote.

]]> en US suggested Ukraine could give up Donbas for NATO membership, Zelenskyy says https://www.politico.eu/article/us-suggested-ukraine-could-give-up-donbas-for-nato-membership-zelenskyy-says/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 14 Nov 2026 10:48:19 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9325917 The U.S. has floated the idea of Ukraine joining NATO in exchange for withdrawing from its eastern Donbas region as part of negotiations to end the war, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday.

“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this had been raised,” Zelenskyy told reporters on Friday, a day after he met with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Dublin. 

The Donbas region in Ukraine’s far east borders Russia, and Moscow declared it had annexed the region in 2022 after its full-scale invasion. The vast majority of the region is occupied by Russian troops.

Giving up Donbas has long been part of the proposals put forward by U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration, including the 28-part plan for a peace agreement proposed by the White House in 2025. Russian President Vladimir Putin has previously demanded that Ukraine abandon its efforts to join NATO and accept strict limits on the size of its military.

“I have said repeatedly: Ukraine is not retreating and is not giving up its land to terrorists,” Zelenskyy told reporters.

The White House and U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Zelenskyy said he was discussing a “comprehensive security package” with partners that would include specific guarantees from NATO and the EU, a strong Ukrainian army with adequate troops, weapons and financial support for a set period and a recovery plan with clear funding attached. 

“If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not? I have no right to make that decision on my own,” Zelenskyy said. “Of course, this would be without any recognition of the occupied territories as Russian,” he added.

“But we need specifics, and we don’t have them yet. All of this is still under discussion,” the president said.

Veronika Melkozerova contributed to this report.

]]> en Finland rejects reported Russian demand to leave NATO as part of peace talks https://www.politico.eu/article/finland-rejects-reported-russian-demand-to-leave-nato-as-part-of-peace-talks/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 14 Nov 2026 09:57:48 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9325851 Finland has rejected a reported Russian demand that it leave NATO as part of Ukraine peace talks, with Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen saying its membership in the alliance wasn’t up for negotiation. 

“Such matters are in no way a matter for negotiation. Russia knows that. This is absolutely outrageous to even suggest such a thing,” Häkkänen told reporters on Friday, according to Finnish broadcaster Yle. Finland, which shares a 1,340-kilometer border with Russia, joined NATO in 2023 in a foreign policy U-turn prompted by the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

German newspaper Bild reported that a Russian proposal made during talks in Abu Dhabi this week included Moscow keeping occupied Ukrainian territories, gaining control of new swathes of land, demilitarizing ports in Ukraine, removing NATO bases from the Baltics, and Finland leaving NATO.

Russia proposed withdrawing its nuclear weapons from Belarus and refraining from stationing intermediate-range missiles there in exchange, Bild reported. 

But it remains unclear which proposals Russian President Vladimir Putin would support after discussions between intermediaries, according to the report. 

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a new security framework for Europe for after the war raised by the Americans “can be dangerous.”

“Russia certainly cannot make decisions on behalf of all the societies that are members of NATO,” he told reporters on Friday.

Zelenskyy’s comments were not in direct response to the demands reported by Bild, but came after a meeting between Zelenskyy and U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on Thursday in Dublin. 

“Putin’s desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe. This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations,” Zelenskyy said.

EUobserver spoke to 12 of the youngest MEPs in the European Parliament to understand the issues at the heart of Gen Z unrest.]]> From Porto to Athens, Europe was taken by surprise by the mass youth protests for better education, an affordable cost of living, and political accountability. EUobserver spoke to 12 of the youngest MEPs in the European Parliament to understand the issues at the heart of Gen Z unrest.

One topic that has been largely misunderstood is political engagement. 

“It is not the apathy some attribute to Gen Z, but a disconnection from the political establishment, because it is not delivering for them,” said Lena Schilling, a 25 year-old Austrian MEP for the Greens.

For instance, an EU study from October found that 55 percent of young Europeans had participated in at least one social initiative.

The issue is that “fewer political candidates take an interest in young people,” 34-year old German Socialist & Democrat (S&D) MEP Delara Burkhardt told EUobserver.

Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, agrees, calling for a wider European security arrangement before a deal to end the Ukraine war. 

European capitals have been alarmed, and with reason.

Read more

The future security of a continent is being discussed with a government that is still bombarding Ukrainian cities every night. European governments are trying to insert themselves into the talks and seemingly now have US backing.

If a new order for Europe is being drawn up, Europeans should insist on writing into it the one word absent on Kushner’s list: nuclear.

It is a striking omission, because every one of his five goals is at heart a nuclear question.

Crisis communication, transparency and escalation risk matter so much precisely because this war is being fought – and  tensions with Moscow are increasing – in the shadow of the bomb.

The gravest danger of the past five years has never been confined to the front line in Ukraine. It is that a nuclear-armed state has used the threat of mass destruction to try to keep others from coming to the aid of its victims.

Since February 2022, president Vladimir Putin has used tacit and overt nuclear threats to try to achieve tactical advantage in the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

And now there are no guardrails. For almost a year, the United States and Russia have had no binding limits on their strategic arsenals.

Who nuclear deterrence really rewards

Defenders of nuclear deterrence say it keeps the peace.

This war shows what it actually does. Russia felt emboldened by its nuclear arsenal to launch a full-scale invasion. Its nuclear weapons were not a shield against aggression. They were the arms holding the spear.

Nuclear deterrence is a contest over who is more believably prepared to kill millions. A system that pays out to whoever appears most reckless is not a source of stability. It is an incentive to aggression. A path to disaster.

This is why any settlement of this war matters far beyond Ukraine. If the terms of peace reward territory seized under nuclear coercion, the message will be heard by every would-be proliferator.

Europe must not copy Moscow’s playbook

Europe’s current response risks mirroring the logic it fears.

In March, president Emmanuel Macron announced the first increase in France’s nuclear arsenal in more than three decades and launched a still undefined “forward deterrence” concept.

Macron has also had himself photographed watching the test launch of a ballistic missile from a submarine accompanied with bellicose rhetoric, eliciting satirical comparisons with the North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

Read more

Lithuania moves to lift ban on nuclear weapons as ‘Russians do not attack the strong’

The fear behind these moves is understandable. But they accept Moscow’s rules of the game: a competition in conveying a credible threat of assured destruction that nobody wins, and in which the risk of miscalculation only grows.

More nuclear weapons in more places is not a security architecture. It is a shorter fuse on the same bomb, and the continent seems willing to hand Vladimir Putin a match

What Europe should put on the table

If Washington wants to talk about European security, Europe should answer with concrete nuclear demands:

First, declare nuclear threats inadmissible. In 2022, G20 leaders, following the lead of states that have joined the UN Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, agreed that the use or threat of use of nuclear weapons is inadmissible. Any framework for European security should turn that principle into a binding commitment, with consequences for breaking it.

Second, Europe can no longer host the nuclear chessboard of Russia and the US. Russian weapons in Belarus should be removed; as should the US weapons in six European countries.

After that, interim verified limits to nuclear weapons must be agreed. Greater military transparency must mean warhead numbers and inspections, not just notifications of exercises. 

Finally, the elimination of nuclear weapons must be anchored in law that already exists. The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, already signed or ratified by a global majority, bans not only the use and possession of nuclear weapons but also the threat to use them. 

Read more

Putin and the threat of a tactical nuclear attack

In three weeks, countries meet at the UN for the treaty’s first review conference. European governments that want a security order resistant to blackmail should be in the room, at the very least as observers.

Moscow and Washington cannot dictate Europe’s future. Neither should nuclear threats, whoever makes them. A peace that leaves the bomb as the final arbiter of borders is not a lasting peace. It is a pause before the next blackmail attempt.

But the judgment the International Court of Justice (ICJ) is due to deliver on 19 November addresses questions that go to the heart of international law: when can a state be held responsible for genocide, what evidence is required to establish genocidal intent, and how should the court assess the conduct of state authorities?

    The case was brought by The Gambia, which alleges that Myanmar violated the 1948 Genocide Convention through its treatment of the Rohingya. The court’s answer will matter not only to the victims of the alleged crimes, but also to the interpretation and application of the Convention in other cases.

    One of the most important precedents is the court’s 2007 judgment in Bosnia and Herzegovina v Serbia and Montenegro. Bosnia brought its case in 1993, alleging that Serbia was responsible for genocide committed during the Yugoslav war. In 2007, the court found that genocide had been committed in Srebrenica in July 1995.

    But it did not find that the acts of genocide could be attributed to Serbia. It held that Serbia had nevertheless breached its obligations to prevent genocide and to punish those responsible.

    The distinction is fundamental. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) dealt with the individual criminal responsibility of those who committed or participated in the crimes.

    The ICJ, by contrast, had to determine whether the conduct could be attributed to a state and whether Serbia had breached its obligations under the Genocide Convention.

    Read more

    After students voted out Vučić, can Serbia’s uprising against ‘evil’ change how the state really works?

    The court also set a demanding standard of proof. It held that allegations involving charges of exceptional gravity, such as genocide, must be established by “fully conclusive” evidence, and that it must be “fully convinced” that the allegations have been clearly established.

    Where genocidal intent is not directly established but inferred from a pattern of conduct, the court added that this intent must be the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the acts in question.

    These requirements attracted criticism. Some considered that the court had effectively approached the question as if it were deciding the criminal guilt of an individual, rather than the international responsibility of a state.

    Others argued that requiring genocidal intent to be the only reasonable inference set an exceptionally high threshold, making it particularly difficult to establish genocide through circumstantial evidence.

    I was an ICTY judge when the ICJ delivered its judgment in 2007. I followed it with particular interest — and some surprise. At the tribunal, we were dealing every day with the individual criminal responsibility of those involved in the crimes committed in Bosnia.

    The evidence concerning Srebrenica and the role of Bosnian Serb political and military leaders was familiar to us. Yet the ICJ was operating within a different legal framework, with a different question to answer.

    Read more

    [Interview] Ex-Bosnia envoy sees no risk of renewed violence, but the fractured country’s EU dream is rotting away

    In its 2015 judgment in Croatia v Serbia, the court largely maintained its approach. It rejected both Croatia’s claim and Serbia’s counterclaim, finding that neither side had established the specific intent required to prove genocide. The demanding standard of proof therefore remains an important feature of the court’s jurisprudence.

    The Gambia v Myanmar proceedings bring these questions back before the court. The judges will have to assess how genocidal intent can be established, including through patterns of conduct and circumstantial evidence, and how the actions of state officials engage the responsibility of the state.

    Myanmar, unsurprisingly, argues for continuity with the court’s established case law. The judgment will show how the court applies that jurisprudence to the evidence before it — and whether it offers further clarification.

    The wider interest in the case is reflected in the participation of eleven states under Article 63 of the court’s Statute: Belgium, Canada, Denmark, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, France, Germany, Ireland, the Maldives, the Netherlands, Slovenia and the United Kingdom. They are not parties to the dispute. They have intervened because they consider that the interpretation of the Genocide Convention is at stake. Under Article 63, the court’s interpretation of the Convention will also be binding on the states that have intervened.

    Belgium’s participation is particularly significant. It is not simply an observer of proceedings taking place far away. By intervening, Belgium has chosen to take a position on the interpretation of a treaty that lies at the centre of the international legal order.

    The judgment will also be closely followed in the case brought by South Africa against Israel. Both proceedings concern the same Genocide Convention, and the ICJ’s reasoning on the interpretation of its provisions, the assessment of evidence and the establishment of genocidal intent may be relevant to the South Africa case.

    The Myanmar judgment will not decide that case, nor should its outcome be prejudged. But the court’s legal reasoning will inevitably attract attention. The two proceedings raise questions that are closely connected, even though their facts and procedural stages are different.

    There is another reason why the composition of the court has attracted attention. Gambia appointed Navi Pillay as its ad hoc judge, while Myanmar appointed the German international law scholar Claus Kreß. Pillay is a distinguished international jurist: she served as President of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, was a judge at the International Criminal Court (ICC) and later served as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. In October, she was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

    Her appointment has nevertheless prompted public comment, particularly because of her previous work and statements concerning Israel. That makes it all the more important to recall the role of an ad hoc judge. Such a judge is not a representative of the state that appointed them. Once appointed, an ad hoc judge has the same duty of independence and impartiality as every other member of the court. I know this responsibility from personal experience, having served myself as an ad hoc judge at the ICJ.

    US sanctions on ICC

    The independence of international judges is not an abstract institutional concern. The ICC has already been subjected to sanctions by the Trump administration, targeting judges and other officials. The ICJ has not faced the same direct measures, but it operates in an international climate in which judicial institutions and those who serve them are increasingly exposed to political pressure.

    The authority of the ICJ ultimately depends on its ability to decide cases independently, according to law and evidence, irrespective of the political consequences.

    The judgment in The Gambia v Myanmar will be important first and foremost for the Rohingya. But it will also help shape the interpretation of the Genocide Convention, influence the debate in other proceedings and test the confidence states place in international adjudication.

    For European countries, this is not a distant legal dispute. Belgium and ten other states have chosen to participate because the interpretation of the Convention matters to them.

    Their commitment to international justice will be tested not only by the positions they take in court, but also by their willingness to defend the independence of the institutions that apply the law — including when the consequences are politically uncomfortable.

    In France, the Senate has just adopted a draft bill that could severely restrict the right to protest. The text still has to go through the National Assembly, but it stands a good chance of becoming law.

    Is Europe slowly killing the right to protest?

    Once again, a draft bill has been adopted by the French Senate, with the full support of the far-right Rassemblement National (RN) party.

    The bill was introduced this summer. Its stated aim is to crack down on violent protesters and make them pay for the damage they cause. But it goes much further than that.

    The proposed text targets not only violent protesters responsible for causing damage, but also people who are simply present nearby. They could face fines of up to €10,000, even if they haven’t committed any criminal offence. Simply because they stayed there after the police ordered them to disperse.

    This shifts the burden onto people who may not have committed any offence, while relieving the authorities of the difficulty of identifying the actual perpetrators.

    But opponents argue that this seriously undermines the right to protest. According to Olivier Cahn, a professor of criminal law quoted by the newspaper Le Monde, the wording leaves considerable room for arbitrary interpretation.

    Read more

    Europe’s youth take to the streets as the post‑war promise of a better life breaks down

    In an opinion piece also published in Le Monde, several public figures warn that protesters could find it impossible to prove that they didn’t hear a police order to disperse. In many cases, such warnings simply aren’t heard, either because they aren’t loud enough or because they were never given in the first place.

    The senators have made the bill even tougher by adding a six-month prison sentence for anyone taking part in a demonstration that hasn’t been authorised by the authorities.

    In some cases, the authorities could even seize part of people’s social benefits once they have identified them as offenders. The Senate has gone as far as proposing to evict them from social housing.

    All of this has drawn strong criticism from civil society organisations and left-wing movements. They fear that the bill will discourage people from taking part in peaceful demonstrations because of the risks involved.

    In the opinion piece I mentioned earlier, the authors even draw a parallel with George Orwell’s novel 1984.

    France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, however, believes that the bill has actually been improved by the senators.

    So that’s the situation in France. What about the rest of Europe? Well, let’s just say that a similar trend can be observed almost everywhere.

    Read more

    Europe’s youth asked for hope – but politicians just offer fear and hate

    In 2024, Amnesty International published a major report examining the right to protest in 21 European countries. Its findings pointed to a clear deterioration in the conditions for exercising this right.

    In eight countries, legislation restricting the right to peaceful protest has been introduced in recent years. These are France, Belgium, Germany, Greece, Italy, Luxembourg, Spain and the UK.

    The report’s authors also found that, across all the countries analysed, protesters are frequently labelled as terrorists, criminals, foreign agents, anarchists or extremists.

    People of colour face systematic discrimination in at least seven countries. Climate activists are targeted in almost every country covered by the report.

    LGBTQ+ people, women, children and people with disabilities also face discrimination in several countries.

    All of this, combined with police violence reported in many countries in recent years, is raising concerns among human rights organisations.

    In France, they are now hoping that members of the National Assembly will take a less restrictive approach to dealing with protesters. Let’s see how the debate unfolds in the coming months.

    Ukraine’s war effort depends heavily on two American tools: Starlink and Starshield. Both belong to Elon Musk’s SpaceX, and both can be switched off. Europe says it wants to reduce that dependence.

    Is it possible, and why is Europe so far behind? Starlink is SpaceX’s satellite internet service. It’s sold to the general public, to companies and to armies. It relies on a constellation of around 10,000 satellites in low orbit, which makes it possible to get a connection almost anywhere on Earth.

    Starshield is the version designed for governments and militaries. It uses the same technology, but with dedicated satellites and dedicated encryption. In other words, it’s more secure.

    Russia faces a strategic crisis and record losses, but thanks to Trump it sees things positively (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,713)

    The problem is that its use completely depends on the goodwill of Elon Musk. But also on the US government. Starshield is a government system, and it’s Washington that actually makes it available to Ukraine.

    This has already led to some awkward situations. A few weeks ago, Ukraine noticed that the speed of its drones had been throttled overnight. The explanation was clear: it was an American move. The issue has since been resolved, but it illustrates a real unease.

    So how did Ukraine end up in this position? At the start of the war, the country’s cable-based internet infrastructure was damaged. On the battlefield, the army now uses SpaceX terminals to receive internet signal, because they’re small and very practical.

    And that is exactly what Europeans don’t offer. Most European satellites are in high orbit. They cover very large areas, but they have two drawbacks in wartime. Because they are further away, the delay in transmission is longer. Second, the equipment needed to receive the signal is much bulkier, so it is not suited to the front line.

    Elon Musk made a very strategic choice: putting tens of thousands of satellites in low orbit.  It’s much cheaper, and much easier to operate. Now could Europeans compete on this market?

    The closest European equivalent, on a smaller scale, is the OneWeb constellation, run by the French company Eutelsat. Eutelsat was originally a European intergovernmental organisation. But it was dismantled and its activity has been taken over by a company.

    The French state is still its largest shareholder, with around a third of the shares. The United Kingdom and an Indian group also hold stakes.

    Through OneWeb, Eutelsat has around 680 satellites, in both low and high orbit. The company says it could replace Starlink in the medium term, meaning sometime in the 2030s.

    It plans to reinforce its fleet with several hundred new satellites. But most of them will actually replace older ones. So it’s not a big increase, compared with Starlink.

    Read more

    Russia’s fake war maps at Abu Dhabi peace talks aren’t fooling anyone (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,721)

    There is also another project designed to secure European connections. It’s called IRIS². This one is a European project, carried out by several companies, including Eutelsat. The EU is its main customer. Unlike OneWeb, it’s not a commercial venture. But both share the same goal: reducing dependence on Starlink.

    The ambition is a constellation of at least 348 satellites by 2030, with deployment starting in 2029. So again, fewer than a thousand. That’s still far from Starlink.

    But here, it’s worth saying that satellites in low orbit are much cheaper to put in place, which also explains the sheer volume SpaceX has been able to launch in recent years.

    With far fewer satellites, but in higher orbit, Europeans can also cover the whole planet. It’s just that the system isn’t as flexible.

    Finally, is money part of the explanation? Yes, of course. The United States spends around six times more on its space programmes, civil and military, than Europeans do.

    There’s also another factor that helps SpaceX deploy thousands of satellites at low cost: it has its own launcher, the Falcon 9.

    Eutelsat, on the other hand, has to buy launches from third parties. So it’s much more expensive, and it doesn’t control the pace at which it can put satellites into orbit.

    Before wrapping up, a quick word about China, another big actor. It’s quite new in the space industry, and it’s not really spending huge amounts of money for the moment. But it’s worth keeping an eye on Beijing on this front too.

    ]]>

      <description><p>CEO behind the meteoric rise of Nvidia stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy </p><p>Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/nvidia">Nvidia</a>, the company at the center of the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/artificialintelligenceai">AI</a> boom, after leading it for more than 30 years.</p><p>Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/12/jensen-huang-affair-timeline">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Rallies are planned at more than US 40 campuses as workers seeking better pay and conditions decry stalled talks</p><p>Starbucks baristas, students, elected officials and allies are planning rallies at <a href="https://starbucksworkersunited.controlshift.app/events?link_id=2&amp;can_id=debd8d2ad19f005d15f9bbdff314d42a&amp;source=email-nov-12-day-of-action-for-starbucks-baristas&amp;email_referrer=email_3490793&amp;email_subject=nov-12-day-of-action-for-starbucks-baristas&amp;&amp;">over 40 college campuses</a> across the US on Thursday to support the Starbucks Workers United <a href="https://www.boycottstarbucks.net/">boycott campaign</a> as the union nears five years of deadlock with the company over contract negotiations.</p><p>Starbucks Workers United is <a href="https://sbworkersunited.org/what-were-fighting-for-updates-on-contract-bargaining/">seeking</a> better pay and stronger staffing levels, including a $17 an hour minimum wage for baristas and a minimum staffing of three workers per store.       <description><p>Sales of built units fell to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, with mortgage rates at nearly three-year high</p><p>US existing home sales hit a 16-year low in October as buyers were driven away by high <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/money/mortgage-rates">mortgage rates</a> and rising inflation, according to new data released on Wednesday.</p><p>Sales of already built units dropped to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, the National Association of Realtors (NAR) reported.       <description><p>Trump-appointed judge Jeffrey T Kuntz partially denies British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss over edit</p><p>Federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz ruled on Tuesday that Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the BBC can proceed, denying in part the British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss the case.       <description><p>Safety campaigners have condemned it and owners have complained about it. Goodbye to a steel monstrosity seemingly designed by a five-year-old</p><p>Elon Musk is having a rough go of it, isn’t he? The world’s richest man spent almost half a billion dollars on the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/04/elon-musk-midterm-spending-analysis">midterms</a> in a failed attempt to defend Republican control of government. Now the tech mogul, who moved from California to Texas to escape Democrats and regulations, finds himself in a newly blue state. He also finds himself the subject of an unflattering <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/08/musk-review-epic-study-worlds-richest-most-banal-man-elon-film">documentary</a> and, if the Democrats follow through on threats to investigate him, could potentially be in a spot of legal bother.</p><p>And to top it all off? Musk’s beloved Cybertruck, the steel monstrosity that looks as if it were designed by a five-year-old, is <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/06/tesla-to-wind-down-cybertruck-production-as-elon-musk-focuses-on-robotics-and-ai">winding down production</a>. According to Musk, this isn’t because it’s an abject failure, but because he is channelling his energy into other things. “This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media,” Musk <a href="https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2119691615774146614?a=pN3ISFVZZ-aU4_-TlJw&amp;s=20">tweeted</a> on Monday. “But rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.” (The Cybercab is a two-passenger robotaxi.)</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/11/farewell-cybertruck-elon-musk-car-repellent">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSun, 15 Nov 2026 14:34:07 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Shareholder faces ‘double taxation’ on shares he owns]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/15/shareholder-faces-double-taxation-on-shares-he-owns/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/15/shareholder-faces-double-taxation-on-shares-he-owns/Sun, 15 Nov 2026 11:06:00 +0000I suspect readers other than me may be interested in the capital gains tax (CGT) liability date arising from the Bluefin acquisition of our Irish Continental Group shares. And also in the relevant dates when calculating capital gains.

I understand that, all things being equal, the sale will be completed during Q4 of 2026. This seems to imply we may all have a very short window to calculate and pay the resulting CGT to Revenue.

From my reading of the scheme document and other announcements, I’m guessing the purchase transaction may end up happening some time in late November. In which case, I understand I will be required to file and pay by December 15th.

On what date will the transaction be deemed to have been made? The date of some announcement by the company or the date that a cheque or bank transfer actually reaches me?

I also need to work out my tax liability. I inherited my shares and, as it happens, the value when probate was granted was significantly (33 per cent) greater than on the date of the death of my mother. As advised, I calculated and paid capital acquisitions tax (CAT) based on the value as of date of probate.

However, I have been told the relevant date for calculating capital gains is the date of inheritance rather than the probate date.

This seems rather unfair as I will be taxed twice on the gain in the value of the shares between the disposer’s death and the probate date. (In my case the CGT bill looks like being 20 per cent greater than natural justice would suggest it should be.)

I am wondering how Revenue justifies this switch in valuation dates? Or perhaps I have been misinformed of the rules?

SN

Your query is timely as the €1.2 billion management buyout of Irish Continental led by long-time chief executive Eamonn Rothwell via the bid vehicle Bluefin was approved by the High Court last week. That clears the way for the deal to be completed within weeks.

The bid by Rothwell, who has run the Irish Ferries business for the past 24 years, and his team was announced in late July. It is the second time he has tried to take the group private, with a previous attempt 19 years ago being frustrated by other interested parties.

The catalyst was a determination – shared over recent years by other companies listed on the Irish Stock Exchange, now Euronext Dublin – that shares in the business, which floated in Dublin in 1988, are not properly valued, a factor that market dynamics suggest is unlikely to change.

It was a close-run thing this time around too, with an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders to approve the offer put back by a fortnight on the eve of the intended vote when it became clear to the company’s board that not enough votes had been secured to seal the deal.

Eventually, on September 10th, 79.2 per cent of votes cast supported the €8-per-share offer, above the 75 per cent threshold required.

That decision required High Court approval given the structure of the deal. That sanction came last Tuesday. As a result, your shares will be compulsorily acquired by the bid vehicle, Bluefin. You have no further say in the matter, nor any option to retain your shares as part of what will now be a privately-owned group

In the immediate aftermath of that ruling, Irish Continental said it expected trading in the shares on Euronext Dublin to stop at close of business next Friday, November 20th.

Payments to shareholders, it said, were expected to be made no more than two weeks after that – by December 4th.

Capital gains tax in Ireland is payable on gains made on the sale of assets. The key date, according to the legislation, is when the gains are realised.

If the gains are realised between January 1st and November 30th of any year, the tax is payable by December 15th of the same year. If the gain is realised in December, tax falls due by January 31st of the following year.

You can be subject to both late payment penalties and to interest if you miss the relevant date.

In addition to paying the tax, you must also make a return to Revenue with the details of the gain. For those filing annual returns – which is a growing number of us, even PAYE workers, as we claim for things such as college and health expenses – the details can be registered with your normal annual return for 2026.

Any individual not otherwise filing an annual return will need to complete and file a CG1 Capital Gains Tax Return and Self-Assessment form.

As the Irish Continental management buyout straddles the capital gains tax deadlines, it is easy to see why people could be confused. The shares will cease trading before November 30th but it could be December 4th before you get your payment.

Technically, I guess, if that payment arrives early – before November 30th – your capital gains tax bill is due by December 15th but, given the stated payment deadline is December 4th and the tight deadline involved, I cannot see Revenue making a fuss as long as payment of any tax due is made by January 31st of next year.

In any case, these “payment due” dates tend to be used in full by companies going through such takeovers as they are highly regulated complex processes.

I would not expect to see payment until December 4th or the days immediately preceding it so I think you can be comfortable with the January 31st deadline. That’s not a lot of time to get things organised anyway, with Christmas intruding in that window, but it should give you a eight-week window to get sorted.

Double taxation

Turning to your second point, I can certainly see your concern.

As you say, for capital acquisition tax (inheritance tax) purposes, the relevant date was something called the valuation date. This can be a very complex notion in itself, unfortunately. It is the date you are deemed to have actually got control of the asset under inheritance and, for most people, this will be the date of probate.

And that is what you did. In terms of assessing the value of your inheritance for tax purposes, you took the value of the shares on the date of probate.

However, shares in Irish Continental have proved fairly volatile at various times over the past six years – especially over the one-year-plus window of a typical probate process. In your case, this meant the valuation date value of the shares was about 20 per cent higher than at the date of your mother’s death.

This becomes a problem because, with capital gains dying with an owner, the successor in ownership of an asset is responsible for any capital gain from the date. So, for capital gains tax, your liability stretches back to what the shares were worth when your mother died, not when you actually got control of them.

There is some relief available under Section 104 of the Capital Acquisitions Tax Consolidated Act 2003 but only where the two separate taxes are charged on the same property on the same event

That is not the case here. The inheritance tax arose on your mother’s death and the capital gains tax arises only on the subsequent sale, via takeover of the business in which you sold the shares.

I can find no provision that would grant you relief in your position.

In terms of how Revenue justifies this, it is simply an accident of fate – the provisions to two separate pieces of legislation.

Unfair? Yes, it would certainly appear so. Have you been misinformed? No. Have you any recourse to relief? I don’t think so.

On the upside, you are still ahead financially on shares you never purchased yourself.

]]><![CDATA[No, people have not fallen out of love with work]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/15/no-people-have-not-fallen-out-of-love-with-work/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/15/no-people-have-not-fallen-out-of-love-with-work/Sun, 15 Nov 2026 10:00:00 +0000Have people lost the will to work? This theory – until now quite wishy-washy – appeared to gain some quantitative heft in the UK last week thanks to the latest edition of the long-running British Social Attitudes Survey.

The results revealed the lowest job satisfaction in the survey’s history and a broad-based decline since 2015 in the proportion of employees who said they were willing to work harder than was required to help their employer succeed. A rising share of Britons said they would prefer to work fewer than full-time hours, driven by men (both fathers and non-fathers).

This has revived a debate that took place in the aftermath of the pandemic, when young workers posted on TikTok about “quiet quitting” their jobs, while overworked youth in China spoke of “tang ping” (or “lying flat”). Some theorised that people no longer wanted to toil in a “bullshit job” that didn’t contribute to society, in the words of social anthropologist David Graeber.

But it is worth examining the rest of the data. The share of people who say they would prefer not to work at all remains a very low and stable 4 per cent. So why might they want to work less? It is not because they think their jobs are “bullshit”.

In fact, the proportion who say their job is useful to society has risen steadily from 54 per cent in 1989 to 73 per cent in 2025 – the highest in the survey’s history.

Nor is it because people have lost all ambition and drive. The workforce’s largest “unmet wants” in 2025 – the gap between the proportion of people rating a certain work attribute as important and those reporting that they actually have it – were for a high income and advancement opportunities. Both of these gaps have widened since 2015. This does not smack of a country that just wants to slack off.

But it does point to a more straightforward reason for people’s decreased willingness to go above and beyond for their employers: not enough money and progression.

Real weekly earnings in the UK have risen overall since 2015, but they’re still barely above where they were in 2008 after a dreadful decade and a half for living standards.

On top of that, the proportion of respondents who said their job had good opportunities for advancement fell from 35 to 26 per cent.

This fits with stories I hear from UK workers and employers about wage compression on the lower rungs due to the rising minimum wage, and from white-collar managers who complain they have to rate each team member’s performance on a forced-distribution curve, even if no one has performed badly.

How ‘workfluencers’ became the new buttoned-up breed of content creator

I suspect there is something else at play, too. We know from a different long-running data set – the Skills and Employment Survey – that Britons have experienced a remarkable loss of autonomy at work over recent years.

In 1992, 62 per cent of surveyed workers said they had a great deal of discretion over which tasks to do and how to do them. By 2024, only 34 per cent said the same.

This decline was initially most evident among people in lower-paid jobs, but between 2017 and 2024, “task discretion” fell among professionals and more highly skilled workers too. This does not appear to be UK-specific: a large continuing survey of workers across Europe has found “a concerning decrease in workers’ ability to influence collective work processes and apply their own ideas”.

My employer cuts maternity top-up payments by half after three months. Is the norm not six months of full pay?

I have begun to think of this as the “routinisation” of professional work. Why has it happened? When I last wrote about the phenomenon, I heard from many readers with whom it resonated. Most of them attributed the trend to increased regulatory demands and technology, which had made it easier for employers to codify, structure and monitor people’s work.

Some pointed out the benefits: allowing less leeway for personal discretion can make for more consistency and fewer mistakes – particularly important in safety-critical sectors such as medicine.

But I also heard from those who said their jobs had become more frustrating and less fun, from academics tied up in bureaucracy to tech workers who said so-called “agile” working practices had morphed into the opposite.

Employers have no doubt been quick to measure the gains of this routinisation process. Now we are beginning to see the costs. It’s not hard to understand why, if you have little control over how you work, you might feel less willing or able to go above and beyond.

Britons haven’t fallen out of love with work itself. They just don’t love to work like this. – The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>Isbjorn<![CDATA[Markets still pricing in two more ECB rate hikes]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/15/markets-still-pricing-in-two-more-ecb-rate-hikes/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/15/markets-still-pricing-in-two-more-ecb-rate-hikes/Sun, 15 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Markets are pricing in at least two more European Central Bank interest rate hikes even with the sharp drop-off in oil prices and the improving inflationary outlook.

ECB officials are expected to increase the deposit rate by a quarter-point to 2.75 per cent at their final monetary-policy meeting of 2026. This will push interest rates to the top of a range that is deemed to be neutral (neither stoking nor restricting economic activity).

Franfurt has raised borrowing costs twice since the conflict in the Middle East pushed energy prices sharply higher.

With inflation now running at twice the ECB’s 2 per cent target level, Klaas Knot, one of two contenders to become the next ECB chief, said this week the bank’s interest rate policy was likely to remain hostage to developments in the Middle East and their impact on energy prices.

He said that if energy prices remained roughly where they were, he saw little need for higher interest rates. “There may be a bit of extra tightening needed, but I don’t think an awful lot of it,” Knot said, adding that any interest rate changes needed to be “very measured”.

Another factor paving the way for another rate hike is euro zone growth, which has been more resilient in the face of inflation that many had predicted, helped in part by multinational exports from Ireland.

Gross domestic product (GDP) across the 21-member currency bloc rose 0.4 per cent in the third quarter, Eurostat said on Friday, matching an initial estimate from October.

This gives the central bank more leeway to counteract inflation with growth-anchoring interest rates.

The global economy is by no means out of the woods on inflation given the ongoing impasse in the Middle East.

Bond market turmoil is also expected to weigh on the growth as countries struggle to service their debts.

The ECB sees growth risks as tilted to the downside and those for inflation as skewed to the upside.

]]>Ben Kilb<![CDATA[Why Anthropic’s IPO is nothing like Google’s]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/15/why-anthropics-ipo-is-nothing-like-googles/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/15/why-anthropics-ipo-is-nothing-like-googles/Sun, 15 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Anthropic still plans to go public next week, despite recent volatility in AI stocks and a sharp reassessment of its prospective valuation. After investors contemplated as much as $2 trillion (€1.8 trillion) only weeks ago, figures ranging from $1.1 trillion to $1.5 trillion have since been floated.

The valuation wobble has irked at least one investor.

“If [public market investors] are not seeing the narrative at this point, they are failing a basic IQ test,” one early Anthropic backer told the Financial Times. “The next Google is dancing naked in front of you. If you can’t see the value of it, you don’t deserve to make money.”

Anthropic may be dancing naked in front of investors, to stick with this unfortunate metaphor, but it may also be asking them to pay some $1.5 trillion for the privilege of watching.

As for Google, it was valued at $23 billion when it floated in 2004 – less than Yahoo, then valued at $39 billion. In contrast, Anthropic’s trillion-dollar status will immediately place it among the S&P 500’s most valuable companies.

Put another way, $1.5 trillion would buy 65 Googles at their 2004 valuation. Even $1 trillion would buy 43. The two opportunities are hardly comparable.

Anthropic may well be worth $1.5 trillion or more. It may outperform in coming years. However, there is only so much excitement in the prospect of buying the “next Google” when it is already valued as though it has achieved Google’s success.

]]>Gabby Jones<![CDATA[How can Ireland afford to be so generous to public sector workers?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/11/14/we-are-giving-out-pay-rises-not-because-productivity-is-up-but-because-we-have-money/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/11/14/we-are-giving-out-pay-rises-not-because-productivity-is-up-but-because-we-have-money/Sat, 14 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Did your Granny have a “good room”? In west Cork in the late 1970s, my Granny had a good room that was so good, I wasn’t good enough to go into it. In fact, none of my immediate family was. The good room was kept for people who were better than us: the parish priest, the solicitor or the local big Fine Gael farmer. After Mass, Granny would usher these better people into the good room, where my cousins and I lined up to meet them, drinking our MiWadi nervously from swanky Waterford glass goblets, terrified lest we drop a thing, not least our Tee Haitches. Once the good people were gone, the Waterford glass was carefully locked back in a press, not to be touched again until the next good room charade.

The aim was not to mortify the family. We were insecure about our position and let on to be richer than we were. The really posh people knew we were playing posh, and we knew that they knew we were putting it on, but everyone went along with the drama to avoid embarrassment.

No one made a Holy Show of themselves.

Good rooms are no longer a thing in Ireland, but the insecurity of good-room mentality pervades. These days the good people are no longer parish priests or local, Ford Granada-driving solicitors, but foreign leaders and dignitaries, the type of folk who arrived in Dublin last week. Our governing class still feels insecure alongside these cosmopolitan, multilingual continentals, and the last thing the lads could countenance was a messy public sector strike on the very day the national good room opened to our upscale visitors.

In terms of negotiating, this was the moment of maximum Government fragility and thus a maximum leverage point for the public sector workers. The unions struck a deal on Wednesday, and a truce was announced predawn, fittingly 106 years to the day of the first World War armistice. Face was saved, and the big event could pass off swimmingly – the good room won the day. But what about the economic and fiscal details of the latest deal? Once the black Mercs have swished the foreign grandees back to the airport, we will have to pick over the details to see who is on the hook for what.

The first thing to appreciate is that the Irish public sector is in overdrive mode, and has been for some time. The ultimate question is whether the expanded public sector offers the sort of value for money that would render legitimate a €5.2 billion pay deal that will deliver pay increases of 10.75 per cent over two years and nine months.

The growth of the public service is unambiguous. Annual expenditure has grown from roughly €15.3 billion in 1994 to €107 billion in 2025: a seven-fold nominal increase in three decades. Even allowing for inflation and population growth, the trajectory is striking. Spending more than doubled between 2000 and 2010 (€26 billion to €61 billion), was reined in through austerity (falling to €54.6 billion by 2015). Spending has since exploded, up exactly 100 per cent in the decade to 2025. Health alone absorbed €25.8 billion in 2025 – more than the entire State budget only 25 years earlier in 2000 – while housing expenditure grew from €1.2 billion in 2015 to €9.3 billion by 2025, a near eight-fold increase in a single policy area within 10 years.

Lots of dough is being spent. But just how much is being spent per head? And how are we doing relative to other countries – are we spending more or less per head than the rest of Europe?

At first blush, things look good. When we stand back, we see that general Government expenditure in 2024 was 39.25 per cent of national income. Based on this, Ireland sits meaningfully below the European high-spenders – Finland (57.7 per cent), France (57.3 per cent) and Italy (50.4 per cent). Ireland is also below Spain (45.5 per cent) and the UK (44 per cent).

Public sector pay deal: What’s in it for me?

Public pay deal will be reviewed if economy deteriorates, Government and unions insist

But drill a bit deeper into the per-capita picture and a more nuanced and revealing story emerges. Last year, Ireland’s general Government expenditure was €133.5 billion, which is how much it costs to run our country of 5,308,039 people. We therefore spend about €25,198 per person. This means that Ireland’s Government actually spends more per person than even France – €25,198 versus €23,300 – and broadly comparable amounts to Finland (€24,200). We spend considerably more than Spain (€17,300) and Italy (€20,100), and somewhat less than the UK (€27,300).

Because our population is much younger, our unemployment levels much lower and our tax revenues more buoyant, this spending per head figure should set off alarm bells. It means Ireland is not spending anywhere near as efficiently as many of our neighbours. Given that productivity in the public service is so hard to measure, the notion that a young country – which should have far fewer demands on its health and welfare systems – is spending significantly more per head than older countries (which have far greater demands on the welfare state) means that productivity in the public sector in Ireland is lower than in other countries.

How can the State afford to be so generous to workers in the public sector without impoverishing other taxpayers? For context, 31.76 per cent of total current expenditure goes to public sector pay. Public sector employment rose from 301,000 in 2015 to 424,000 in 2026. Meanwhile, the average annual public sector pay is €56,496, compared to €40,200 in the private sector – a premium of approximately 40 per cent. If public sector workers are paid more, get more holidays, can’t be fired and have guaranteed pensions, something must give, surely? Are other workers shouldering this burden, and why are they not more pissed off?

The reason is simple: the money for the public sector pay rises is not coming from the tax paid by their neighbours, but from tax paid by foreign multinationals, which will amount to €34 billion this year, predicted to rise to €39 billion in 2027 and to €44.7 billion by 2030. Some of that hasn’t been for the right reasons – reports of failing screens and stock shortages, for example – but on the whole, the opinion seems to be that Apple has done something good here, even if it is eye-wateringly expensive.

Foldable phones have always been a great idea in theory; the reality has often fallen far short. The early days were marred by screens that peeled or a less than stellar multitasking experience. Later models struggled to find the perfect size that would make the folded version as good as a standard smartphone for everyday tasks while accommodating a folding screen without making the whole thing too thick.

The iPhone Duo manages to neatly sidestep that problem. At less than half an inch thick when closed, the phone is not far off the iPhone 18 Pro, which comes in at 0.34 inches. It weighs in at 254 grams, a little heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro’s 211 grams.

The closest comparison is with the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, a passport-sized folding phone that manages to bridge the gap between the phone that people want and the one they can actually use.

The nano texture on the inner display certainly disguises the crease, especially when content is on the screen, although nothing can eliminate it entirely. The crease is far less visible than anything I’ve seen on any other foldable phone, and it will be interesting to see how that holds up over the course of a year or two with the product.

It supports Apple Pencil too – the USB C version – so you can use it to take notes, draw or just as a smart stylus.

But there are downsides. The main sacrifice comes with the camera, which only has the wide and ultrawide lens, leaving the telephoto lens out. If you are coming from the standard iPhone, that will not be a big issue as the more powerful telephoto lens has been primarily on the iPhone’s Pro models.

The front-facing camera is only 12 megapixels instead of the 18 that we have come to expect, although it retains the centre stage capabilities that keep you in the middle of the frame. The downgrade is small, admittedly; you also get the under-display FaceTime camera on the inner display, which is only really useful for video calls and is of much lower quality.

Apple has built in extras for the camera such as KidCue – similar to Google’s Made You Look feature – that displays an animation of Snoopy on the outer screen when you are using the camera with the display folded out to keep a child’s attention. There is also Smart Take, which will detect when everyone is looking at the camera and then snap a shot.

But the camera doesn’t use the inner display to its fullest, sticking with the same layout as every other iPhone despite the extra screen real estate. And the Duo lacks some of the more advanced features of the 18 Pro, including the ability to shoot RAW format and the pro controls.

So the Duo gives, and the Duo takes away. Multitasking with some apps works well, pinning two apps side by side. But there are others that would do well from a redesign to take advantage of the extra space that the Duo offers, either in how they are displayed (Gmail) or just simply by making them fit the screen and ditch the black bars (Duolingo).

You can get around this a bit by using multitasking, where you have an app open in each half of the Duo’s folded out display. For example, I like to have Google Docs and Safari open side by side. Once I open Docs and drag it to one side of the screen, I can open Safari in Split View, and the phone will remember that pairing for as long as I need it to.

Apple iPhone 18 Pro review: New smartphone makes advances but feels like a place holder

What you also don’t get is FaceID; the iPhone Duo uses TouchID instead to log you in to websites or unlock payments. Again, not a huge deal, but when you have been used to the seamless Face ID process, TouchID is a bit of a throwback.

Some of these issues can be resolved with software updated, including the app support, the decision for which rests with the developers. But it makes using the phone a little less pleasant.

Good

When it comes to design, the iPhone Duo is almost perfect. Closed it is the ideal size for one-handed use; open you get almost as much space as an iPad Mini.

Battery life was better than I expected, with the batteries in both sides of the fold giving me most of a day out of the device while using the outer display for most tasks. That inner display can really suck up the battery, though.

Multitasking is very useful. I can run two apps side by side, and the Duo will remember the app pairing for the future.

Bad

The front display looks great but when it comes to apps, there is a lot of wasted space. There are a lot of apps that don’t make full use of the iPhone Duo’s larger inner screen, including its own camera app. Think thick black bars everywhere.

You can’t mention the downsides without talking about the price. At almost €2,400, the iPhone Duo is out of reach of many consumers. Even with a contract, you are talking about a sizeable investment.

Everything else

The under-screen camera is fine, but should only be used for video calling. And invest in a good case, which should also help with the impact of the camera bump on the back of the phone.

Verdict

As a first attempt at a folding phone, Apple has learned from the mistakes of its rivals. The good outweighs a few flaws, but the price will be a stumbling block for most would-be Duo owners.
