City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Sun, 15 Nov 2026 13:11:47 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Innocent and Charles Tyrwhitt founders urge government to back UK startups https://www.cityam.com/innocent-and-charles-tyrwhitt-founders-urge-government-to-back-uk-startups/ Sun, 15 Nov 2026 13:10:05 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2477926

The founders of Innocent Drinks, Charles Tyrwhitt and Justpark have joined a group of leading British entrepreneurs calling on the government to cut employment costs and strengthen support for startups, warning that the UK risks losing its most promising businesses overseas. In an open letter seen by City AM, 13 entrepreneurs urged ministers to expand [...]]]>

The founders of Innocent Drinks, Charles Tyrwhitt and Justpark have joined a group of leading British entrepreneurs calling on the government to cut employment costs and strengthen support for startups, warning that the UK risks losing its most promising businesses overseas.

In an open letter seen by City AM, 13 entrepreneurs urged ministers to expand financial support for young founders, improve enterprise education and address the rising cost of hiring staff.

The intervention comes as Global Entrepreneurship Week UK kicks off on Monday, bringing together founders, investors and business leaders to discuss how startups can drive economic growth.

Signatories include Innocent Drinks co-founder Richard Reed, Charles Tyrwhitt founder Nick Wheeler, JustPark founder Anthony Eskinazi and Love Home Swap founder Debbie Wosskow.

While welcoming the government’s recent Budget rhetoric on entrepreneurship, the founders argued that more action was needed to help businesses start, scale and remain in Britain.

“We are mindful of the anecdotal and empirical evidence of entrepreneurs leaving the UK,” the letter said.

“We must stem the tide, and see the necessity, importance, and potential for our great founder-led businesses to stay and flourish in Britain.”

The group called for an expansion of the Young Entrepreneurs Allowance to help founders cover living costs during their first year in business.

They also urged ministers to reconsider the cost of employing staff, specifically highlighting employers’ National Insurance contributions and minimum wage levels.

“It should also think about what more it can do over the coming months to stem the cost of employing people.”

Founders warn over Britain’s scale-up problem

The warning adds to growing frustration among British entrepreneurs over taxation and the challenges of scaling businesses domestically.

Former Treasury entrepreneurship adviser Alex Depledge stepped down last month after accusing ministers of treating high-growth companies as a “sideshow” while prioritising traditional industries.

Meanwhile, ohn Healey’s recently announced Founders’ Relief has faced criticism from economists over eligibility rules that could discourage growth.

The scheme offers a 10 per cent capital gains tax rate on up to £10m of lifetime gains, but the Treasury estimates that just 600 founders annually will qualify.

Recent research from Rathbones also found that 5,774 British businesses were sold last year, the highest number in eight years, raising concerns that entrepreneurs are choosing to exit rather than expand.

Despite the challenges, the letter highlighted Britain’s strengths as an entrepreneurial economy, with 815,000 new companies incorporated last year and one in five adults either starting or running a business.

The founders also pointed to the UK’s position as the world’s third-largest venture capital market and its ranking among countries with the most unicorn businesses.

“As entrepreneurs who have started and scaled businesses in the UK, we are passionate that entrepreneurship has the capacity to bring about the much-needed growth in our economy,” they wrote.

Other signatories include Childs Farm founder Joanna Jensen, Primary Health Properties founder Harry Hyman and Arora Group chairman Surinder Arora.

The letter coincides with the Enterprise Summit on Monday, which opens Global Entrepreneurship Week UK, running until 22 November.

]]> 2477926Saskia Koopman Saskia Koopman Burnham says UK has ‘lost more than it gained’ from Brexit https://www.cityam.com/burnham-says-uk-has-lost-more-than-it-gained-from-brexit/ Sun, 15 Nov 2026 11:28:03 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2477916

Andy Burnham has warned Britain has “lost more than we’ve gained” since Brexit as he prepares for a Brussels summit aimed at cutting trade barriers and boosting economic growth. Speaking at the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday, Burnham accused the Conservatives of delivering a harder Brexit than voters expected, arguing that closer ties with the [...]]]>

Andy Burnham has warned Britain has “lost more than we’ve gained” since Brexit as he prepares for a Brussels summit aimed at cutting trade barriers and boosting economic growth.

Speaking at the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday, Burnham accused the Conservatives of delivering a harder Brexit than voters expected, arguing that closer ties with the European Union could help bring down food prices and support British exporters.

The prime minister will meet European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and European Council president António Costa on Friday, with negotiations focused on food and farming, emissions trading and youth mobility.

The government hopes the agreements could boost UK GDP by 0.4 per cent, equivalent to around £17bn.

Burnham said a food and farming deal would particularly benefit Welsh lamb and shellfish exporters by reducing the paperwork and border checks imposed after Brexit.

“We must be prepared to make difficult decisions to bring down the cost of living,” he told delegates in Llandudno.

However, he insisted Labour would respect its manifesto commitments, which rule out rejoining the single market, customs union or restoring freedom of movement.

The comments follow his suggestion that Britain could explore a closer long-term relationship with Brussels after the next general election.

Businesses warn over EU reset

The proposed food agreement would bring British regulations into closer alignment with EU standards, removing many of the health certificates and routine checks currently required for agricultural exports.

Ministers estimate the deal could add £5.1bn annually to the UK economy by 2040, although the final terms have yet to be agreed.

But Karen Betts, chief executive of the Food and Drink Federation, warned the changes could place additional pressure on manufacturers already struggling with high energy costs and regulation.

“The sector finds it must rapidly prepare to re-comply with EU food law, in the UK and for exports, under the UK-EU reset about to be signed,” she said.

“This is all diverting precious resources – people and capital – from investing in the manufacturing capacity, efficiency and jobs that underpin our food system’s resilience.”

The negotiations also come amid concerns over proposed EU “Made in Europe” rules, which could restrict subsidies for manufacturers using components produced outside the bloc.

Britain’s automotive industry is particularly exposed, with the proposed measures threatening to disadvantage UK carmakers supplying European markets.

David Bailey, professor of business economics at the University of Birmingham, said securing access to the scheme was “mission-critical” for British manufacturing.

“If Europe introduces a Made in Europe regime that protects its industrial base, the UK needs to be inside it,” he said.

He suggested Britain should consider tariffs on Chinese imports if necessary to secure an agreement with Brussels.

Meanwhile, Tories have criticised the cost of Britain’s planned return to the Erasmus student exchange programme, estimated at £570m next year.

]]> 2477916Saskia Koopman Saskia Koopman UK to expand jobs scheme to tackle Neets crisis https://www.cityam.com/uk-to-expand-jobs-scheme-to-tackle-neets-crisis/ Sun, 15 Nov 2026 10:10:22 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2477910

The government will expand its youth employment scheme nationwide to guarantee jobs for more than 90,000 young people, as ministers seek to tackle Britain’s growing number of people not in education, employment or training (Neets). The Jobs Guarantee will be rolled out across Great Britain from the end of November, offering eligible 18 to 24-year-olds [...]]]>

The government will expand its youth employment scheme nationwide to guarantee jobs for more than 90,000 young people, as ministers seek to tackle Britain’s growing number of people not in education, employment or training (Neets).

The Jobs Guarantee will be rolled out across Great Britain from the end of November, offering eligible 18 to 24-year-olds claiming Universal Credit six months of paid employment, with the government covering wages for up to 25 hours a week.

From April 2027, young people will qualify after 12 months out of work, rather than the current 18, under plans aimed at reducing the number of young people economically inactive.

The government expects the scheme to help more than 90,000 young people into work by March 2029, with over 400 employers, including Lidl, Boots and Leonardo Hotels, already backing the programme.

The expansion comes ahead of a major review by former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn, due on Tuesday, which is expected to recommend fundamental changes to the benefits system amid concerns over almost one million young people being out of work or education.

Welfare shake-up could see benefits cut

Speaking to the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg programme, Milburn warned that some young people would lose benefits under his proposals, but argued that spending should be redirected towards employment opportunities.

“There will be some young people who lose out, of course,” he said. “We’re already spending £22 billion a year keeping young people inactive and on benefits and not in a job.”

Milburn said his proposed reforms would take a decade to deliver, requiring billions of pounds in additional investment before savings from lower welfare spending and higher employment could be realised.

He also called for a legal “opportunity guarantee”, under which the government would have a duty to provide young people with employment, education or training opportunities.

In return, young people would be expected to take up those opportunities, with sanctions remaining available for those who refused.

He also proposed allowing young people to keep more of their benefits when entering part-time employment, arguing that the current system penalised those attempting to return to work.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden backed the need for a “complete reset of the system”, acknowledging that existing government measures were insufficient.

“I’m not here to say that what we’re doing at the moment is enough,” he told the BBC.

The minister also confirmed that the reforms would include an “element of compulsion”, arguing that the welfare state should offer both financial security and opportunities to work.

The expansion forms part of the government’s £2.5bn youth employment package, which aims to create 500,000 opportunities for young people.

The government is expected to respond to Milburn’s recommendations following the publication of his review on Tuesday

]]> 2477910Saskia Koopman Saskia Koopman City law and accountancy firms face cash flow crunch in HMRC shake-up https://www.cityam.com/city-law-and-accountancy-firms-face-cash-flow-crunch-in-hmrc-shake-up/ Sun, 15 Nov 2026 10:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2477671

City partnerships could be forced to take on expensive debt to fund their own partners’ tax bills after the government confirmed a major shake-up of HMRC’s self-assessment regime. As part of the Budget, Chancellor John Healey confirmed the government announced plans to introduce more timely payments for income tax self assessment (ITSA) from April 2029. [...]]]>

City partnerships could be forced to take on expensive debt to fund their own partners’ tax bills after the government confirmed a major shake-up of HMRC’s self-assessment regime.

As part of the Budget, Chancellor John Healey confirmed the government announced plans to introduce more timely payments for income tax self assessment (ITSA) from April 2029. This will replace the current system, where those who report tax via self-assessment pay twice a year, with ‘regular’ payments.

According to the government, ITSA taxpayers are “a vital part of the UK economy”, with around 12m people filing a self-assessment return, bringing in £48bn of income tax revenue in 2024 to 2025. One of the larger users of the ITSA is limited liability partnership (LLP) firms and equity partners in law, accountancy, and consulting firms.

Healey said he wants to ensure tax is paid closer to real time, reducing the likelihood of late payments or taxpayers falling into tax debt.

However, experts have warned the move could significantly affect professional services firms.

Nimesh Shah, chief executive, Blick Rothenberg, said: ‘The government’s clear objective is to collect tax sooner – but for LLPs, it could have a significant impact on investment in the business and ultimately how profits are managed and distributed.”

“A switch to more regular tax payments will hit cash flow at a time when professional service firms are already being squeezed by more general economic issues including increases in staff costs and national insurance,” explained David Portman, partner at Lubbock Fine.

In a recent report, the Law Society said it did “not believe this is justified”, and added that it had responded to a government consultation on the plans.

Slow-billing City firms face ‘double-hit’ squeeze

“This is not simply a change to the frequency of partners’ tax payments,” Adam Craggs, tax partner at law firm RPC, said. “It potentially changes the way professional partnerships manage cash, partner remuneration, drawings, capital and financial performance.”

Under the current system, equity partners and member firms file tax returns twice a year: the first by 31 January and the second by 31 July.

“Partners are generally taxed on their share of LLP profits, and many firms set aside money to meet those personal tax bills,” explained Sue Robinson, principal at Ryan Tax. “More frequent payments may mean releasing those reserves sooner and revisiting how much working capital the firm retains.”

At a time when lock-up, the time it takes to convert billable work into cash in the bank, is under constant pressure at firms as clients are being chased to pay bills. The average lock-up days for British law firms in 2026 is 134 days, according to the Law Society Financial Benchmarking Survey.

But the upcoming tax change means there needs to be a renewed focus on lock-up, early invoice raising, and collection. “Firms with slow billing or collection would be likely to feel that pressure most,” Robinson said.

In addition, because tax may be due to HMRC before a firm bills the client, some LLPs may have to dip into credit facilities, extend overdrafts, or take out working capital loans, industry figures warned.

Shah added, “Some partners could see lower take-home distributions as a result.“

The cost of servicing that debt could cut directly into the firm’s bottom line should interest rates rise as many economists expect.

As the ‘regular’ payment has yet to be defined, and further guidance from HMRC on the changes is expected in 2027, concerns have been raised that a potential ‘double-hit’ squeeze could cause a cash flow issue.

Portnam said “the government should consider delaying this proposal”, to give people more time to prepare.

When approached for comment, a government spokesperson said: “This government wants the tax system to work better for working people and small businesses. No one will owe more tax, and moving to smaller, more regular payments will make it easier for millions of taxpayers to manage their money and avoid the shock of large tax bills.”

]]> 2477671Maria Ward-Brennan Maria Ward-Brennan Riner, Khan, Klitschko: The sport stars that go from pitch to politics https://www.cityam.com/riner-khan-klitschko-the-sport-stars-that-go-from-pitch-to-politics/ Sun, 15 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2476542

After Teddy Riner announced his candidacy for French president, City AM took a look at the stars that swapped the pitch for politics, sport for service “If refusing to bow my head and refusing to accept chaos makes me crazy, then yes, I am completely crazy.” Those are the words of the latest person to [...]]]>

After Teddy Riner announced his candidacy for French president, City AM took a look at the stars that swapped the pitch for politics, sport for service

“If refusing to bow my head and refusing to accept chaos makes me crazy, then yes, I am completely crazy.” Those are the words of the latest person to throw their name into the ring to become the president of France in 2027, in what is seen as a wide open race to replace Emmanuel Macron. 

“France does not need a professional politician lecturing and bickering all day long. It needs common sense, firmness, justice, and a state that puts things back in order,” they added.

The aforementioned one-line zingers aren’t those of someone inside the traditional bubble, however, but instead of five-time Olympic champion judo fighter Teddy Riner – one of the republic’s most popular sportspeople.

He will challenge the likes of Marine Le Pen to lead L’Hexagone, but by no means is he the first sports star to swap the sport for service.

Sport for service

Notably, former cricketer Imran Khan, footballer George Weah and hurler Jack Lynch went from the pitch to politics, becoming heads of state. Khan was leader of Pakistan before his imprisonment, while Weah led Liberia between 2018 and 2024 and Lynch was the elected Taoiseach for much of the 1970s.

Riner isn’t the only combatant to seek office, either. Former heavyweight boxer Vitali Klitschko answered the call from Ukraine to become Mayor of Kyiv in 2014, while Manny Pacquiao served as both a congressman and senator in his native Philippines between 2010 and 2022 and even attempted a run at the presidency. On these shores, London 2012 gold medal winner Luke Campbell is currently serving as Reform UK’s Mayor of Hull and East Yorkshire.

Sticking in Blighty, former national 100m record holder Menzies Campbell was briefly leader of the Liberal Democrats while few can look past Lord Sebastian Coe’s involvement in politics; he went from a glittering 1,500m career to the green benches of the House of Commons before going on to leading World Athletics and having a crack at being elected as president of the International Olympic Committee. Less successful was rower James Cracknell, who failed in an attempt to become an MP in 2024.

Pitch for the future

Former Georgian centre-back Kakha Kaladze was elected as the mayor of the country’s capital, Tbilisi, while ex-Manchester City striker Mikheil Kavelashvili was in 2024 sworn in as the country’s president. And in India World Cup winner Gautam Gambhir was elected to parliament for a five-year term in 2019. Australian back-row David Pocock is now a senator Down Under, too.

The most recent major elections saw the Democrats take control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the US. And while the likes of NBA champion Bill Bradley and NFL star Jack Kemp have previously been legislators – the latter as a secretary of state in George Bush’s administration – last week’s election saw former New York Yankees baseball player Mark Teixeira, former Tennessee Titans linebacker Colin Allred and wheelchair basketball gold medallist Josh Turek all elected for the first time.

So when Riner sits at his grand desk and calls for change, he does so off the back of many other sports stars who have ditched the sporting limelight for podiums and politics. A win wouldn’t make him the first to succeed, but the attributes sport may have developed in him and others have precedent in translating into votes.

]]> 2476542Matt Hardy Matt Hardy The HMRC stealth powers to take your taxes  https://www.cityam.com/the-hmrc-stealth-powers-to-take-your-taxes/ Sun, 15 Nov 2026 00:01:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2477786

HMRC is set to receive sweeping new tax powers to seize cash from bereaved families, scour the AI chatbot history of taxpayers and slap huge fines on those who made inadvertent errors in documents, under changes quietly pushed through after the Budget. Following John Healey’s maiden Autumn Budget a raft of new proposals were added [...]]]>

HMRC is set to receive sweeping new tax powers to seize cash from bereaved families, scour the AI chatbot history of taxpayers and slap huge fines on those who made inadvertent errors in documents, under changes quietly pushed through after the Budget.

Following John Healey’s maiden Autumn Budget a raft of new proposals were added the Finance Bill, dubbed ‘Budget Resolutions’, which survived the first reading on 3 November.

While some resolutions centre on tax hikes discussed by Healey at the despatch box, including the hike to savings, property and income tax, others dramatically beef up the powers of the tax authority.

The shake-up to the system comes as HMRC aims to close the UK’s staggering tax gap.

According to the latest estimates from the government body, the shortfall cost the Treasury nearly £60bn in lost tax receipts during the 2024/25 financial year.

Healey has pledged to close the gap, but as Labour’s manifesto prevents hikes to income tax, VAT and employee national insurance, the government is leaning on compliance and greater enforcement powers for HMRC to raise revenue.

Healey said restoring fiscal discipline was his “first commitment as Chancellor”, including “raising revenue from those who can afford to pay”.

Punishing tax mistakes

HMRC will introduce a statutory ‘Duty to Correct’ regime from April 2028, which will legally require taxpayers to rectify mistakes on old tax returns upon becoming aware of them.

Currently, a mistake discovered after filing is treated by the authority as “careless” which carries a lower penalty of up to 30 per cent of the unpaid tax over six years. But the new regime will see an inaccuracy – even if unintentional – branded as “deliberate”, the term used by HMRC when it believes it is intentionally fed false figures or withheld information in order to pay less tax.

It is the highest penalty tier for the authority, carrying a fine which can be up to 100 per cent and a scrutiny period of 20 years.

The changes have raised concerns among tax barristers, who have called out the lack of minimum threshold on tax errors as well as the two-decade long window, as it clashes with statutory record-keeping rules for the self-employed.

They are only legally required to keep records for up to five to six years, meaning those facing a 20 year audit may be unable to produce needed receipts and bank statements.

Fiona Fernie, partner at Blick Rothenberg, said: “This legislation needs clearer safeguards and a finite time limit for making corrections. Otherwise, a measure intended to modernise compliance could undermine it.”

An HMRC spokesperson said: “We know most of our customers act in good faith and want to get their tax right. These changes make it quicker and easier for taxpayers to correct errors when we flag them.

“They won’t be penalised for innocent mistakes, and deliberate penalty charges only arise where taxpayers fail to take reasonable steps to correct an inaccuracy they were already aware of.”

Bereaved families hounded for longer

HMRC can currently demand information from the families of deceased taxpayers for up to four years after their death if they suspect they’ve paid the wrong amount of tax. This covers inheritance tax, capital gains tax and income tax.

Under Labour’s proposals, HMRC will be granted the right to demand information about the dead for an unlimited period, and the right to gather evidence for existing tax investigations that reach back up to 20 years.

This could see families by the government years after an estate has been settled, which advisers have warned could lead to disputes among relatives or leave them buckled by tax bills they cannot afford to pay.

Draft legislation states HMRC will have to apply to a tax tribunal to send an information demand more than four years after death, but it will not be required to inform the executors of the estate, or the family, until after the tribunal has made a decision.

A government spokesperson said: “This does not mean new powers and will not affect the vast majority of taxpayers.

“The updates to HMRC’s existing information powers reflect how tax information is stored and processed digitally, and updates powers in line with the international standards of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.”

AI chatbot histories set to be snooped on

The tax authority will soon be able to view taxpayers’ messaging records with AI chatbots under new powers that will allow HMRC to probe digital records.

HMRC currently has powers to request and obtain copies of digital “records” if it has a legitimate reason to do so to determine whether a taxpayer has paid the correct amount of tax.

However, under the government’s newly proposed rules, the definition of digital information will be expanded to allow access to “relevant” digital records, which may include AI chatbots.

The move will also require third parties, including software providers, to give HMRC people’s tax information if they hold it.

“Conversations between a taxpayer and their advisor are confidential and AI conversations should be treated in the same way, so without the right checks and balances HMRC’s new powers could cross the line between a legitimate investigation and overreach,” Praveen Gupta, head of tax at accountancy and advisory firm Azets, said.

Gupta added it “cannot be one sided” and “robust safeguards around these powers will be critical”. Doing so would allow people to “understand why they’re being investigated and that the information being requested is relevant and a reasonable request for HMRC to understand their tax affairs”. 

“Will individuals be able to request and be granted access to HMRC’s own internal notes and AI research into their tax affairs? In the interests of fairness, they should be,” he said. 

Matthew Greene, partner at Stewarts, said while HMRC accessing AI chat histories “could help uncover tax irregularities”, it “also risks dragging innocent taxpayers into unnecessary investigations.”

Prepping young people for work is no good unless the government lowers the cost of employment to create more jobs, writes Helen Dickinson ahead of the release of the Alan Milburn’s NEET report

There is little point making young people work-ready if there are no jobs waiting for them. This is why government must address the rising costs and regulation that make entry-level jobs harder to create.

Picture a single decker bus. Forty young people, aged 16 to 24. The bus stops by the school and university; 23 get out to study. Next, it pulls up in the business district; another 12 get out for work. That leaves five young people not in education, employment or training (NEET).

This bus represents a whole generation of young people. The five people still on the bus represent nearly 1m young people who are NEET and cost the economy an eye-watering £125bn a year. A figure currently expected to rise.

But it’s more than the money. These young people miss out on the purpose and recognition that comes with a job, as well as opportunities to develop skills, build confidence and gain independence. Without experience, they struggle to find work; without work, they cannot gain experience. It’s a doom loop that risks leaving hundreds of thousands of young people behind.

Milburn report should focus on stimulating job creation

One in every eight young people is neither learning nor earning, failed by the system. They might be your child, your neighbour, your friend. We have a moral and economic duty to act.

This is what Alan Milburn’s upcoming report into Young People and Work, expected to be published next week, will set out to do. What he says, and how the government responds and acts, will determine whether this moral and economic imperative will be addressed.

Milburn will call on government to do more to prepare young people for the world of work. We need a benefits system that incentivises work. This might be helping people into part-time roles or changing the balance between in-work and out-of-work support. Doing so should reduce pressure on the welfare system and strengthen public finances.

But unless government also stimulates job creation, it simply won’t be enough. We need more jobs, including entry-level roles for those without experience or qualifications.

Retail is a vital source of these. Its 2.8m jobs offer flexible, local opportunities that don’t require qualifications. But between 2024 and 2027, retail’s employment costs will have risen by around £8.5bn. Over the same period, retail has lost over 120,000 roles. That’s a lot of full buses of young people with no job to head to.

Red tape is stifling employers

Economic growth has slowed to a crawl. The cost of employing young people has skyrocketed, so retailers have scaled back recruitment. When jobs are scarce, employers are choosy, leaving inexperienced young people at the back of the queue.

Government has two levers to boost job creation. First, put more money in people’s pockets, boosting spending power and giving employers a reason to hire. Secondly, cut the cost and risks of employing people. They must start to reverse the devastating employer National Insurance rises which have made entry-level jobs unaffordable for too many retailers. And they must ensure the implementation of new employment rights legislation avoids the adverse impacts on part-time and flexible work, so often relied upon by young people entering the workforce.

Retailers are taking action. Through Opening Shift, a BRC-DWP work experience initiative, over 50 retailers have pledged 11,000 placements, with the ambition of helping 100,000 young people into jobs. By giving young people the experience they need to get their foot on the career ladder, we can help break the cycle of unemployment. But only if these are new jobs. Simply moving the problem from one group of people to another won’t solve anything.

All eyes are now on the forthcoming Milburn report. Its recommendations must provide a turning point. But making young people work-ready is not enough. We must lower the costs of employment for businesses, and build a welfare system that rewards hard work. What the government does next will determine whether we get this generation moving or leave another million young people stuck on the bus.

Helen Dickinson is chief executive at the British Retail Consortium

Feldspar’s founders believe its sensor plate technology can revolutionise sport by providing data to improve athlete performance and prevent injury but also enhance the spectacle.

Feldspar’s two products are a super-fast track layer that allows athletes to race or train harder, and the cloud-connected sensor-plate technology that can be installed beneath it.

The latter is, the company says, “the world’s first modular platform for continuous, real-time force measurement across sports surfaces”, and could facilitate recurring subscription revenues.

The smart track – created by the Cambridge Design Collective – collects data on horizontal, vertical and lateral force as well as centre pressure, delivering real-time insights that can be applied to training or turned into sophisticated content.

“What we’re doing here is potentially very transformational,” says executive director Tim Godfrey, formerly of SailGP, Formula E and triathlon’s PTO. “Because the underlying surface in which sports are played on is, in our mind, going to change forever if we get a lot of things right.”

He adds: “Nobody has been able to solve this particular problem of getting this level of biomechanical force data at scale. People do it already, but in a single force plate. No one’s done it to the scale we’ve done before. That’s the technological innovation.”

Feldspar’s first three years have been funded this far by the family of athlete-turned-entrepreneur Chen but the company is now in talks with investors over a seed round.

It is aiming to raise £5.5m to £6m, Chen says, and is keen to attract backing from sports organisations which may be able to play a role in the products’ evolution.

Godfrey adds: “We think it’s going to be strategic partners who understand, first and foremost, the value of the technology in a sporting environment.

Smart track tech at the Olympics and new Man Utd stadium?

“If a whole stadium wanted eight lanes, 400m with the sensors, today the price is not something that we would look to do, because we need to do a lot more development and get the manufacturing and the production and the supply chain,” says Godfrey.

Nvidia chief’s defenestration underlines the importance of governance ESG’s overlooked category, Ali Lyon writes in today’s Midday Markets newsletter.

At City AM, we pride ourselves on making the cross-pollinating worlds of business, finance, economics and wealth, fun. Indeed, so averse are our higher-ups to conforming to the industries’ love of complexity, jargon and – dare we say – pretence, that ‘business with personality’ has been the paper’s strapline for the entirety of its 21-year existence.

And so when, today, I suggested devoting this newsletter to the the subject of ‘governance’ I was met with more than a few raised eyebrows.

I’ll concede, 700 words on the processes and structures that a company implements to protect the long-term interests of its stakeholders doesn’t scream ‘business with personality’.

But this week’s defenestration of Jensen Huang – the scandal-hit co-founder of chip giant Nvidia – has thrust the thorny, unsexy issue firmly into the limelight, and thrown up some interesting talking points, to boot.

To many in the public and among some of the company’s shareholders, Huang was not the face of Nvidia; he was Nvidia. And for good reason: the leather jacket-toting, ever-energetic ‘AI rockstar’ had been both chief executive and president of the semiconductor colossus for more than 30 years.

He oversaw its evolution from niche computer-gaming chipmaker to the undisputed weathermaker of the AI evolution. And now, he’s gone, leaving a vacuum of leadership, not just at the world’s second-largest company, but at the heart of the most financially consequential industrial revolution in history.

This is, to borrow a technical phrase, not good. Nvidia’s shares are down 10 per cent since the start of the week, and 20 per cent in the past month. In one day, they shed more value than the total market capitalisation of HSBC, the FTSE 100’s most valuable company, all because of the poor judgement of a single, highly consequential individual.

UK Corporate Governance Code, I was not familiar with your game

The unseemly episode has laid bare the sheer amount of power and influence wielded by those at the top of the largest companies in history. In Nvidia’s case, Huang reportedly had up to 60 executives reporting directly into him at any one time. And despite the totemic founder’s multi-decade tenure, Nvidia’s toothless – and, until this week, chairless – board appears to have done next to no succession planning.

As Imperial Business School associate professor Dr Porneetha Luthra wrote in the pages of City AM this week: “While charismatic’ leaders can seem intoxicating – admired, respected and sometimes loved – this is a very dangerous hierarchy.”

It’s worth noting that, had the same indiscretions been committed by any of the other founder-led tech giants, things would have been even worse. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, SpaceX and Tesla’s Elon Musk and Palantir’s Alex Karp are all, essentially, impossible to fire, thanks to the company’s dual-share structure.

And to a number, those emblematic entrepreneurs also personally own much more of the company than Huang’s 3.6 per cent. Just imagine the chaos had it been Elon Musk – who owns a fifth of Tesla and nearly half of SpaceX – who fraternised with an alleged Chinese spy.

In the good times, this concentrated power is a blessing. It allows for fast, bold decision-making unhindered by pesky shareholder votes and board oversight. When you’re dealing with some of the biggest brains in the world, who know their company and industry back to front – those decisions are more often than not, correct and lucrative. But either in – or in the run-up to – crises, robust governance is worth its weight in gold.

Which is why, today at least, we should be grateful for the UK’s rather old-fashioned approach. Thanks to the UK Corporate Governance Code, there is not a single FTSE 100 chief executive who also serves as chair of their company’s board (on the US’s S&P 500, more than four in 10 do). Under London-listing rules, any public company that allows its most senior executive to serve in both roles must explain its rationale to shareholders every year.

In a recent overhaul, the London Stock Exchange chose to water down some of its rules in what is, so far, a vein attempt to attract founder-led fintech and tech unicorn IPOs. But those changes don’t come close to mirroring the free-wheeling approach adopted by the bourse’s counterparts across the pond. And after this week’s Nvidious episode, that is probably no bad thing.

His admission of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy had him on the ropes – reports of two further relationships with women inside Nvidia finished him off. Huang quit after 33 years at the helm following an emergency board meeting, casting the company into chaos and wiping nearly $600bn from its value at one point.

Finance chief Colette Kress has been installed as interim chief executive and Harvey Jones named chairman while the board begins a desperate for a permanent successor. Huang, meanwhile, faces a grilling from US lawmakers over his relationship with Alice Huang, with a closed-door House Foreign Affairs Committee briefing already set for 1 December. To be a fly on that wall… It’s a hell of a downfall for a man who was until recently on Donald Trump’s speed-dial.

Sporting his trademark black leather jacket, it should perhaps not come as too much of a surprise that his midlife crisis also extends to affairs with younger women. Their relationship had already raised eyebrows, with Huang (no relation) posting pictures of the pair enjoying intimate dinners together, which Jensen had previously claimed were “related to [her tech company] Megaspeed… it was all completely normal and not unusual”. 

He was being more accurate than he intended: in the heated arena of the corporate boardroom, affairs are surprisingly “normal and not unusual”, although they do tend to cause something of a ruckus when they are inevitably exposed.

Remember the Coldplay kisscam?

Who could forget the infamous Coldplay kisscam footage from last year, when data startup Astronomer boss Andy Byron was caught red-handed – and red-faced – in a clinch with his “chief people officer” Kristin Cabot. Their reaction – attempting to duck from the prying eyes of the camera – caused the footage to go viral and by the next morning, the pair were infamous across the world. Both resigned from the company and they are, rather unfairly, still hounded over it to this day.

In 2023, BP boss Bernard Looney was stripped of a remuneration package worth millions after failing to admit relationships – with an “s” – with various colleagues, with the BP board claiming it had been “knowingly misled”.

The incident recalled Lord Browne’s infamous departure from the same company in 2007, when he was forced to quit after lying under oath about a four-year relationship with Jeff Chevalier.

In an ill-fated attempt to block the Mail on Sunday from publishing the story, Lord Browne went to the High Court, lying under oath about meeting his beau while jogging in a London park, rather than through an escort website. He forfeited a leaving package worth some £15m.

Jensen Huang has joined a large club

Former McDonald’s boss Steve Easterbrook, a rare Brit to reach the summit of corporate America, was fired over an affair in 2019 – it later emerged that, like Jensen Huang, he had engaged in multiple relationships with people at the fast food company. Easterbrook was subsequently fined by the US financial watchdog for misleading investors: as the saying goes, the cover-up is always worse than the crime.

The same story repeats ad nauseam: in 2005 Boeing CEO Harry Stonecipher was forced out of the firm after admitting to an affair with his vice-president for operations and commercial activities Debra Peabody. In 2006 Walmart’s marketing executive Julie Roehm had an “inappropriate romantic relationship” with Sean Womack, a former marketing VP at the retailer (Walmart claimed the pair had been spotted in a compromising position in a bar).

None of these adulterers survived their indiscretion – Huang has proved nobody is too big to fail. If you’re running a company, take heed.

Rising GDP figures may be welcome, but they’re no reason yet to celebrate Labour, writes shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith

Often in politics, people look to you to be excessively partisan. As someone who came to politics only after a career in business, that isn’t my style. I welcome the positives from this week’s GDP figures whilst cautioning ministers trying to take a celebratory lap from a decidedly mixed picture.

First, let’s consider what this week’s figures show: 0.7 per cent growth in Q3 of 2026, up from 0.5 per cent in Q2. Compared to last year, that’s GDP 1.9 per cent higher. This is by no means a boom, nor is it far off from expectations, but in the context of global shocks and rising inflation, it is still welcome. The devil is, as ever, in the details which show a deeply uneven picture across the economy.

The ONS data shows that big growth drivers have been tech and business services, including IT and computer equipment. These benefit from the global AI boom and Britain’s services sector is well placed to catch it, especially because our position outside the EU has kept us safe from overzealous AI regulation. The key then, is to let this winner run.

Last week, the Bank of England estimated that AI-related activity accounts for a staggering fifth of all growth since the start of the year. An EU reset that jeopardises that growth by adopting Brussels regulations could be enormously damaging.  

The worrying trends behind the figures

Now for the less good news: behind the headline figures there lies the continuation of some worrying trends.  

The resolutely domestic construction sector shrank by 0.7 per cent in Q3, under a government that promised to get Britain building. In fact, construction sector indices have been in negative territory ever since Labour took office. The Office for Budget Responsibility now expects 190,000 fewer new builds than it forecast as recently as March. It’s a big sector of the economy and one at the sharp end of government policy. The verdict isn’t good.

The macroeconomic picture also shows up an oddity. Unpicking the public and private sector components of GDP, it becomes clear that the former has soared while the latter has flagged. Public sector spending and investment have grown 20 per cent since 2019, while the same components in the private sector have only grown 3.2 per cent. This is not a wholly new problem, but it is getting worse not better. It is no more sustainable than a hungry snake eating its own tail.

Brits are still being squeezed

Finally, in the real world, families are bracing for harder months ahead, with expensive energy bills, inflation remaining high and rising interest rates. The households and businesses that have kept this economy moving are about to be squeezed even further, which is why today is no moment for a victory lap.

The tangible help the economy urgently needs is to cut energy costs by getting Britain drilling again and removing the tangled web of levies and obligations that have held back industry and raised costs for families. Second, lift the ongoing burden on employers from Labour’s ‘back to the 1970s’ (Un)Employment Act alongside adopting the Conservative policy halving the jobs tax for young people. And to help construction, speed up planning and cut gold plated regulations to get Britain building again.

This week’s growth figures remain a testament to the strength and resilience of British businesses. Such growth as there is has come despite, not because of, the government. Just imagine what those businesses could do with a government properly on their side.

Andrew Griffith is shadow chancellor

Having laid down its spirit in 2015, it became the 8th English distillery since 1903 to release an authentic English whisky. Its very first whisky, Cattle Creep, named after the narrow livestock underpasses along the Grand Union Canal, was aged in 55-litre Madeira casks and bottled at 58.8 per cent ABV.

Wharf then released the Equinox and Solstice single malts, matured in 160-litre Port quarter casks and chestnut wood. It then launched Fyr Drenc, an English single malt grain spirit distilled in copper pot stills using four types of malted barley.

Operating out of Towcester in Northamptonshire, founder Laurence Conisbee has spent the past seven years proving his liquid can hold its own.

An English whiskey named after a moment in time

Now, however, he is ditching the folklore altogether. Wharf’s latest release, bottled at 55.3 per cent ABV, dispenses with themed names in favour of a timestamp: 17.05.23 15:18 Single Malt English Whiskey.

In a market increasingly sceptical of over-packaged craft releases, that stripped-back naming convention, coupled with the ‘e’ in whiskey, helps the bottling stand out in an increasingly crowded market.

“Every whiskey takes its own path,” says Conisbee. “We wanted to create something that celebrates that individuality, stripping away the elaborate names and unnecessary embellishments and allowing the whiskey to speak for itself. Each release is identified simply by the moment its cask was filled. The rest of the story is there for people to discover and interpret in their own way.”

The whiskey was matured in an ex-bourbon cask and is an individual expression of English single malt whiskey. With only one cask filled, it’s a rare item in a crowded market.

“We’ve been releasing English whiskey since 2019, but this represents an evolution in how we present what we make,” Conisbee notes. “This particular whiskey began its maturation journey in an ex-bourbon cask on 17 May 2023 at precisely 15:18. Samruk-Kazyna said on Thursday in a statement on its website the wealth fund and its companies within the group “continue to operate as normal”.

“All commitments to investors, creditors, international financial institutions and business partners remain in full force and are being honoured in accordance with the terms of existing agreements,” it said.

Samruk-Kazyna also controls major assets across various sectors in Khazakhstan, including transport, telecoms, and infrastructure. Alongside Air Astana it also operates the country’s state gas and oil company, KazMunayGaz.

Air Astana’s 2024 London IPO

Air Astana, which was previously half-owned by British defence giant, BAE Systems until March this year, officially listed on the London Stock Exchange in February 2024, as well as two domestic exchanges in Kazakhstan.

The group looked to raise $120m across both exchanges before the dual-jurisdiction listing to pump into a series of new routes and bolster its low-cost airline Flyarystan.

Samruk-Kazyna and Air Astana Group did not respond immediately when contacted for comment.

The financial watchdog’s proposals to relax pension charge cap rules could help boost investment in start-ups and private companies, bosses have said, after efforts to unleash a wave of investment from Britain’s retirement funds have stalled in recent years.

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) yesterday floated excluding certain performance-linked fees from the charge cap for default funds in workplace pensions in its latest consultation paper.

Critics have argued that a 0.75 per cent fee cap has restricted pension providers from investing in private markets assets including private equity and venture capital, which historically have struggled to fit their fees below the regulatory ceiling.

The watchdog argued the reforms provide “greater flexibility”, allowing access to investments which can “improve long-term returns for value”, while industry figures said it could lead to more capital entering these riskier assets.

“The FCA’s proposals are a welcome recognition that the cheapest pension investments do not necessarily deliver the best outcomes for savers,” said Kelly Parsons, head of DC proposition at Broadstone.

“Private market investments can offer valuable diversification and access to growth opportunities, while potentially unlocking more pension capital for investment into UK businesses.”

Not an excuse

But the regulator warned the changes would not be a “licence to charge more”, telling providers that higher charges must be justified by the additional value delivered to savers.

“Bigger does not automatically mean better…robust governance, transparency and scrutiny of investment performance will be essential,” Parsons added.

Alongside the proposal to overhaul the cap, the FCA suggested safeguards covering transparency, fair allocation of fees and greater scrutiny of private asset valuation.

The consultation comes as the government shifts its focus to improving long-term retirement outcomes, underpinned by the incoming Value for Money framework.

The regime will see workplace schemes assessed on net investment returns and quality of service instead of solely on headline fees.

It could also enable Mansion House signatories to boost their allocations to risker private assets. As of December 2025, the 17 signatories had allocated 3.3 per cent of assets to UK private markets, but the vast majority has been pushed into property.

 Just £500m was invested into private equity.

Gareth Trainor, director of investment propositions at Royal London, which is a Mansion House signatory, said: “Supporting greater investment in private markets could create greater opportunities for pension savers, while also unlocking potentially more investment in the UK economy.” 

Greater alignment

The changes would also align FCA-regulated pension schemes with trust-based schemes, which have been excluded from performance fee restrictions since 2023.

James Wilson, long-term savings policy director at the Association of British Insurers, said ending the differences between the two regimes would remove unnecessary complexity and create a “consistent pensions market”.

“For ultimate success, we need consistency in the fine print too. Regulators must be able to adopt any new protections in lockstep, so all savers have access to the same wide range of investment opportunities,” he said.

The consultation closes on 14 January 2027.

Pro Climbing League returning to London in 2027 season

PCL organisers plan to expand to five events in 2028, including at least one in the US, and will also use their latest funding to build out the business.

Wen-Chieh Liang, deputy minister at Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council, told City AM that the scandal surrounding the chipmaker’s founder had prompted fresh scrutiny of security arrangements for executives in the strategically important sector.

When asked whether the allegations would lead Taiwan to review security advice for senior figures in its AI industry, Liang replied: “Of course.”

“For the past five years, Jensen Huang has done a lot for Taiwan’s AI supply chain and AI industry, so we are very sorry that he’s in this situation right now,” he said.

However, Liang questioned reports that Taiwanese authorities had been warned about the suspected espionage threat as early as 2024.

“Regarding the New York Times report that Taiwan’s government was warned in 2024 regarding a potential spy situation, I have to say that at least from my department, the Mainland Affairs Council, we were not notified about this,” he told City AM.

“So I am not sure that the report is 100 per cent correct.”

The comments come after Taiwan revoked the entry permit of Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman whom US intelligence officials suspect of gathering information for Beijing.

Taiwanese authorities said she had entered the island multiple times in 2024 and 2025, including during visits by Jensen Huang.

Beijing has dismissed the espionage allegations as unsubstantiated.

Third affair emerges after Nvidia resignation

The intervention comes as new reports reveal that Huang had an intimate relationship with another Nvidia employee, bringing the number of alleged extramarital affairs to three.

The latest report follows revelations of a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reported directly to Huang.

Huang has acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife over his relationship with Alice Huang but has not publicly confirmed the two other alleged affairs.

The 63-year-old resigned on Thursday after 33 years leading Nvidia, with finance chief Colette Kress appointed interim chief executive.

His departure sent shares in the AI chip giant plunging 16 per cent at the open, wiping nearly $600bn off its market value.

The sell-off also spread to AI infrastructure firm Coreweave, whose shares fell around six per cent, while the Nasdaq and S&P 500 opened lower.

Trump defended the Nvidia founder, saying Huang had told him he had “absolutely no idea” the woman was a suspected spy and that he believed him.

Aviva has recorded a boost in general insurance premiums after its acquisition of Direct Line granted it more command over the UK market.

Total group remiums rose 19 per cent in the first nine months of the year to £11.8bn, up from £10bn the prior year.

UK and Ireland premiums also grew 27 per cent to £8.5bn. Its personal lines segment, which covers motor, health and travel insurance, increased 54 per cent to £5.5bn, after receiving a boost from its acquisition of Direct Line.

The £3.7bn acquisition, which was completed in July 2025, has allowed Aviva control of a fifth of the UK motor insurance market. 

Chief executive Amanda Blanc said she is eyeing “many opportunities to continue our profitable growth in general insurance”. 

She noted further extension of Direct Line policies, the introduction of pet insurance and growing it reach in international markets Canada and Ireland, where it is among the leaders of general and life insurance.

But commercial lines insurance, aimed at businesses, suffered a five per cent decline to £2.9bn, reflecting “softer market conditions”.

Shares increased 2.1 per cent in early trading to 754.6p.

Wealth flows rise

Its wealth arm reached net flows of £10.9bn, compared to £8.3bn the prior year.

Assets under management also ticked up 19 per cent to £267bn, while customer numbers climbed to 6.1m, which Blanc said has caused its wealth business to be the “number one UK player”.

“We see significant opportunities for Aviva to expand further, across our workplace, adviser and direct businesses, giving us confidence that we will achieve at least £280m in operating profit in wealth by 2027,” Blanc said.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst UK at investing and trading platform IG, said: “The strong trading in its wealth division provides another string to Aviva’s bow, and has played a big part in the rally in the shares.

“While we’re all used to thinking of Aviva as an insurer, it is growth in wealth management that offers the real potential for the future. With tech stocks looking wobbly again, Aviva’s combination of dividend and share price growth is a compelling proposition.” 

Division stumbles

Despite headline growth, the insurance giant faced pressure in several divisions.

Its retirement business saw nine-month bulk purchase annuities (BPA) volumes, insurance policies used by defined benefit schemes to transfer liabilities to insurers, halved to £1.9bn, amid increased competition in the market.

But Aviva noted that BPA deals signed or ones in the pipeline which refer to the insurer as the “preferred provider”, reached £5.8bn, ahead of the £4.6bn written across the entirety of 2025.

Meanwhile, health insurance sales fell 31 per cent to £81m amid slower market growth across consumer and small-business channels. 

Severe weather and catastrophe claims in Canada, its second-largest market, weighed on underwriting profits, while premiums for the year to date rose by just two per cent to £3.2bn.

A global Microsoft outage has disrupted NHS services, police forces and Britain’s electricity grid, prompting fresh warnings over the UK’s reliance on American technology giants for critical infrastructure.

The technology giant is struggling to restore Outlook, Teams and its AI assistant Copilot after a disruption that began on Thursday and has affected users across 74 countries.

Britain’s National Energy System Operator (Neso) was forced to revert to fax machines to communicate with power stations, while police forces, schools and hospitals reported widespread problems.

The Metropolitan Police warned that officers were unable to access emails and some online crime reports might not reach them, although emergency response services remained operational.

NHS England said the outage was “inevitably” disrupting staff, with some trusts reverting to paper records and alternative IT systems to keep services running.

Microsoft said it was making “additional progress toward service recovery” on Friday, with traffic gradually being restored across parts of its infrastructure in Asia-Pacific.

However, the company warned that some users could continue experiencing intermittent problems as it worked to clear email backlogs.

The outage was caused by servers becoming unexpectedly unavailable, placing additional strain on remaining infrastructure. Microsoft said there was no evidence of malicious activity.

Microsoft outage exposes reliance on US tech

Mark Boost, chief executive of British cloud provider Civo, said the outage exposed the risks of concentrating essential public services within a single technology ecosystem.

“Outages happen to every provider. The real problem is how much of our public services now depends on just one or two US hyperscalers,” he said.

“When the same company runs the cloud, email, documents and collaboration tools, a single failure takes everything down together.”

Nicky Stewart, senior adviser to the Open Cloud Coalition, said the disruption highlighted the economic costs of businesses becoming locked into individual technology providers.

“Over-reliance on a single provider leaves businesses and public services vulnerable to disruption and creates wider economic risks,” she said.

She called on regulators to take action to restore competition and reduce dependence on dominant cloud providers.

Mon, 19 Oct 2026 04:13:59 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 Researchers tracked the passwords 154 people used online for an average of 147 days and found them logging into 26 websites with fewer than 10 unique passwords — roughly 60 percent were reused outright or built from pieces of passwords they were already using elsewhere https://siliconcanals.com/d-researchers-tracked-the-passwords-154-people-used-online-for-an-average-of-147-days-and-found-them-logging-into-26-websites-with-fewer-than-10-unique-passwords-roughly-60-percent-were-reused/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:30:40 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109740

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

]]> Agility’s 284-pound Digit 5 runs for 90 minutes and recharges in nine, a 10-to-1 work-to-charge ratio the company says can deliver more than 20 productive hours a day, with early customer access planned for the first half of 2027 https://siliconcanals.com/n-agilitys-284-pound-digit-5-runs-for-90-minutes-and-recharges-in-nine-a-10-to-1-work-to-charge-ratio-the-company-says-can-deliver-more-than-20-productive-hours-a-day-with-early-customer-access/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 19:00:38 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109721

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

What a 20-hour day actually means

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. Agility has not published an independent customer-floor validation of a Digit 5 working day yet.

Independent reporting on the launch has generally repeated the 20-hour figure as Agility’s claim rather than as a verified outcome. IEEE Spectrum’s Evan Ackerman, reviewing Digit 5, raised a broader doubt about Agility’s underlying assumption that the robot can function as what he called “a more or less effortless drop-in replacement for human labor,” noting he was not sure that had happened yet with any robot, anywhere. The one field metric that has been independently reported involves the previous generation, not Digit 5: at a GXO logistics facility, Digit 4 reportedly 98% accuracy sorting totes over more than 100,000 units, a real operational number — though it speaks to picking accuracy, a separate metric from hours worked per day.

Heavier lifts, taller reach than the last generation

Alongside the battery changes, Agility increased what Digit 5 can physically do. The robot can repeatedly lift loads of up to 50 pounds, which the company describes as a 40 percent jump over Digit 4’s payload, and it can reach items up to 7.2 feet high, up from about 5.5 feet on the previous version, according to Forbes’ coverage of the launch. Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo.
