]]> Any FinTech founder raising in the UK this year will have seen the numbers – according to KPMG’s Pulse of FinTech, investment fell to €2.1 billion (£1.8 billion) in the first half of 2026, down around two-thirds on the same period last year and the lowest since the report began in 2016. Deal count hit a ten-year low. The capital that is still moving is going to AI, and within AI it is going to where the results can be seen fastest. 

Alongside the numbers runs a story: AI has collapsed the sales cycle. Products that used to take a year to sell now close much more quickly, and founders who can’t match the pace should question whether they are building the right thing, or building it in the right country.

For anyone selling into regulated financial services, the story is a little different. Worse, believing the first version of the story is one of the fastest ways to put a good company out of business. Rather than being an issue, the long sales cycle is one of the few things in this market that is a strength and cannot be copied in other industries. 

What a sale actually looks like

Here is what selling AI to a mortgage network, a wealth manager or an advice firm actually involves. It means integrations into systems that were not built with an innovative AI provider in mind. It means lengthy security reviews, several boards and committees, each on its own calendar. It takes several internal sponsors, who need to be won over separately and who do not all agree with each other. You also need trust in the system, trust in the output, and the certifications to prove it, from the usual ISOs through to the new AI equivalent, ISO/IEC 42001.

In the UK at least, the procurement cycle has not sped up. Regulated financial services firms are accountable to the FCA for what their systems decide, a point the regulator’s own Mills Review made quite plainly this summer, and in compliance much of the work is straight-through: a file review or a financial promotions check is either right or it is a regulatory problem. A highly regulated product, with many integrations, that has to pass several boards and several sponsors, moves as slowly as it always has. The sales cycle is long, and that is fine and normal.

Founders arriving with consumer expectations miss this. They hear about the fastest sales cycle in AI without noticing that the companies telling that story are B2C, or B2B businesses that behave like B2C. The lesson travels but the conditions do not.

Surprise is what kills a startup, not the cycle

A long cycle only becomes dangerous when it is a surprise. If a founder expects deals to close in weeks and sizes their future round, their hiring plan and their investor conversations around that timeline, the business can find itself in real trouble by month nine, with nothing closed and no fault in the product. If the cycle is a known quantity from day one, it is simply a parameter to design around.

Designing around it means a few unglamorous things. Size rounds so the money lasts through more than one full cycle. Hire people who have sold into regulated institutions before and know that a fourth meeting with the risk committee is normal rather than a warning sign. Set investor expectations before the term sheet, not after the first missed quarter – and get the certifications done early, because the security review will ask for them either way.

Our investors describe the length of our sales cycle as a moat, and they are right. The entrants it protects against are the naive ones, and in this market they are usually people from inside the industry – they have very good product knowledge, a real understanding of the problem yet no experience of how running a startup works. They build something credible, start selling, and run out of money before the first contract lands. The technology can be copied and the domain knowledge is widely held. Being set up to wait is the hardest thing to copy, because it has to be built into the funding, the hiring and the expectations from the beginning.

Build in the slow lane, and build it here

The other conclusion founders are drawing from the funding numbers is that conditions will be better in the US and while for some companies it is, for others it would be wise to question what they are actually aiming to build before making that move. The most compliance in the world is in Europe, not America: the most demanding regulators, the most complex rulebooks, and the customers with the strongest reason to buy. Leaving the market where your problem is most prominent, because the deals there take longer, is a strange trade. The US may not be the answer for everyone.

The slow lane has three things going for it. There are fewer competitors, because most cannot afford to wait and many of those that do try, fail. The customers you win stay, because a firm that has just spent a year taking you through three committees has no appetite to repeat the exercise with someone else. And the market rewards the one thing that is hard to fake: a company designed, from its first round, to survive the wait.

FinTech is not dying. Parts of it are, but companies using AI to do work that firms could not do before are growing quickly but selling slowly. The nine-month deal is not a flaw in regulated FinTech. It is the entry fee, and the founders still standing in two years will have paid this on purpose.

]]> Swiss SpaceTech startup SWISSto12 and French startup UNIVITY are advancing Europe’s ambitions for sovereign satellite communications after successfully completing a Critical Design Review (CDR) for two active antenna systems designed to deliver 5G connectivity from space.

The milestone brings the companies closer to demonstrating broadband and direct-to-device connectivity through a single satellite architecture, combining European satellite manufacturing expertise with a homegrown approach to space-based telecommunications infrastructure.

The collaboration brings together two startups that have attracted significant investment in 2026.

Switzerland-based SWISSto12 secured €73 million in January from European Space Agency member states for its HummingSat programme, and then closed a €61 million Series C in July. While Paris-based UNIVITY raised €27 million in April from Blast, Expansion, the Deeptech 2030 fund managed by Bpifrance on behalf of the French State, and two family offices.

Emile de Rijk, CEO and founder of SWISSto12, says: “UNIVITY set us an ambitious schedule; reaching Critical Design Review in less than one year was possible due to SWISSto12’s proprietary and differentiated payload and antenna technology and a vertically integrated delivery model. It’s a significant milestone for the program and the start of the next phase as we move into hardware production and an extensive verification and acceptance campaign.”

Founded in 2011 by Emile de Rijk as a spin-off from his doctoral research at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne (EPFL), SWISSto12 specialises in satellite payloads, antenna systems and compact geostationary satellites, using proprietary manufacturing technologies including 3D printing. UNIVITY, founded in 2022 by Charles Delfieux and previously known as Constellation Technologies & Operations, is developing a Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) satellite constellation designed to enable telecom operators to extend their existing 5G services into space.

At the centre of their collaboration are two active phased-array antennas being developed by SWISSto12 for UNIVITY’s 5G non-terrestrial network (NTN) demonstration satellites. The first, an S-band direct radiating array, is designed to connect standard 5G smartphones directly to satellites. The second, a Ka-band antenna operating at 26 GHz, will support broadband services and feeder links connecting satellites with terrestrial infrastructure.

By integrating both capabilities into a single satellite, UNIVITY aims to enable telecom operators to provide broadband and direct-to-device services under their own brands, complementing existing terrestrial networks rather than replacing them.

The development forms part of UNIVITY’s uniShape programme, supported by France 2030 and the French Space Agency (CNES). The programme aims to demonstrate high-throughput, low-latency 5G connectivity using VLEO satellites, with the longer-term objective of developing a shared, neutral space infrastructure that enables European and international telecom operators to maintain greater control over their connectivity services.

For SWISSto12, the partnership puts its HummingLink antenna and payload technologies to work on a European connectivity project. The company manufactures passive radiating antenna components through 3D printing, integrating miniaturised, low-loss filters with beamforming electronics and digital controls. Design and manufacturing are carried out at its Swiss facilities, providing a vertically integrated process from technical specifications through to finished hardware.

Completing the Critical Design Review means the antenna designs can now progress towards hardware production, verification and acceptance testing. While the milestone does not yet demonstrate operational connectivity in orbit, it represents a step towards validating a satellite architecture capable of supporting two different 5G services simultaneously.

Charles Delfieux, Chief Executive Officer of UNIVITY, adds: “Active antennas are central to our 5G payload architecture: they will enable a single satellite to deliver both broadband and direct-to-device connectivity. This dual capability is essential to our ambition of providing telecom operators with a shared space-based infrastructure that complements their terrestrial networks. By reaching this milestone in less than a year, SWISSto12 has demonstrated its ability to support our ambitious roadmap for the uniShape program.”

Their collaboration comes amid broader investment activity across Europe’s SpaceTech sector. In October 2026, EU-Startups highlighted financing announcements exceeding €1.3 billion across a selected group of European companies, including €450 million in primary financing for Finland’s ICEYE and €387 million for Germany’s The Exploration Company.

Investment has also reached smaller startups developing technologies essential to future space operations. Switzerland’s Stellar Alpina raised €3.8 million to develop propulsion systems for in-space mobility, while France’s ArcSpace secured more than €2 million to advance technologies for satellite servicing and repair.

Against this backdrop, the SWISSto12–UNIVITY collaboration illustrates how European startups can combine specialised technologies to develop more independent space infrastructure. Rather than relying on a single company to manufacture satellites, develop payloads and operate connectivity services, their partnership brings together complementary capabilities across borders.

Their progress could help establish whether Europe can turn its growing investment in SpaceTech into infrastructure that provides greater technological and commercial autonomy.

]]> Every startup faces the same squeeze: big ambitions, small team and limited budget. Free open-source software, which can be used, modified, and redistributed under its license, can help founders ease the squeeze. It lets a small startup build products that once required a large engineering department.

But a shortcut is not a strategy. To make good use of open source, founders must decide what they should build themselves, what to borrow, and which skills their team needs to retain. Here is what to consider, from saving time and standing out to staying secure and talking to investors.

Saving time

Microsoft’s Edge browser shows how this can work. I co-authored a study of its move to Chromium, the open-source engine also behind Google’s Chrome, found faster releases and closer alignment with Chrome’s supported web features. Edge remained Microsoft’s own product, on a shared foundation. For founders, the question is how much development work a shared foundation can save, and what trade-offs come with it.

Artificial intelligence offers a similar shortcut. Free toolkits such as TensorFlow and PyTorch help developers build AI applications. “Open-weight” models, such as Meta’s Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen, let teams download an AI system that has already been trained and adapt it, rather than start from scratch.

But open-weight does not necessarily mean open source. Founders should read the license carefully: downloading a model does not necessarily provide access to its training data or unrestricted rights to sell products built on it.

Before committing, startups should build a small prototype around a real customer task. A polished demo can hide missing features, thin documentation or fiddly integration work. Founders should also factor in the costs of computing power and upkeep. Access to the code lets teams tailor software or run it in a customer’s own systems, provided they have the skills and resources to manage it.

Standing out

If competitors can use the same technology, a startup needs to give customers a reason to choose its product. That might mean specialist features, smoother links with the systems customers already use, or reliable support. Founders can use the development time saved to find out what customers value enough to pay for.

Take an AI tool for manufacturers. It could pair a widely available model with a factory’s equipment records and tests designed around how engineers work. Tying the technology to a real job can make a product useful even when the model underneath is available to everyone.

Some companies make money from their own open code. Strapi, a French startup, offers a free content management system and charges for extra features and support. Founders who publish their code need to be equally clear about what customers pay for. They also need to allow time for users’ questions, documentation and outside contributions.

Keeping expertise in-house

Startups need staff who understand how the product works and can change it. In research I led on German firms, I found that product innovation was strongest among companies that outsourced a moderate amount of IT work. In related research I co-authored, we found that excessive reliance on outsourcing raises the risk of intellectual-property infringement.

The practical question for founders is which skills they need to retain as they draw on outside work. Early choices can become expensive to reverse. A team learns one framework; data takes on its format, and other parts of the product grow around it.

Before the business relies on a critical component, the team should test how easily it could be replaced. Design decisions and the ability to investigate failures should stay within the team. When working with outside developers, founders should agree who owns the work and what stays confidential.

Engineers also need time to experiment. If all their effort goes into stitching together other people’s software, they may struggle to build the know-how needed for the startup’s next product.

Maintenance and security

Joining an open-source community can help a startup’s developers learn. Research on larger companies found that contributors got more value from using open source, partly through feedback from other developers.

An active community can help spot and fix problems, but security still needs an owner inside the startup. 

The Open-Source Security Foundation advises tracking outside components, checking their origins and maintenance, and monitoring newly discovered vulnerabilities. Someone within the startup should be responsible for testing and installing updates.

Some popular projects rely on a single volunteer. Paid support may be worthwhile for critical components, while startups publishing their own code also need time for handling security reports and maintaining new versions.

Making the case to investors

Founders should show what the head start delivered, whether they have a working product, paying customers, or evidence of demand. They should explain what they didn’t have to build because they used open source, and what they developed themselves.

Our study found that US startups that engaged with outside projects on GitHub, a popular code-sharing site, were more likely to have raised their first funding round. The link was stronger for novel technologies and weaker in crowded markets. However, the research does not imply that publishing open source code alone will win over investors.

Founders should be ready to explain their own contribution to the product, the cost of maintaining it and how they would manage problems with a critical dependency. The test is whether open source helps them build something customers value while leaving the team able to maintain and improve it.

Founded in 2026 by Aistis Šimaitis, Alexander Blessing, and Christian Garrett, Onodrim, like Palantir, takes its name from The Lord of the Rings: the Elvish term for the tree-like Ents, creatures roused to go to war. Šimaitis, co-founder and CEO, is a former adviser to the Lithuanian government and one of Palantir’s first hires in Europe in 2013. Blessing, co-founder and CTO, previously served as a Forward Deployed Engineer at Palantir and was closely involved in developing and deploying Palantir’s flagship Foundry software platform, used by companies and governments to streamline data and digitise workflows. Garrett, Partner at 137 Ventures, is also a co-founder.

Onodrim acquires controlling stakes in established European defence, aerospace, and industrial businesses, particularly small and medium-sized, founder-led family companies. It then scales them up using permanent capital, technology, and business development expertise. The company also encourages existing founders to remain and help grow their businesses as part of the Onodrim group. It expects to announce its first acquisitions in the coming months.

“Europe has no shortage of exceptional companies. The challenge has been access to the resources needed to help them grow at the scale and speed the moment demands. We are bringing permanent capital, technology and world-class operators to Europe’s best companies, giving them the resources to expand, compete and strengthen the continent’s defence industrial base,” said Šimaitis, co-founder and CEO of Onodrim.

European defence companies are sitting on record order backlogs following the continent’s sharp increase in military spending after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine over four years ago. Most of these companies are struggling to expand capacity fast enough to meet government orders. Onodrim says the market is not only under significant pressure but it is also an opportunity for an operator to plug the gap and build Europe’s defence sovereignty.

“Our approach at Onodrim is rooted in long-term partnership and collaboration. We believe Europe’s industrial champions are built by investing in great businesses, empowering the people behind them and giving them the resources to grow for the long term,” said Blessing, co-founder and CTO, Onodrim

The fresh capital will fund Onodrim’s acquisition programme. It is also expanding its European presence by opening Onodrim Germany in Munich and Onodrim Italy in Turin, joining its existing offices in Amsterdam, London and Vilnius. The company says it has already identified several targets but declined to name them. Additionally, Onodrim has flagged supply chain bottlenecks in areas including propulsion systems for drones, sensing and radar, energetics used in explosives, and aero-structures as priority areas.

]]> Calogena, a French nuclear startup developing a small modular reactor (SMR) designed to supply low-carbon heat to district heating networks, has secured €40 million.

The funding came in the form of a grant from the European Commission’s Innovation Fund ,and it marks the first time that European funding has been given to an SMR earmarked for the direct construction of a commercial facility.

“This funding marks a major milestone for Calogena. Having developed our technology and brought it to industrial scale, we are now entering the construction phase of our first commercial reactor,” said Julien Dereux, Executive Chairman of Calogena.

Calogena was founded in 2021 as a subsidiary of Groupe Gorgé, a Paris-based high-tech industrial group with approximately 3,500 employees and €600 million in revenue. The company is developing a 30-thermal-megawatt, water-cooled SMR specifically designed to decarbonise district heating networks.

Its reactor is based on pool-type research reactor technology, a design proven in hundreds of installations worldwide. It operates at low temperature (100°C) and low pressure (6 bar), less than a bicycle tyre, making it simpler and safer to operate than conventional power reactors.

Another strength of Calogena’s SMR is its compact footprint, requiring just 3,000 square metres of land and under 1,000 square metres of building. The design also does not require major water or electricity supply, and refuelling requires only one lorry delivery every two years. Each module can supply heat to around 20,000 households and produces less than 80ml of nuclear water over a lifetime of use.

The grant follows more than €50 million already secured under France’s national industrial strategy programme, France 2030, which helped the company develop its technology and bring it to industrial readiness. 

The €40 million grant will be used to fund the construction of Calogena’s first commercial reactor in Pierrelatte, which would serve as the company’s inaugural commercial reference project. The company says the town will receive locally produced, low-carbon heat, an alternative to the carbon-intensive and largely imported energy sources that currently account for nearly one-third of Europe’s total energy demand. 

“The European Commission’s support confirms the maturity of our project and its potential to address one of Europe’s major energy challenges: producing local, low-carbon, cost-competitive heat at scale while strengthening energy sovereignty. Pierrelatte would be our first commercial reference and should pave the way for wider deployment across Europe,” added Dereux.

In addition to the Pierrelatte project, the company is also pursuing projects across Europe and is in contention to supply more than fifteen reactors in Finland, where it opened a subsidiary in 2025. In June, Calogena signed a cooperation agreement with Veolia, a European leader in district heating, to explore the deployment of its SMRs across Central and Eastern Europe.

“To make better decisions, data access must be immediate and actionable. Europe and many of its global partners lack this capability today. We at Marble are determined to close this gap, and Cherry’s trust helps us achieve this faster,” said Robert Hook, co-founder and CEO of Marble Imaging.

Marble highlighted that although VHR imagery is a core input for security and commercial intelligence, Europe and many of its partners rely on non-European providers. “This makes them vulnerable to being cut off from coverage over key areas of interest, as materialised in Ukraine or the Strait of Hormuz, creating massive economic as well as security knowledge gaps,” it stated. 

Marble is therefore setting up Germany’s first commercial constellation of very-high-resolution (VHR) satellites. The German startup is also building an AI-powered analytics platform that converts multi-source data into insights. It also notes that as Marble’s constellation scales, the interplay of these segments will create a uniquely well-trained AI solution that delivers actionable decision support for users in the defence, civil security, and critical infrastructure sectors, and beyond.

AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ Aerospace Global News Sun, 15 Nov 2026 13:07:01 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cropped-AGN_Icon_Jet-32x32.png AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ 32 32 Exclusive: Düsseldorf’s Asian network ambitions hindered by aircraft delivery delays https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/exclusive-dusseldorf-asian-ambitions/ Sun, 15 Nov 2026 13:07:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56807 In an interview, SVP Aviation Henning Pfisterer discusses the airport's Asian network ambitions and the arrival of La Compagnie's New York route.

The post Exclusive: Düsseldorf’s Asian network ambitions hindered by aircraft delivery delays appeared first on AGN.

]]> Düsseldorf Airport’s (DUS) long-haul network has shrunk considerably compared to 2019. It has taken steps to rebuild it, with La Compagnie announcing it would introduce an all-business class flight to New York from next spring.

It will use its Airbus A321LRs to fly the service beginning April 2027, capturing higher-yielding premium demand from the region, including from neighbouring countries.

Rebuilding a long-haul network is no easy feat, and adding new destinations is even harder – but talks are progressing well for DUS, SVP Aviation Henning Pfisterer tells Aerospace Global News in an interview. However, he shares that aircraft delivery delays are hindering its network growth ambitions.

Asian growth plans and 777X delivery delays

Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, Düsseldorf Airport had links to several destinations in Asia. Cathay Pacific flew to Hong Kong, All Nippon Airways to Tokyo Narita, Air China to Beijing and Singapore Airlines to Singapore.

Lufthansa Group’s low-cost branch Eurowings also offered A330 flights to Bangkok. The airline no longer operates long-haul services as these have been shifted to the newly-created Discover Airlines which offers flights exclusively out of Lufthansa’s Frankfurt and Munich hubs.

DUS hopes to recover part of its Asian network, including services to Tokyo Narita. Pfisterer points out that the return of a service to Japan depends largely on slot availability, bilateral traffic rights and capacity constraints at Tokyo’s Narita Airport.

All Nippon Airways continues to prioritise growth from Haneda Airport and will do so through fiscal year 28, it said earlier this year. From FY29, it will take advantage of Narita Airport’s planned expansion which will increase takeoff and landing capacity to 500,000. It hopes to grow by a factor of 1.7x. Aviation Week reports that its focus lies on growing US and Europe flights.

“With deliveries of long-haul aircraft being delayed, there is currently no opportunity to serve this route, but we hope to see it return in the coming years,” Pfisterer said, referencing the airport’s discussions with ANA on the topic.

All Nippon Airways is awaiting deliveries for Boeing 777X aircraft, originally meant to begin service with them in 2021. This would potentially free up lower-capacity jets (such as the 787) for a return to Düsseldorf.

He confirmed that the return of the Tokyo connection was possible with another airline too, but did not comment further.  Japan Airlines is the other major long-haul operator out of Tokyo.

“We also aim to get maybe one or two direct services to the big Asian hubs,” he added. “My vision for the future is that in the coming years we are linked to one, two or three Asian hubs, and from there ensuring connections within Asia, to Australia and the broader Pacific region.”

He confirmed that talks were in progress, but 777X delivery delays were a “challenge”. “There are some talks in progress, but there is still the issue of long-haul aircraft availability. We’re somewhere in the pipeline with a couple of carriers.”

When asked whether he was hinting at Cathay Pacific or Singapore Airlines, he acknowledged that both were natural candidates given their respective networks and the markets Düsseldorf is looking to reconnect with.

The airport also wants to be connected to markets it may not previously have had experience with. 

“We spoke with Vietnamese carriers and we see potential for future connections,” he said.

La Compagnie brings New York back to the DUS network

La Compagnie is expanding its network which has historically been focused on connecting France and Italy with Newark with its all-business class configured aircraft. Supported by the arrival of its third A321LR next year, its new Düsseldorf-Newark connection marks its first foray into the German market.

Pfisterer describes the connection as “vital” for the whole region. “New York and Tokyo are basically the most important connections we need to build back,” he said, reflecting on the impact of the pandemic. DUS last had regular flights to the Big Apple until March 2020 with Eurowings, data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows. Since 2022, Condor has offered a handful of charter services in September and October each year.

DUS has also previously had all-business class flights to New York with PrivatAir on behalf of Lufthansa in the early-2000s.

“La Compagnie studied the market very intensively and, as a niche carrier with a premium product, identified a lot of premium potential here. Also, we have very strong corporations. We are the economic powerhouse of Europe. We have numerous blue-chip companies in our catchment.”

Düsseldorf Airport’s target market is not limited to Germany. It is actively promoting its position in the Dutch market. Pfisterer expects around 10% of La Compagnie’s Newark customers to come from the Netherlands.

“Currently we have about 1.6 million Dutch passengers per year, and we’re continuing to see strong growth in this market. So Düsseldorf is growing as a departure point for Dutch passengers, particularly from the provinces close to the German border.

Leisure and VFR markets see strong growth

Its catchment area is also what drove its ability to offer new services to Curaçao, a country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. “It gives Dutch travelers a new travel option on a well-established route to a well-established destination, and at the same time it brings a new destination to the German market,” Pfisterer explains.

The Middle East conflict also had a considerable impact on the airport’s network, though Pfisterer assures that this is not a “structural challenge.” 

He added: “We have seen demand recovering, and we’re already back in stable operations. What is missing a little bit is cruise tourism, because the Gulf region – Dubai, Doha – used to be ports of origin for German cruise ship operators.”

Instead, there has also been a surge to destinations across the Western Mediterranean, Egypt and Türkiye. Sharm el-Sheikh is returning with TUI, joining Corendon which has a strong Egyptian network using its four based aircraft. Air Cairo, Nesma Airlines and Nile Air are also growing their Düsseldorf services.

Düsseldorf Airport is also maintaining its position as a strong hub catering to Visiting Friends and Relatives (VFR) traffic. It was the first European airport to regain links to Syria (with LEAV Aviation). FlyCham and Eurowings are both expected to begin Damascus flights soon. Pfisterer highlights that it is the only airport in Central Europe with links to two destinations in Libya: Tripoli and Benghazi.

Frankfurt’s proximity and traffic rights pose challenges for long-haul growth from Düsseldorf

Nearby Frankfurt Airport (FRA) is Germany’s largest air hub, home to both Lufthansa and Condor. It boasts an expansive long-haul network with flights to almost every corner of the globe. From Düsseldorf, railway connections are particularly convenient. 

Pfisterer concedes that this proximity is “definitely a challenge.”

“We have some leakage, where passengers go by surface transport to Frankfurt and embark on their long-haul flights that are not available from Düsseldorf. Another challenge is bilateral traffic rights. Certain markets cannot be connected with Düsseldorf because of restrictions under bilateral air services agreements,” he continues.

“Certain routes are limited by the number of frequencies and the number of points of entry in Germany. So we are effectively prevented from accessing certain markets that are very important to us, as airlines tend to prioritise the hubs.”

However, he adds that as passengers prefer to avoid surface transportation, there is a desire to grow the number of nonstop connections from Düsseldorf.

]]> The world’s top 5 fastest business jets in 2026 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/top-5-fastest-business-jets-2026/ Sun, 15 Nov 2026 11:59:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56286 For business executives, entrepreneurs and high-profile travellers, these five aircraft offer an exceptional combination of speed, comfort and convenience.

]]> Speed is one of the most impressive achievements in modern business aviation. Today’s private jets combine extraordinary performance with luxurious interiors, advanced technology and the ability to travel thousands of miles without stopping to refuel.

For business executives, entrepreneurs and high-profile travellers, these aircraft offer an exceptional combination of speed, comfort and convenience. But which business jets are the fastest in the world?

From Bombardier’s record-breaking Global 8000 to Gulfstream Aerospace’s impressive G800, manufacturers are continually pushing the boundaries of aviation performance. Here, Aerospace Global News explores the top five fastest business jets, ranked from fastest to slowest according to their published maximum operating speeds.

1. Bombardier Global 8000 – Mach 0.95

The Bombardier Global 8000 takes the number one position as the fastest business jet currently in service. With a maximum operating speed of Mach 0.95, equivalent to approximately 729 mph (1,173 km/h) under standard sea-level conditions, it represents the pinnacle of modern business aviation.

Manufactured by Canadian aerospace company Bombardier, the Global 8000 has been designed for travellers who demand exceptional speed without compromising on long-distance capabilities.

One of its most impressive features is its remarkable range of approximately 8,000 nautical miles, allowing it to connect major international destinations with fewer interruptions. It also features four distinct living spaces, offering passengers plenty of room to work, relax and sleep during longer journeys.

The aircraft’s advanced cabin technology, sophisticated flight systems and luxurious interior make it particularly attractive to international business travellers.

The Global 8000 has also attracted attention for its flight-testing achievements, reaching Mach 1.015 during testing. Although this was a test-flight milestone rather than its certified operating speed, it demonstrated the aircraft’s impressive aerodynamic capabilities.

Key specifications:

  • Maximum operating speed: Mach 0.95
  • Approximate range: 8,000 nautical miles
  • Passenger capacity: Up to 19
  • Category: Ultra-long-range business jet

For travellers seeking the ultimate combination of speed, range and luxury, the Global 8000 sets an impressive benchmark.

2. Gulfstream G800 – Mach 0.935

Taking second place is the Gulfstream G800, one of the most advanced long-range business jets produced by American manufacturer Gulfstream Aerospace.

With a maximum operating speed of Mach 0.935, the G800 can travel at approximately 717 mph (1,154 km/h) under standard sea-level conditions. Its performance places it among the fastest private aircraft available.

Speed, however, is only part of its appeal. The G800 has an impressive maximum range of approximately 8,200 nautical miles, making it one of the longest-range business jets in the industry.

Its spacious cabin can accommodate passengers across multiple living areas, creating an environment suitable for working, dining and resting during intercontinental flights.

Gulfstream has also incorporated advanced avionics and flight-deck technology to support operational efficiency and enhance pilot awareness.

The G800 is particularly appealing to multinational business leaders and organisations that regularly require long-distance international travel.

Key specifications:

  • Maximum operating speed: Mach 0.935
  • Approximate range: 8,200 nautical miles
  • Manufacturer: Gulfstream Aerospace
  • Passenger capacity: Up to 19
  • Category: Ultra-long-range business jet

Although slightly slower than the Global 8000, the G800 offers an exceptional combination of range, performance and passenger comfort.

Also read: Gulfstream G800 completes longest and fastest flight in business aviation history Also read: Gulfstream G800 completes longest and fastest flight in business aviation history

3. Gulfstream G700 – Mach 0.935

Another impressive aircraft from Gulfstream, the G700, shares the same published maximum operating speed of Mach 0.935 as the G800. This places it firmly among the world’s fastest business jets, offering exceptional performance alongside one of the industry’s most luxurious cabins.

The G700 has a maximum range of approximately 7,750 nautical miles and is capable of high-speed cruising at Mach 0.90.

One of its biggest selling points is its exceptionally spacious interior. The aircraft features up to five living areas, allowing passengers to enjoy separate spaces for business meetings, dining, relaxation and sleeping.

Its cabin also benefits from Gulfstream’s advanced environmental technology, designed to provide a comfortable atmosphere during long-haul journeys.

/i

For businesses that regularly transport senior executives, clients and international teams, the G700 offers an attractive balance between speed and comfort.

Key specifications:

  • Maximum operating speed: Mach 0.935
  • Approximate range: 7,750 nautical miles
  • Manufacturer: Gulfstream Aerospace
  • Passenger capacity: Up to 19
  • Category: Ultra-long-range business jet

While the G700 matches the G800 in maximum operating speed, the G800 has the advantage in published maximum range.

4. Cessna Citation X+ – Mach 0.935

The Cessna Citation X+ deserves a place among the fastest business jets ever produced. Despite being a smaller aircraft than the Global and Gulfstream flagship models, it delivers remarkable performance.

With a maximum operating speed of Mach 0.935, the Citation X+ matches the G700 and G800, demonstrating that extraordinary speed is not exclusive to large, ultra-long-range business jets.

Manufactured by Textron Aviation, the Citation X+ was developed as an evolution of the original Citation X, which earned a reputation as one of the fastest civilian aircraft in the world.

Its maximum range is approximately 3,460 nautical miles, making it better suited to shorter international journeys and transcontinental travel than some of the larger aircraft featured in this ranking.

The Citation X+ also offers a comfortable cabin designed for business travellers who value efficiency and performance.

Although production ended in 2018, it remains an important aircraft in the history of private aviation and continues to attract attention for its exceptional speed.

Key specifications:

  • Maximum operating speed: Mach 0.935
  • Approximate range: 3,460 nautical miles
  • Manufacturer: Cessna (Textron Aviation)
  • Passenger capacity: Typically up to 12
  • Category: Super-midsize business jet

For those who prioritise speed over maximum cabin size and intercontinental range, the Citation X+ remains an impressive example of aeronautical engineering.

5. Bombardier Global 7500 – Mach 0.925

Completing our list is the Bombardier Global 7500, another outstanding aircraft that combines impressive speed with exceptional long-distance capabilities.

With a maximum operating speed of Mach 0.925, approximately 710 mph (1,142 km/h) under standard sea-level conditions, it is slightly slower than the aircraft ranked above it.

However, the Global 7500 is far more than simply a fast business jet. It has a maximum range of approximately 7,700 nautical miles, making it capable of connecting major international destinations without requiring a fuel stop in suitable operating conditions.

Its cabin is divided into four living spaces, providing passengers with opportunities to work, relax, dine and sleep comfortably. The aircraft also features Bombardier’s advanced wing design, sophisticated flight systems and carefully designed cabin environment.

The Global 7500 has established itself as a popular choice among high-net-worth individuals, corporate organisations and international travellers who require a combination of performance and luxury.

Key specifications:

  • Maximum operating speed: Mach 0.925
  • Approximate range: 7,700 nautical miles
  • Manufacturer: Bombardier
  • Passenger capacity: Up to 19
  • Category: Ultra-long-range business jet

Although it takes fifth place in this ranking, the Global 7500 remains one of the most capable and prestigious business jets in the world.

Which is the fastest business jet?

Modern business aviation has reached extraordinary levels of performance, with the fastest aircraft capable of operating at speeds approaching the speed of sound. The Bombardier Global 8000 currently leads the field with its maximum operating speed of Mach 0.95, followed by several aircraft capable of reaching Mach 0.935.

However, speed is not the only consideration when choosing a private jet. Range, passenger capacity, cabin comfort, operating costs and overall performance all play important roles.

For those who want the fastest aircraft available, the Global 8000 is an exceptional choice. Meanwhile, the Gulfstream G800 and G700 offer outstanding alternatives, combining impressive speed with luxurious long-distance travel.

Ultimately, these five aircraft demonstrate just how far business aviation has progressed, offering travellers an increasingly sophisticated way to move around the world.

]]> Who is responsible for cleaning up space? https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/responsible-for-cleaning-up-space Sun, 15 Nov 2026 09:59:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56336 Thousands of defunct satellites and fragments of debris are putting Earth's orbital environment under increasing pressure. The aerospace industry is therefore facing a growing challenge over responsibility, accountability and the cost of keeping space safe.

The post Who is responsible for cleaning up space? appeared first on AGN.

]]> Space is getting busier. Every year, more satellites are launched to support communications, navigation, weather forecasting and Earth observation. The problem is, not everything sent into orbit comes back down.

Thousands of defunct satellites, discarded rocket stages and fragments from past collisions are now travelling around Earth at enormous speeds. Even a small piece of debris can damage an operational spacecraft.

As launch activity increases, so does the risk.

Who is legally responsible for space debris?

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty provides the starting point. It establishes that countries are responsible for their national space activities, whether carried out by government agencies or private companies. Governments therefore retain responsibility for commercial operators operating under their jurisdiction.

The 1972 Liability Convention also explains who is responsible if a space object causes damage. Countries are held responsible for damage caused on Earth, while damage to other spacecraft in orbit depends on who is at fault.

However, neither treaty says countries must remove old satellites or clear up space debris. While there are rules about who is responsible when damage occurs, there is no clear international system requiring countries or companies to clean up after themselves.

What are the rules around preventing space debris?

For now, preventing additional debris is more practical than trying to remove everything already in orbit.

The United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space has developed guidelines encouraging operators to minimise debris, avoid collisions and safely dispose of spacecraft at the end of their missions.

Regulators are also tightening the rules around space debris. NASA recommends that certain spacecraft are removed from orbit within 25 years of completing their missions.

In 2022, the US Federal Communications Commission went further, introducing a five-year limit for certain satellites in low Earth orbit.

With more companies launching large groups of satellites, these rules are becoming more and more important. However, requirements are still very different between countries, making it harder to ensure space debris is managed consistently across the industry.

Wargames in space: US rehearses satellite ‘dogfight’ across three orbits Wargames in space: US rehearses satellite ‘dogfight’ across three orbits

Can we clean up Earth’s orbit?

Satellites are rarely designed to be collected once they stop working, and approaching an uncontrolled object travelling at orbital speed requires sophisticated technology.

The European Space Agency’s ClearSpace-1 mission, developed with Swiss company ClearSpace, is intended to demonstrate how a dedicated spacecraft can capture and remove debris from orbit.

There are practical and legal obstacles, though. Space objects remain under the jurisdiction and control of their state of registry, meaning permission is generally needed before another country or organisation can remove them. Liability is another concern if a removal attempt damages the object or creates further debris.

Read next: NASA unveils nuclear-powered Moon rover as $1.3bn lunar transport contracts awarded Read next: NASA unveils nuclear-powered Moon rover as $1.3bn lunar transport contracts awarded

Who should pay for cleaning up space?

The financial responsibility remains one of the industry’s biggest unanswered questions. Should governments fund the removal of abandoned satellites, or should operators contribute towards clearing up after their own missions?

A polluter-pays approach would place more responsibility on those creating the debris, potentially encouraging better spacecraft design and end-of-life planning. However, putting such a system into practice would require international agreement on funding, liability and enforcement.

There is also a strong commercial reason to act, with aviation, telecommunications, navigation and weather forecasting all depend on reliable satellite services. Worryingly, a growing debris problem threatens the infrastructure behind them.

Cleaning up space will ultimately require cooperation between governments, regulators, satellite manufacturers and operators. Better disposal planning can limit future waste, while dedicated removal missions could gradually tackle the debris already in orbit.

Space may be vast, but the orbital regions we depend on are not limitless. Although the industry has made significant progress in understanding the problem, the next challenge is agreeing who takes responsibility for solving it.

Japan Airlines, Delta, Air New Zealand, Malaysia Airlines and SAS each found different routes to survival.

]]> Airlines can lose billions and vanish, practically overnight. Others shed aircraft, renegotiate debts and emerge from court protection looking remarkably different.

These airlines prove it is possible for carriers to recover from financial troubles and become major international competitors again. They survive through state intervention or private investment, and face years of rebuilding.

Five airlines’ turnaround stories show different ways an airline turnaround can succeed. Japan Airlines returned to the stock market less than three years after filing for corporate rehabilitation. Delta Air Lines emerged from Chapter 11 and reshaped its network. Air New Zealand survived largely thanks to a government rescue. Malaysia Airlines and SAS have also restructured for survival.

Japan Airlines: From bankruptcy to stock market relisting

Japan Airlines entered corporate rehabilitation proceedings on 19 January 2010 after years of losses and a mounting debt burden. For one of Asia’s best-known flag carriers, the filing represented a dramatic reversal.

The airline’s restructuring involved debt forgiveness, a complete reduction in existing shareholder capital and an injection of ¥350 billion (roughly $3.9 billion at the time) from the Enterprise Turnaround Initiative Corporation of Japan. 

The airline reduced its size, withdrew from unprofitable activities and changed management practices. It also pursued a stronger focus on costs and route profitability, instead of trying to preserve the scale of the pre-bankruptcy business.

JAL completed its corporate reorganisation proceedings in March 2011. On 19 September 2012, it returned to the Tokyo Stock Exchange, about two years and eight months after filing.

JAL later said its market capitalisation at relisting was ¥687.3 billion and that the public investment had been repaid without a loss on the capital injection. However, creditors and existing shareholders bore substantial losses.

Today, Japan Airlines is a profitable, publicly listed airline, although its earnings, like those of all carriers, are still vulnerable to fuel costs and exchange-rate movements. For the six months to September 2026, JAL reported record first-half revenue of ¥1,098.9 billion and EBIT of ¥70.1 billion. Revenue rose 11.7% year on year, while EBIT fell 36% as expenses increased. 

Delta Air Lines: Chapter 11 and a new competitive position

Delta filed for Chapter 11 protection in the United States on 14 September 2005, facing intense competition, high costs and a difficult financial position.

Chapter 11 allowed the carrier to continue flying while renegotiating obligations and implementing a reorganisation plan. Delta used the process to restructure costs and develop a more internationally oriented network.

The airline emerged on 30 April 2007 after approximately 19 months in bankruptcy protection. At the time, it reported that its restructuring had delivered $3 billion in annual financial improvements. Its emergence was supported by $2.5 billion in exit financing.

Delta also reported four consecutive quarters of operating profits, including $155 million in the first quarter of 2007. The airline later merged with Northwest Airlines in 2008, enlarging its global network.

Delta is now one of the major US network airlines and continues to generate substantial profits. 

In October 2026, it reported September-quarter operating revenue of $20.2 billion and GAAP pre-tax profit of $1.1 billion, despite elevated fuel costs. It also projected approximately $4.5 billion in pre-tax profit for the full year, showing how far the business has come since its Chapter 11 restructuring.

Air New Zealand: A government rescue preserves the flag carrier

Air New Zealand’s crisis stemmed from its investment in Ansett Australia, which quickly became a major burden. Ansett entered voluntary administration in September 2001. The global downturn in aviation following the September 11 attacks compounded the financial pressure.

The New Zealand government intervened to prevent the loss of its national carrier. In November 2001, it finalised an NZ$885 million recapitalisation package that gave the Crown an 82% ownership stake.

The government also committed to make up to NZ$150 million in additional funding available before June 2003 if required. Officials emphasised the airline’s importance to tourism, international connectivity and the wider economy.

Air New Zealand survived, refocused its business and continued to operate as a publicly listed carrier. The state later reduced its holding, including a sell-down in 2013.

The airline reported a NZ$242 million net loss for the year ended June 2026, compared with a NZ$108 million profit a year earlier. Revenue increased to NZ$7.0 billion, but higher fuel and maintenance costs and continuing engine-availability problems weighed on earnings. 

Malaysia Airlines: Rebuilding after tragedy and financial distress

Malaysia Airlines’ restructuring followed years of financial difficulties and the devastating loss of flights MH370 and MH17 in 2014. Those tragedies intensified an already difficult period for the airline.

A recovery plan launched in 2014 led to the establishment of a new operating company in 2015, with Malaysia Aviation Group later serving as the parent organisation. The process included changes to staffing, capacity and the airline’s financial structure.

The COVID-19 pandemic forced another round of negotiations. In 2021, the group completed a recapitalisation and restructuring process that it said would reduce liabilities by more than RM15 billion. 

The airline group later reported its first net profit after interest and tax since its 2015 formation: RM766 million for 2023. It recorded a further RM54 million net profit in 2024, marking a third consecutive year of positive operating profit. Malaysia Aviation Group faced maintenance and aircraft-delivery disruptions, which forced capacity cuts.

Its 2024 net profit benefited from a RM426 million reversal of earlier impairment charges. Still, Malaysia Airlines’ restructuring and improved commercial performance have brought financial stability.

Malaysia Aviation Group reported net profit after interest and tax rose to RM137 million in 2025, from RM54 million in 2024, while revenue reached RM14.5 billion. The group has also received high preliminary ratings for a proposed sukuk financing programme, although the ratings agency has highlighted continuing financial constraints, including high borrowings and negative shareholders’ funds. 

SAS: A new ownership structure for Scandinavia’s airline

SAS began voluntary Chapter 11 proceedings in the US in July 2022 as part of its SAS FORWARD transformation programme. The Scandinavian airline was dealing with heavy debt, aircraft costs and pressure to improve its competitiveness.

SAS also undertook company reorganisation proceedings in Sweden and negotiated changes to aircraft leases, creditor obligations and financing.

On 28 August 2024, SAS announced that it had completed both processes. The company said it had restructured more than $2 billion of debt and secured a $1.2 billion investment package comprising $475 million in new equity and $725 million in secured convertible debt.

The new ownership group included Castlelake, Air France-KLM, Lind Invest and the Danish state. SAS also moved from Star Alliance to SkyTeam, changing its strategic airline partnerships and financial structure.

The airline’s former shareholders received no recovery under the restructuring plan, and their shares were cancelled.

For the year ended 31 October 2025, SAS’s revenue rose 7% to SEK 49.1 billion, and the airline recorded an operating profit of SEK 3.03 billion, compared with an operating loss of SEK 2.11 billion a year earlier. It carried 28.3 million passengers, up 12%, and reported a SEK 517 million net profit.

As of November 2026, SAS is also expanding its Copenhagen hub, with additional intercontinental and European capacity announced for summer 2027.

]]> Disruption to flights is easing after the United States lifted its nationwide ground stop on Friday that left airports overloaded with aircraft and passengers stranded. Authorities pointed to ageing Air Traffic Control infrastructure to be associated with the issue, with US Transport Secretary Sean Duffy calling for more funding to upgrade systems.

Flights were grounded as of 20:54 UTC (15:54 EST), with all departures halted and en-route international arrivals allowed on a “case by case basis.” Any further departures from around the world to the US were cancelled. Services were allowed to resume as of 01:15 UTC (20:15 EST).

Friday’s disruption was the longest ground stop in the United States since 9/11.

What went wrong?

Answers are few and hard to come by. In a press conference, Duffy shared that his teams were “still working on the details of what went wrong today” and was unable to specify the root cause. He did point to ageing ATC infrastructure, adding that all “new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down.”

Authorities noted “instability for our radar and our communications and our centers and our TRACONs across the country” at 20:36 EST (15:36 EST). Less than 20 minutes later, flights were grounded. All 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs) that handle high-altitude flying were impacted.

The Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON) are FAA-run facilities that handle aircraft between 2,500 and 10,000 feet around busy areas surrounding airports. Once below 2,500 feet, aircraft are passed on to the airport towers. As mentioned by Duffy, these TRACON facilities were also impacted. The FAA lists 25 spread across the United States.

What happens to planes already in the air when the FAA grounds all flights? What happens to planes already in the air when the FAA grounds all flights?

“We didn’t lose all telecom we didn’t lose all radar but that instability, because of abundance of caution and making sure we keep the American fliers safe, we did the ground stop,” Duffy clarified. “But we were going to allow those lifesaving movements to still occur, as well as with law enforcement as well.”

There are two types of telecommunications services supporting air traffic management. This includes the older Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) technology and the more advanced Internet Protocol (IP)-compatible service.

Talking about the TDM technology that was central to the errors, Duffy says that its routers were “overloaded with data” and began producing “inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down.”

He added: “And our new IP switches did not go down; it’s the old hardware that went down.”

Duffy calls for more investment in ATC infrastructure

Duffy called for more investment into the overall ATC architecture, arguing that the President’s request for $30 billion from congress may need to be adjusted: “The President has asked for $30 billion. I want $50 billion.”

“And I think the question for the American people is, do you want your congress to fund this? President Trump has asked for the money, he’s asked the congress on a bipartisan approach to say, give us the resources to build a state-of-the-art air traffic control system.”

He highlighted the non-partisan aspect of the issue, arguing that it is “American” rather than Democrat or Republican. “Now, if you look to the past administrations going back 25 years, $15 billion has been given to the FAA to fix this air traffic control system. And guess what? Barely anything was done.”

He cautioned against a “patchwork fix” adding that the system is critical for “every single family.”

The administration already sought $12.5 billion in funding to help renovate the air traffic systems. “But that’s a partial funding,” Duffy says.

“I want new towers. We should also invest in many of the airports around the country that, frankly, many of them are embarrassing. Let’s get the money.”

]]> Why are there not enough planes? The global commercial aircraft shortage explained https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/commercial-aircraft-shortage-explained/ Sat, 14 Nov 2026 15:06:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56116 While the main manufacturers have enormous order books, the delivery of new commercial aircraft continues to struggle to keep pace with demand. But why?

The post Why are there not enough planes? The global commercial aircraft shortage explained appeared first on AGN.

]]> The global aviation industry is experiencing an unusual problem. Airlines want more aircraft, passengers are returning to the skies in growing numbers, and manufacturers have enormous order books. Yet the delivery of new commercial aircraft continues to struggle to keep pace with demand.

Airbus, Boeing and other manufacturers are facing a combination of production restrictions, component shortages, engine supply problems and difficulties recruiting skilled workers. The result is a growing backlog of aircraft orders, leaving airlines waiting longer for new aeroplanes and forcing them to reconsider their fleet expansion plans.

The scale of the problem is considerable. According to figures published by ADS Group, the global commercial aircraft backlog reached a record 17,037 aircraft in July 2026. Although manufacturers are delivering more aircraft than in previous years, the gap between airline demand and available production capacity remains significant. So why can’t the industry simply build more aircraft?

A record backlog and a manufacturing challenge

Commercial aircraft production is a complicated industrial process involving thousands of businesses across numerous countries. Although Airbus and Boeing are responsible for final assembly, they depend on an extensive network of suppliers to provide everything from engines and landing gear to electrical systems, avionics and specialist materials.

An aircraft cannot be completed until all its essential components are available. This means that a shortage affecting even one relatively small, but critical part can delay the delivery of an entire aeroplane.

Increasing production is therefore not simply a question of opening another assembly line or asking factory workers to build more aircraft. Every part of the manufacturing network must be capable of supporting the higher production rate. This is one of the biggest challenges facing the aerospace industry as it attempts to reduce its enormous order backlog.

Engine shortages are holding back production

One of the most significant restrictions is the availability of aircraft engines. Modern commercial jet engines are among the most technologically advanced products manufactured anywhere in the world.

They contain highly specialised components that must withstand extreme temperatures, pressures and mechanical stresses while operating reliably over many thousands of flight hours.

Producing additional engines requires specialist manufacturing equipment, precision engineering and extensive testing. Engine manufacturers must also support existing airline fleets by supplying replacement parts, maintenance services and overhauled engines.

This creates competing demands on production capacity. While airlines need engines for newly manufactured aircraft, they also need spare engines and replacement components to keep existing aircraft flying.

Other essential systems, including avionics, landing gear and electrical equipment, face similar supply challenges. Finding alternative suppliers is not a quick solution because aviation components must undergo rigorous testing and certification before they can be used.

The problem starts with raw materials

Behind the shortages of components lies another challenge: securing the raw materials needed to manufacture them.

Aircraft construction relies on specialist materials such as titanium, advanced aluminium alloys, high-performance metals and carbon-fibre composites. These materials are selected for their strength, durability, weight and ability to withstand demanding operating conditions.

Some materials are sourced from relatively limited geographical areas, making the supply chain vulnerable to political tensions, trade restrictions and transport disruption.

The 2026 Global Aerospace Supply Chain report, produced by Roland Berger in collaboration with ADS Group and European aerospace associations, highlights the scale of this problem. Around 80% of surveyed aerospace companies anticipate constraints involving critical raw materials.

Increasing supplies is difficult because new sources must be identified, production facilities established and materials qualified for aerospace use. Manufacturers cannot simply substitute one material for another without demonstrating that it meets the required engineering and safety standards.

For aircraft manufacturers, this means that material shortages can affect production long before components reach the final assembly line.

A shortage of skilled aerospace workers

The availability of experienced workers is another factor limiting aircraft production. Building commercial aircraft requires highly trained engineers, technicians, machinists, quality-control specialists and production managers.

Many roles require years of experience, particularly where workers are responsible for manufacturing safety-critical components.

Although manufacturers and suppliers are recruiting, expanding the workforce takes time. New employees need extensive training, while experienced staff possess specialist knowledge that cannot easily be replaced.

The aerospace sector must also compete with other industries for engineering talent. As production targets increase, companies need to invest in apprenticeships, technical education and workforce development to ensure they have the people required to support future manufacturing programmes.

Without sufficient skilled workers, additional factories and machinery will not necessarily translate into higher aircraft production.

Smaller suppliers face financial pressures

Much of the aircraft manufacturing supply chain is made up of smaller specialist businesses. These companies may produce relatively inexpensive components, but their products are essential to the completion of an aircraft.

Increasing production can place considerable financial pressure on these suppliers. They may need to purchase new machinery, expand factory space, recruit additional employees and hold larger stocks of materials before receiving payment for increased production.

For smaller businesses operating on limited margins, financing this expansion can be difficult. Uncertainty over delivery schedules also makes financial planning more complicated.

Suppliers need confidence that higher production levels will be sustained before committing substantial investment.

This creates a potential bottleneck for the entire industry. Even if Airbus or Boeing has the capacity to assemble more aircraft, production can remain restricted if a smaller supplier cannot deliver components quickly enough.

Strengthening the financial resilience of these businesses is therefore an important part of resolving the aircraft shortage.

Why aircraft production cannot increase overnight

Aircraft manufacturers operate within one of the most tightly regulated industrial environments in the world. Every aircraft must meet demanding safety, reliability and quality requirements before it can enter commercial service.

Any changes to manufacturing processes, production facilities or component suppliers must be carefully assessed. Alternative materials and components may require extensive testing and certification before they can be approved for use.

This makes aerospace manufacturing very different from industries where production can be increased relatively quickly by adding another production line.

There is also a difference between temporarily increasing output and maintaining a higher production rate over several years. Sustainable expansion requires reliable suppliers, sufficient materials, trained employees and consistent quality control throughout the manufacturing process.

The 2026 Global Aerospace Supply Chain report found that more than 70% of surveyed companies considered themselves well prepared for increased production. However, continuing shortages and capacity constraints demonstrate that preparedness does not automatically translate into additional aircraft deliveries.

How the shortage affects airlines and passengers

The consequences of restricted aircraft production extend well beyond the manufacturers themselves.

Airlines typically order new aircraft several years before they are required. These orders allow carriers to plan fleet replacement, introduce new routes, increase flight frequencies and improve fuel efficiency.

When deliveries are delayed, those plans can be disrupted.

Airlines may have to retain older aircraft for longer than originally intended, extend existing aircraft leases or acquire additional capacity through the second-hand market. Older aircraft can require more maintenance and generally consume more fuel than newer equivalents, potentially increasing operating costs.

The shortage can also restrict airline growth. A carrier expecting to receive several new aircraft may be unable to introduce planned routes or increase frequencies if those aircraft arrive months or even years behind schedule.

Passengers may experience the consequences through reduced seat availability on popular routes and potentially higher ticket prices where demand exceeds available capacity. However, airfares are also influenced by fuel prices, competition, airport charges and wider economic conditions.

Aircraft leasing companies are affected too. With fewer new aircraft entering the market, airlines may compete more strongly for available leased aircraft, increasing the importance of existing fleet assets.

Is there any light at the end of the tunnel?

Despite the challenges, there are signs of improvement. ADS figures show that 794 commercial aircraft were delivered worldwide during the first seven months of 2026, representing the strongest January-to-July delivery performance since 2018.

This suggests that manufacturers and their suppliers are making progress in restoring production capacity. However, the industry still has a considerable distance to travel before deliveries can match the enormous volume of outstanding orders.

Airbus, Boeing and their suppliers will need to continue investing in manufacturing facilities, equipment, workforce training and more resilient supply chains.

Greater diversification of material sources, improved cooperation between manufacturers and suppliers, and better long-term production planning should also help reduce the risk of future disruption.

Ultimately, the objective is not simply to produce more aircraft in the short term, but to establish a manufacturing system capable of delivering higher output reliably and consistently.

The commercial aircraft shortage is an industry-wide problem

The commercial aircraft shortage is not the result of a single manufacturing failure or one company struggling to meet its targets. It reflects a combination of interconnected problems affecting the entire aerospace industry.

Engine shortages, limited supplies of specialist materials, component manufacturing constraints, workforce gaps and financial pressures on smaller suppliers are all restricting production.

For airlines, this means longer waits for new aircraft and difficult decisions about fleet planning. For manufacturers, it means finding ways to increase output without compromising safety, quality or reliability.

The record order backlog demonstrates the strength of demand for commercial aviation, but turning those orders into completed aircraft will require sustained investment across the global aerospace supply chain.

The industry is making progress, but the aircraft shortage is unlikely to disappear quickly. Until manufacturers and their suppliers can increase production together, airlines and passengers will continue to feel the effects of a global industry struggling to build enough aircraft to meet demand.

What went wrong, and what might have been?

]]> Military aviation has produced some incredible aircraft, but not every promising design makes it into service.

Rising costs, political decisions and changing defence priorities have ended some fascinating projects. Here are four that could have taken military aviation in a very different direction.

Avro Canada CF-105 Arrow: The Mach 2 interceptor that never entered service

Developed to protect North America against Soviet bombers, the Avro Arrow was intended to replace the RCAF’s ageing CF-100 Canuck.

With a projected top speed of Mach 2, advanced aerodynamics and an integrated weapons and fire-control system, it was a major achievement for Canada’s aerospace industry.

The Arrow first flew on 25 March 1958, but its future was short-lived. On 20 February 1959, the Canadian government cancelled the programme, citing rising costs and changing assessments of the Soviet threat, particularly the growing importance of ballistic missiles.

Five pre-production aircraft had flown, while a sixth, intended for the more powerful Orenda Iroquois engines, remained unfinished. Another 31 were in production.

Cancellation came just as the Arrow was beginning to show what it could achieve.

BAC TSR-2: Britain’s ambitious supersonic strike aircraft

Britain’s BAC TSR-2 was designed to replace the RAF’s Canberra bombers with a high-speed strike and reconnaissance platform capable of penetrating heavily defended territory.

It was expected to reach Mach 2.35 at altitude and Mach 1.1 at low level, using terrain-following navigation to avoid enemy defences. Its planned weapons included conventional and nuclear payloads.


Prototype XR219 first flew on 27 September 1964 and completed 24 flights by the end of March 1965. Despite promising results, technical challenges involving the engines and undercarriage remained.

The programme was cancelled in April 1965 amid escalating costs and political disagreements. Britain subsequently pursued the American F-111, only to abandon that purchase too.

The TSR-2 remains one of British aviation’s most intriguing missed opportunities.

Sukhoi T-4: The Soviet Mach 3 bomber that never reached its potential

The Soviet Union was developing its own high-speed contender in the Sukhoi T-4, nicknamed the Sotka. Conceived as a strategic strike and reconnaissance aircraft, it was built around the ambition of reaching Mach 3 and taking on high-value targets, including naval task forces.

Extensive use of titanium and stainless steel helped withstand the extreme temperatures associated with sustained supersonic flight. It also incorporated fly-by-wire flight controls, an impressive feature for the early 1970s.

The prototype first flew on 22 August 1972, with Vladimir Ilyushin, a prominent Soviet test pilot and son of aircraft designer Sergei Ilyushin, at the controls. However, it completed just ten test flights, reaching approximately Mach 1.3 rather than its intended Mach 3.

Technical complexity, development costs and changing military priorities contributed to its cancellation. The Soviet Union instead favoured Tupolev’s Tu-22M Backfire, a more practical alternative for its strategic strike requirements.

Northrop YF-23: The stealth fighter that lost to the F-22 Raptor

Developed for the US Air Force’s Advanced Tactical Fighter competition, Northrop’s YF-23 offered a distinctive approach to next-generation air superiority. Its rival was Lockheed’s YF-22.

The YF-23 featured diamond-shaped wings and a carefully sculpted airframe to reduce radar visibility. It also demonstrated supercruise, maintaining supersonic speeds without afterburners.

Two prototypes were built: PAV-1, Black Widow II, and PAV-2, Gray Ghost. During testing, the first prototype reached Mach 1.5 in supercruise.

In 1991, the US Air Force chose the YF-22, which became the F-22 Raptor. Northrop’s aircraft never entered production, although its distinctive approach to stealth, range and aerodynamic efficiency still attracts considerable interest.

The lasting legacy of cancelled military aircraft

The Arrow, TSR-2, T-4 and YF-23 came from very different countries and generations, but each challenged contemporary aerospace engineering.

Their stories show that technical excellence alone is not enough to secure a place in military service. After all, political considerations, budgetary constraints and evolving defence requirements can be just as decisive as performance.

Each programme certainly offers a fascinating glimpse into the alternative paths military aviation history might have taken.
