]]> The next challenge for hydrogen aviation: Refuelling before the next flight https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/hydrogen-aviation-refuelling-h2fly-hyprime/ Sat, 14 Nov 2026 10:12:09 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54966 Hydrogen-powered flight is advancing from proving concept feasibility to tackling airport ground operations. European initiatives H2FLY and HyPRIME are currently testing liquid hydrogen refuelling infrastructure and boil-off management to align with standard commercial airline turnarounds.

The post The next challenge for hydrogen aviation: Refuelling before the next flight appeared first on AGN.

]]> Hydrogen-powered aviation is moving beyond proving that aircraft can fly on the fuel, with developers now concentrating on how to refuel them quickly, safely and repeatedly at commercial airports.

Two European programmes are working on different parts of that challenge. Germany’s H2FLY is developing hydrogen-electric propulsion and mobile refuelling systems, while the UK’s HyPRIME project is preparing to test equipment capable of delivering liquid hydrogen at rates relevant to commercial aircraft operations.

In exclusive interviews with Aerospace Global News, representatives of both programmes described the progress made in handling liquid hydrogen, the problems that remain and the changes airports will need before hydrogen-powered aircraft can operate regular services.

For H2FLY, which completed what it describes as the world’s first piloted flight of an electric aircraft powered by liquid hydrogen in 2023, the experience has also changed where the company is concentrating its engineering efforts.

Ralph Muller, H2FLY’s chief executive, said the equipment and procedures needed to handle the fuel on the ground are no longer the fundamental obstacle.

“Through our flight test programme, we have built up the capabilities to handle and refuel liquid hydrogen safely. Taking this to routine airport operations is mainly a matter of time and resources,” Muller told AGN.

“The harder engineering challenge lies in the aircraft-based systems: they have to be lightweight, reliable and cost-efficient enough for commercial operation.”

Refuelling within an airline turnaround

For hydrogen-powered aircraft to operate scheduled services, refuelling must fit into the time an aircraft normally spends on the ground between flights.

Muller said that, depending on the aircraft and its mission, the refuelling process would need to take between 15 and 60 minutes.

“For airline-style operations, refuelling has to fit within a normal commercial turnaround without extending it,” he said. “The required refuelling rate therefore depends on the aircraft size and tank capacity.”

Unlike conventional aviation fuel, liquid hydrogen must be kept at approximately minus 253°C. Its extremely low temperature means that tanks, transfer equipment and refuelling connections require specialised designs.

One way to increase refuelling rates is to cool the aircraft’s hydrogen tank before transferring the fuel.

Muller said this could become part of the normal ground-handling process.

“Pre-cooling the aircraft’s liquid hydrogen tank to cryogenic temperatures before refuelling allows higher flow rates, and this step can be integrated into the turnaround procedure,” he explained.

He also identified common standards for connections and handling procedures as important to making refuelling simpler.

H2FLY plans to demonstrate the third generation of its mobile liquid hydrogen refuelling unit through the European Union-funded GOLIAT project, working with partners from across the aviation industry.

The programme forms part of the company’s efforts to develop equipment that can eventually support routine aircraft operations rather than individual flight demonstrations.

HyPRIME prepares to test airport equipment

In the UK, HyPRIME is approaching the challenge from the airport side.

The project is designed to demonstrate that liquid hydrogen can be transported to airports, handled safely and dispensed at flow rates relevant to commercial aviation.

Chris Tye, senior technical project coordinator for HyPRIME, said the aviation industry has already spent considerable time examining the requirements for hydrogen infrastructure.

“The industry is under no illusions about the challenges associated with introducing hydrogen at airports, and the collective knowledge about how to do it has been growing steadily through activities across the world including feasibility studies, techno-economic studies and regulatory work,” he told AGN.

The next task is to test the equipment under conditions that resemble actual airport operations.

“What HyPRIME, and other projects within the DFT zero emission competition, brings is the opportunity to advance the industry into physical testing of commercially relevant assets, in commercially relevant environments,” Tye said.

The programme is developing a mobile liquid hydrogen refuelling system using high-flow-rate cryogenic equipment.

It aims to demonstrate refuelling within operationally relevant turnaround times, although the final performance targets are still being developed alongside airport operating procedures.

Tye said HyPRIME is addressing two central requirements: whether hydrogen refuelling can work in an airport environment and whether the equipment can eventually be operated economically.

“The project will demonstrate that liquid hydrogen can be safely transported to airports and dispensed at commercially relevant flow rates for aviation, while also showing how, through systems integration, this can support decarbonisation of the wider airport ecosystem through use of boil-off gas in ground equipment, simultaneously reducing waste and improving economics.”

The project is working with Bristol and Birmingham airports on operational concepts that will help define the refuelling performance it needs to demonstrate.

What happens to hydrogen that evaporates?

One of the difficulties of handling liquid hydrogen is that some of the fuel can evaporate as heat enters the storage or transfer system.

This is known as boil-off. Unless managed, the resulting gas can represent lost fuel and must be handled safely.

Tye identified boil-off management and refuelling speed as two of the most important technical issues still facing airport hydrogen systems.

“Boil-off gas is unavoidable in LH2 systems; left unmanaged it is a safety hazard, an economic loss of fuel, and an indirect emissions source,” he warned.

HyPRIME intends to capture the gas and put it to use elsewhere at the airport.

Its mobile liquid hydrogen refuelling system is designed to recover boil-off for use in ULEMCo’s hydrogen tow truck and GeoPura’s hydrogen power units.

The approach is intended to reduce venting and improve the overall efficiency of the hydrogen supply system.

HyPRIME will also examine the safety requirements associated with liquid hydrogen storage and refuelling. Its work includes dedicated cryogenic tank design and staged hazard identification, hazard and operability studies, and quantitative risk assessment.

Tye said the project would draw on ZeroAvia’s existing liquid hydrogen operational experience and its participation in UK Civil Aviation Authority sandbox trials at Exeter.

H2FLY, meanwhile, believes careful planning can substantially reduce the amount of hydrogen lost during routine airport operations.

“Boil-off is predictable and can be managed. In scheduled operations, today’s ground operations make it possible to largely avoid it,” Muller said.

He explained that airlines already have detailed information about their schedules and expected fuel consumption. That information could help airports decide when hydrogen needs to be produced, liquefied and made available for refuelling.

“Hydrogen can be produced locally, and gaseous hydrogen can be liquefied on site in line with flight schedules. Supply follows demand rather than sitting in storage,” he added.

Such arrangements would require hydrogen production and supply to be coordinated with aircraft operations, particularly at airports where demand may initially be limited.

How airports would have to change

Neither H2FLY nor HyPRIME expects every airport to require large permanent hydrogen facilities from the outset.

Muller said the infrastructure could develop alongside the aircraft entering service.

“In the early phase, flexible, mobile solutions allow airports and operators to start operations without large fixed installations,” he said.

“As fleets grow, these will be replaced step by step by permanent infrastructure, with dedicated liquid hydrogen storage and a reliable supply.”

Hydrogen could be produced at airports using electrolysers and then liquefied, or delivered from external suppliers by truck or pipeline.

Airports would also need new ground-handling procedures, personnel training and safety zones adapted to hydrogen.

For HyPRIME, the choice of infrastructure would depend heavily on the location.

Tye said hydrogen could arrive by tanker, be delivered as a gas and liquefied at the airport, or be produced and liquefied on site.

“The optimum approach will depend on the airport’s requirements, real estate and region’s availability of power and options for hydrogen production,” he said.

At larger scales, he expects dedicated storage and liquefaction facilities, together with mobile refuellers or cryogenic pipelines, to become necessary.

HyPRIME is also examining what these different arrangements would cost. One of its planned outputs is a techno-economic model covering capital expenditure and operating costs for a representative mid-sized airport.

The project intends to use actual testing data to identify which parts of the infrastructure have the greatest effect on commercial viability.

“Airports and investors will need confidence not only that the technology works, but also that the associated CAPEX and OPEX are commercially viable,” Tye said.

Smaller hydrogen aircraft expected first

H2FLY’s experience has also influenced its expectations for the types of aircraft likely to adopt hydrogen propulsion first.

Muller said the industry initially concentrated heavily on the possibility of developing large hydrogen-powered aircraft. He does not regard that early ambition as misplaced, but believes the transition will take longer and proceed in smaller steps.

“What proved too optimistic was the idea that aviation could make that leap in one step,” he said. “The lessons learned since then have led to a strategic shift: we see hydrogen aviation developing step by step, starting with smaller aircraft, where the technology, certification and infrastructure are less complex, and scaling up from there.”

H2FLY expects smaller hydrogen-electric aircraft to begin entering service in the early 2030s, with larger aircraft following around 2045.

These are the company’s expectations rather than confirmed commercial service dates. The company is continuing to develop the propulsion systems that would support that progression. Its HY4 aircraft has completed several flight demonstrations, including the liquid hydrogen-powered flights in 2023.

Since then, Muller said H2FLY has tripled the power density of its systems. “Our HY4 aircraft, demonstrated in flight several times, showed early on what is possible, and since then we have tripled the power density of our systems,” he said.

The company develops most of its key components in-house, allowing it to work on the weight and performance of the complete propulsion system rather than treating individual components separately.

Muller said improvements in electrification and digital technologies, including developments in drones and air taxis, have also benefited hydrogen-electric propulsion.

Nevertheless, reducing weight, improving reliability and bringing down costs remain central to its work.

What comes after the airport trials?

HyPRIME’s immediate objective is to produce evidence from operating the refuelling equipment, rather than simply demonstrating that the individual technologies work.

The project has identified four areas against which it intends to measure progress: refuelling performance, hydrogen losses, operational efficiency and costs.

It plans to examine repeatable refuelling cycles, including filling, transporting and dispensing liquid hydrogen, as well as recovering boil-off gas under different environmental conditions. The results will feed into its economic modelling.

Further demonstrations at different airports, continued work with airlines and airport operators, and the development of regulatory and certification frameworks would follow a successful trial.

Tye said HyPRIME is intended to provide information that can guide future infrastructure investment in the UK and elsewhere.

For H2FLY, the next steps include demonstrating its latest mobile refuelling equipment through GOLIAT while continuing to improve the aircraft systems needed for commercial hydrogen-electric flight.

Both programmes are working towards the same practical requirement: aircraft must be able to arrive, refuel and depart without hydrogen handling becoming an obstacle to scheduled operations.

The technology has already flown. The next challenge is making it part of an ordinary day at an airport.

The post SpaceX aborts Super Heavy catch as Starship reaches orbit and deploys 26 satellites appeared first on AGN.

]]> SpaceX abandoned an attempt to catch its returning Super Heavy booster during Starship’s 15th test flight on Friday, sending the giant rocket stage into the Gulf of Mexico, where it erupted in flames on reaching the water.

The setback ended the first half of the company’s ambitious plan to recover both stages of Starship during a single mission.

However, the upper stage successfully reached orbit, deployed 26 Starlink satellites and continued a flight that could culminate in the first-ever catch of a spacecraft returning from orbit on 14 November.

The 124-metre-tall Starship lifted off from SpaceX’s Starbase facility in South Texas at 4:47 p.m. local time on 13 November (22:47 GMT), powered by 33 Raptor engines on its Super Heavy booster.

The initial climb proceeded as planned. About two and a half minutes after launch, the upper stage ignited its engines and separated from the booster. The manoeuvre, known as hot-staging, allows the spacecraft to begin accelerating towards orbit before the two stages have completely separated.

Super Heavy then turned towards Starbase, where SpaceX had intended to catch it using two enormous mechanical arms or chopsticks, attached to the launch tower.

Instead, the company called off the catch and directed the booster towards a designated area offshore. It reached the water approximately six and a half minutes after liftoff, with a large fireball visible during its final descent.

SpaceX did not immediately explain what prompted the decision to abandon the catch.

“Well, that certainly isn’t the news that we had hoped to hear for today,” SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice said during the live broadcast.

The company stressed that protecting the launch infrastructure and surrounding area takes priority over attempting a recovery.

“Safety is always the number one priority, and we’re still testing out things that we haven’t done before on these vehicles, and so we are prioritising making sure that we can perform each maneuver safely,” a SpaceX commentator said during the livestream.

Why SpaceX wanted to catch the booster

Starship consists of two sections. The Super Heavy booster provides the power needed to lift the rocket off the ground, while the upper stage, called Ship, carries satellites or other payloads into space.

Unlike conventional rockets, which generally discard their boosters after launch, SpaceX wants both sections to return to the launch site for reuse.

Its recovery system uses two large arms, nicknamed chopsticks, to support the descending rocket at specially designed attachment points.

The booster must slow almost to a hover and position itself precisely between the arms. Computers monitor its speed, position and other operating conditions before allowing the catch to proceed.

SpaceX has already demonstrated the technique three times, beginning with Flight 5 in October 2024. However, Friday’s mission involved a newer Version 3 booster equipped with Raptor 3 engines.

The company had not previously caught this upgraded version.

The aborted recovery does not necessarily mean the booster suffered a mechanical failure. SpaceX has built safety checks into the flight sequence that allow the vehicle to be diverted away from the tower if the conditions for a catch are not met.

The precise reason for Friday’s diversion has yet to be established. Although SpaceX has not yet disclosed the cause, multiple reports indicate an onboard anomaly triggered an automatic abort of the catch sequence.

Starship reaches orbit and deploys satellites

While the booster recovery ended unsuccessfully, the upper stage continued its journey.

Its engines completed the initial ascent burn just over eight minutes after liftoff. A second engine firing, lasting approximately 20 seconds, placed the spacecraft into an orbit about 275 kilometres above Earth.

“We’ve got a nominal orbit insertion, so Starship now in orbit around Earth for the second time ever,” SpaceX commentator Dan Huot said during the webcast. “That’s a really great moment.”

The spacecraft subsequently deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, completing the operation over approximately 42 minutes.

These larger satellites are designed to increase the capacity of SpaceX’s broadband network. According to the company, the latest batch can add roughly one terabit per second of network capacity, equivalent to approximately ten Falcon 9 launches carrying the smaller Starlink V2 satellites.

Three of the satellites also carry cameras intended to photograph Starship’s heatshield and other external components while the spacecraft is in orbit.

The images will help engineers assess whether the vehicle is in suitable condition for its planned return.

A second catch attempt remains possible

The most demanding part of Flight 15 may still lie ahead.

Starship is expected to spend approximately 22 and a half hours in flight, completing about 14 orbits before returning towards Texas.

If SpaceX approves the manoeuvre, the spacecraft will fire an engine to leave orbit, descend through the atmosphere and attempt to return to the launch tower.

Unlike the booster, which operates for only a few minutes before returning, the upper stage must survive the intense heat generated as it re-enters Earth’s atmosphere at orbital speed.

Its heatshield consists of thousands of protective tiles. SpaceX has introduced changes to improve tile retention and reduce the risk of extremely hot gases penetrating gaps in the shielding.

During descent, Starship uses four movable flaps to control its orientation. Near the ground, its engines must restart to slow the spacecraft and rotate it into a vertical position before the tower arms can catch it.

No Starship upper stage has previously been recovered this way.

SpaceX has established several decision points during the mission when engineers can abandon the return-to-launch-site plan and direct the spacecraft towards an ocean splashdown instead.

The final decision will depend on the condition of its heatshield, engines and other critical systems.

If approved, the catch is scheduled for approximately 21:17 GMT on Saturday, November 14.

Why the test matters

Friday’s flight follows Starship’s first successful orbital mission in September, when Flight 14 deployed another 26 Starlink V3 satellites.

The latest mission is intended to demonstrate that Starship can carry operational payloads into orbit while progressing towards recovery of both rocket stages.

SpaceX already routinely reuses the first stages of its smaller Falcon 9 rockets. Starship is designed to go further by recovering the upper stage as well.

That capability is central to the company’s plans for frequent satellite launches and future missions to the Moon and Mars.

NASA has also selected a version of Starship to support its Artemis lunar programme, which will require the spacecraft to demonstrate reliable flight, manoeuvring and landing capabilities.

]]> What is a ground stop and why does the FAA order one? https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/what-is-a-ground-stop-faa-why-order-one Sat, 14 Nov 2026 00:07:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56727 A single disruption can send delays rippling through the aviation network. Here's a closer look at the decisions behind keeping aircraft on the ground and how controllers manage the knock-on effects.

The post What is a ground stop and why does the FAA order one? appeared first on AGN.

]]> The last thing you want to hear when you’re about to depart is that a ground stop is in effect. But for airlines, airports and air traffic controllers, it is an essential tool for maintaining safety and managing congestion across the aviation network.

A ground stop is an air traffic management measure issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) that temporarily prevents aircraft from departing for a specified airport or location. Instead of allowing flights to take off and potentially join an already congested arrival queue, airlines are instructed to hold affected aircraft at their departure airports.

It does not necessarily mean the destination airport has closed. Arrivals may continue, depending on the circumstances, while flights already airborne are managed by air traffic controllers.

Read next: All US flights grounded nationwide over major communications issue Read next: All US flights grounded nationwide over major communications issue

Why might the FAA order a ground stop?

The most recent ground stop occurred on 13 November 2026, due to a communications issue with air traffic control.

However, weather is another common reason the FAA might issue a ground stop. Thunderstorms, heavy snow, strong winds and poor visibility can significantly reduce an airport’s capacity. An airport that normally handles dozens of arrivals an hour may suddenly be able to accept far fewer.

When this is the case, keeping aircraft on the ground is often safer and more efficient than allowing them to depart, only to spend extended periods in holding patterns or divert to alternative airports.

Operational problems can also trigger a ground stop. Runway closures, aircraft incidents, equipment failures and cyber attacks can all affect an airport’s ability to handle normal traffic volumes.

Staffing shortages may also play a part. If an air traffic control facility cannot safely manage the expected number of aircraft, the FAA can restrict incoming traffic until sufficient capacity is restored.

How does a ground stop work?

The FAA’s Air Traffic Control System Command Center coordinates traffic management across the United States, working with individual air traffic control facilities to respond to changing conditions.

When a ground stop is introduced, airlines receive instructions specifying the affected airport, which flights are covered and the anticipated duration. Departures are held at their origin airports, with airlines adjusting schedules and passenger arrangements accordingly.

Ground stops are not necessarily issued for a fixed period. The FAA regularly reassesses conditions and can extend, modify or lift restrictions as circumstances change.

Read: How much extra fuel does an airliner need to carry in case something goes wrong? Read: How much extra fuel does an airliner need to carry in case something goes wrong?

Ground stop vs ground delay programme

Although often confused, these are two distinct traffic management measures.

A ground stop temporarily prevents specified flights from departing for an affected destination. A ground delay programme takes a less restrictive approach, assigning departure delays and calculated arrival times to regulate the flow of traffic.

The FAA uses both to balance demand with available airport and airspace capacity. The appropriate measure depends on the severity and nature of the disruption.

Keeping the skies moving safely

Ground stops can cause significant inconvenience, particularly when disruption spreads across multiple airports. However, they are an important part of managing an aviation system in which a problem at one location can have consequences hundreds of miles away.

By controlling departures before congestion becomes unmanageable, the FAA can give airports and controllers the breathing space needed to restore normal operations.

Unfortunately for passengers, it may mean a rather longer wait at the gate. But for the wider aviation network, it is a practical way of putting safety ahead of schedule.

 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-dest-hero__label{display: block;
 font-size: 13px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-dest-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-dest-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}
.sie-dest-hero__title{font-size: clamp(32px, 5vw, 56px);
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #ffffff;
 margin: 0 0 14px;
 line-height: 1.1;
 letter-spacing: -0.02em;
 max-width: 800px;}
.sie-dest-hero__tagline{font-size: clamp(15px, 2vw, 19px);
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 margin: 0 0 28px;
 max-width: 1100px;
 line-height: 1.5;
 font-weight: 400;}
.sie-dest-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 8px;
 padding: 12px 24px;
 background: #1E56B0;
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 15px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 6px;
 text-decoration: none;
 transition: background 0.2s;}
.sie-dest-hero__cta:hover{background: #163e82;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-dest-hero__actions{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 12px;
 margin-top: 4px;}
.sie-dest-hero__cta--secondary{background: transparent;
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);
 color: #fff;}
.sie-dest-hero__cta--secondary:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border-color: #fff;
 color: #fff;}
.sie-country-heart--hero{position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 padding: 10px 20px;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 600;
 gap: 8px;
 border-radius: 6px;
 min-width: unset;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.92);
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);
 box-shadow: none;
 backdrop-filter: none;
 white-space: nowrap;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-family: inherit;
 line-height: 1;
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;}
.sie-country-heart--hero:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.22) !important;
 border-color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.9) !important;
 color: #fff !important;
 transform: none;}
.sie-country-heart--hero.voted{background: rgba(239, 68, 68, 0.28) !important;
 border-color: #f87171 !important;
 color: #fff !important;}
.sie-country-heart--hero.voted i{color: #fca5a5;}
.sie-country-heart--hero .sie-country-heart__count{display: none;
 font-size: 12px;
 opacity: 0.85;}
.sie-country-heart--hero.has-votes .sie-country-heart__count{display: inline;}
.sie-dest-body{max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px 80px;}
.sie-dest-stats{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 0;
 background: #f0f4fb;
 border: 1px solid #d4e0f5;
 border-radius: 10px;
 margin: 32px 0;
 overflow: hidden;}
.sie-dest-stat{flex: 1;
 min-width: 150px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 18px 20px;
 border-right: 1px solid #d4e0f5;}
.sie-dest-stat:last-child{border-right: none;}
.sie-dest-stat__label{font-size: 11px;
 font-weight: 600;
 color: #505a6b; 
 text-transform: uppercase;
 letter-spacing: 0.06em;}
.sie-dest-stat__value{font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #003B73;
 line-height: 1.3;}
.sie-admreq-cta-strip .sie-dest-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 0.5rem;
 padding: 0.75rem 1.5rem;
 background: #fff;
 color: #1d4ed8;
 border-radius: 6px;
 font-weight: 700;
 text-decoration: none;
 font-size: 0.97rem;
 transition: opacity 0.2s;}
.sie-admreq-cta-strip .sie-dest-hero__cta:hover{opacity: 0.9;}

.leo-confirm-yes:hover{background:#1E3354 !important}
.leo-confirm-no{background:#fff !important;background-image:none !important;color:#12233D !important;border:1px solid #C3C9CE !important;border-radius:4px !important;box-shadow:none !important}
.leo-confirm-no:hover{border-color:#12233D !important}
.leo-sat{background:#F4F2ED !important;background-image:none !important;border:1px solid #E4E0D8 !important;border-radius:6px !important}
.leo-visit-website{background:#12233D !important;border-radius:4px !important}
.leo-visit-website:hover{background:#1E3354 !important}
.leo-score-pill{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important;border-color:#E4E0D8 !important;border-radius:3px !important}
.leo-ovv2{border-color:#E4E0D8 !important;border-radius:6px !important;box-shadow:none !important}
.leo-ovv2>summary{background:#F4F2ED !important;border-bottom-color:#E4E0D8 !important}
.leo-ovv2-hl{color:#12233D !important;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace !important;font-weight:500 !important;letter-spacing:.06em !important}
.leo-ovv2-toggle{background:#12233D !important;border-radius:4px !important}
.leo-ovv2>summary:hover .leo-ovv2-toggle{background:#1E3354 !important}
.leo-ovv2-mapwrap,.leo-ovv2-tile{background:#FAF8F4 !important;border-radius:4px !important}
.leo-ovv2-filterbar{border-color:#E4E0D8 !important;border-radius:6px !important;box-shadow:none !important}
.leo-ovv2-search:focus{border-color:#12233D !important;box-shadow:0 0 0 3px rgba(18,35,61,.10) !important}
/* "What are you looking for?" composer: site-wide overlay (#slo-, leo-entry-overlay JS)

#slo-backdrop,.lh-chat-backdrop,.lh-chat-overlay.lh-discover-mode .lh-chat-backdrop{background:rgba(18,35,61,.55) !important;backdrop-filter:blur(2px) !important;-webkit-backdrop-filter:blur(2px) !important}
#slo-drawer,.lh-chat-drawer,.lh-chat-overlay.lh-discover-mode .lh-chat-drawer{background:#FAF8F4 !important;background-image:none !important;border-radius:8px 8px 0 0 !important;box-shadow:0 -12px 40px rgba(18,35,61,.25) !important}
.slo-orb,.lh-chat-orb{display:none !important}
.slo-brand,.lh-chat-drawer-brand{background:#12233D;margin:0 -36px 26px !important;padding:16px 36px !important;border-bottom:0 !important}

.slo-title,.lh-chat-drawer-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif !important;font-weight:600 !important;font-size:26px !important;color:#12233D !important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#12233D !important;letter-spacing:-.01em}

.slo-input-wrap,.lh-chat-drawer-inner .lh-input-wrap{background:#fff !important;border:1px solid #C3C9CE !important;border-radius:6px !important;box-shadow:none !important}

 space for unsized images. They were removed — those same images are also
 used as DECORATIVE icons sized purely by CSS (e.g. the Leonardo lynx in
 the chat header), and "height:auto" overrode that sizing and let them
 balloon to full intrinsic size. The real, measured CLS cause is the font
 swap handled above; any genuinely-unsized content image should get
 width/height attributes on the tag itself, not a blanket src selector. */
 /* Homepage auto-playing chat demo: the typing animation appends message
 bubbles and result cards, which used to GROW the demo window and push
 everything below it on every cycle (measured: CLS 0.258 on the
 homepage). Fixed internal heights make the animation play inside a
 constant-size box — newest messages stick to the bottom like a real
 chat, the results tray keeps its space reserved. */
 #lh-demo-chat {
 height: 240px;

 justify-content: flex-end;
 overflow: hidden;
 }
 #lh-demo-flow {
 height: 250px;
 overflow: hidden;
 }

 /* ── Make the search the priority, not an afterthought ────────────────
 Measured before this change at 1440x900: hero 1028px tall, search bar
 top at y=694. Tightened the vertical rhythm and moved the trust row
 below, which lifts the bar roughly 230px — comfortably in view. */
 .lh-hero.lh-hero{padding:clamp(28px,4vw,56px) 0 clamp(32px,4.5vw,64px)}
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-center{gap:clamp(16px,2vw,26px)}
 /* ⚠️ THE CAUSE OF THE BIG EMPTY GAP, and it was mine. The stylesheet sets
 .lh-hero-text{flex:1 1 380px} and .lh-portals{flex:1 1 420px}. Those were
 written for the original ROW layout, where flex-basis is a WIDTH. Turning
 the container into a column silently turned both into fixed HEIGHTS: the
 text box stayed 380px tall although its content ended after 187px, and
 the search row stayed 420px tall although the cards are 195px. That is
 ~420px of enforced emptiness. Resetting the basis is the whole fix —
 never set flex-direction on an inherited flex container without checking
 what flex-basis meant before. */
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-text{flex:0 0 auto}
 .lh-hero .lh-portals--search{flex:0 0 auto}
 .lh-hero .lh-badge{margin-bottom:10px}

 /* ── Results as a responsive grid, not a single strip ──────────────────
 .sie-res-list holds the program cards as direct children (verified live:
 18 cards, one parent, no headers in between), so one grid rule is enough.
 ⚠️ SCOPED TO THE HOMEPAGE ON PURPOSE. .sie-res-list is the shared
 SieFlowView markup — Leonardo renders into it too, with its own
 per-card animation offsets. Re-layouting it globally would change his
 results as a side effect of a homepage fix. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(320px,1fr));gap:16px;align-items:start}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list > .program-card{width:auto;max-width:none;margin:0}

 per country. Each branch carries max-width:560px inside a 798px rail, so
 two never fit and they stack — the "single strip". Releasing the cap and
 tiling the branches gives two country panels per row at this width, and
 more on a wider screen, without touching the cards inside.
 ⚠️ Scoped to .lh-herosearch: Leonardo renders the same flow markup. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branches{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(360px,1fr));gap:18px;align-items:start}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branch{max-width:none;width:100%}
 /* ── The figures strip ────────────────────────────────────────────────
 Serif numerals, monospaced labels, hairline rules, no card, no shadow,
 no colour fill behind each figure. The register of a register. */
 .lh-stats.lh-stats--figures{background:#F4F2ED;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-bottom:1px solid #E4E0D8;padding:0}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stats-grid{max-width:1200px;margin:0 auto;padding:0 clamp(16px,4vw,48px);display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(4,minmax(0,1fr));gap:0}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat{padding:clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) clamp(14px,2vw,28px) clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) 0;border-right:1px solid #E4E0D8;text-align:left;background:none;border-radius:0;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat:last-child{border-right:0}
 /* Every cell except the first gets inner space on its left, so each rule
 sits with equal air on both sides instead of crowding the next figure.

 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat + .lh-stat{padding-left:clamp(18px,2.4vw,34px)}

 /* #6B7A8D measured 3.92:1 against the warm band — under the 4.5:1 that
 11.5px text needs. The cool grey was fine on the old cold background and
 quietly failed when the palette warmed up; #4F5967 measures 6.2:1.
 Worth remembering when warming any other background. */
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat-label{margin-top:8px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:1.3px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#4F5967}

 .lh-inst-body{margin:0 0 26px;font-size:clamp(15.5px,1.4vw,17px);line-height:1.65;color:#C6D2E0;max-width:54ch}

 /* ── Institutional pass, part 2 (2026-11-08, evening) ──────────────────
 Brings the sections below the hero onto the palette and type the hero
 already uses, so the page reads as one document instead of two designs
 stacked on top of each other. Everything here is homepage-only (it lives
 in this template) and is pure CSS: delete this block to revert. */
 /* The page itself: the site-wide body is cold pale blue (#E8F1FA), which
 showed through every transparent section (the institutions carousel and
 the study fields block) as a blue band between warm ones. */
 body.page-id-150{background:#FAF8F4}
 /* ⚠️ THE HEADLINE NEVER WAS SERIF. leonardo-homepage-css.min.css carries
 `.lh-wrap .lh-title{font-family:system-ui !important; font-size:44px
 !important; font-weight:800 !important; color:#003b73 !important}`, so
 the Source Serif rule earlier in this block lost on every device. Only
 !important with equal-or-higher specificity can beat it. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title,.lh-wrap .lh-hero h2.lh-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif !important;font-weight:600 !important;font-size:clamp(34px,4.4vw,58px) !important;line-height:1.08 !important;letter-spacing:-.6px !important;color:#12233D !important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#12233D !important}

 EUROPE") already does that job; the extra pill only added noise. */
 .lh-hero .lh-badge{display:none}

 the screen edge while the centred text did not. Left-aligned, with the
 same 20px gutter as the rest of the page, it matches the desktop. */
 @media(max-width:900px){
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-center{padding-left:20px;padding-right:20px;box-sizing:border-box;text-align:left}

 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title{text-align:left}

 }

 Serif headings and a small monospaced label instead of the rounded blue
 pills, which were the last "app" element on the page. */

 .lh-wrap .lh-section-badge{display:inline-block;margin-bottom:14px;padding:0;background:none;border-radius:0;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;font-weight:500;letter-spacing:1.8px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#8C5A23}
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-sub{color:#4A525C}
 /* Section rhythm: paper / white / paper, so each block has an edge. */

 .lh-wrap .lh-unis{background:#fff;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8}
 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--origins{background:#fff;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8}

 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--countries a[class*="card"],.lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--countries [class*="card"]{border-radius:6px}
 /* ── Study fields block (rendered by [sie_study_fields] after .lh-wrap) ─
 Six bright category colours, gradient pills and a gradient CTA made it

 The branch colours arrive as INLINE custom properties and inline
 backgrounds, so these overrides need !important to apply. Scoped to the
 homepage: the study-field pages keep their colour coding. */
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-weight:600;font-size:clamp(28px,3vw,40px);letter-spacing:-.4px;color:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-subtitle{color:#4A525C}

 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__junction-dot{background:#12233D}

 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-count{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important}

 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-icon{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__leo-link{color:#0B5FA5 !important}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-leonardo{background:#12233D !important;background-image:none !important;border-radius:6px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-leo-btn{background:#fff !important;color:#12233D !important;border-color:#fff !important;border-radius:4px}
 /* Alignment: the search widget carries its own 24px side padding, so the
 bar sat indented from the headline above it; and the trust row was
 centred under a left-aligned column. Both now share the text's edge.
 Only the LEFT padding goes: removing the right one too pushed the
 "AI-enhanced matching" toggle across the seam into the navy side. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-wrap{padding-left:0 !important}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{justify-content:flex-start}
 /* Institution cards: the stylesheet tints each card top a different pastel

 monogram or logo is the only thing that differs between cards. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-card:nth-child(n) .lh-uni-card-top{background:#F4F2ED !important;background-image:none !important;border-bottom:1px solid #EDEAE3}
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-cta{color:#0B5FA5 !important}
 .lh-wrap .sie-dest-hub__name{color:#12233D}
 /* Europe silhouette on the navy side. Present, never loud: a lighter blue

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.
 loading="lazy" means the browser only fetches each image when the
 panel opens and the card enters the viewport — saving ~30 MB of
 upfront image requests on every page that includes this panel. */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-img {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 transform: scale(1.07);
 }
 /* Gradient overlay + text */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-body {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 padding: 10px 12px 10px;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .72) 0%,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .30) 55%,
 transparent 100%
 );
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-name {
 color: #fff;
 font-weight: 700;
 font-size: .92rem;
 line-height: 1.2;
 text-shadow: 0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,.55);
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 display: block;
 color: rgba(255,255,255,0);
 font-size: .75rem;
 margin-top: 2px;
 transition: color .2s ease, transform .2s ease;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 color: rgba(255,255,255,.9);
 transform: translateX(4px);
 }
 /* ── Body-scroll lock ── */
 body.sie-dest-panel-open {
 overflow: hidden;
 }
 /* ── Country interest heart ── */
 .sie-country-heart {
 position: absolute;
 top: 8px;
 right: 8px;
 z-index: 10;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 border: none;
 border-radius: 20px;
 padding: 4px 8px 4px 7px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-size: 13px;
 color: #94a3b8;
 box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.22);
 backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 transition: color .18s, transform .18s, background .18s;
 line-height: 1;
 min-width: 28px;
 justify-content: center;
 }
 .sie-country-heart:hover {
 transform: scale(1.12);
 background: #fff;
 color: #ef4444;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted {
 color: #ef4444;
 background: #fff;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted i {
 animation: sie-heart-pop .35s cubic-bezier(.36,.07,.19,.97);
 }
 @keyframes sie-heart-pop {
 0%   { transform: scale(1); }
 40%  { transform: scale(1.45); }
 70%  { transform: scale(.88); }
 100% { transform: scale(1); }
 }
 .sie-country-heart__count {
 font-size: 11px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: inherit;
 display: none;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.has-votes .sie-country-heart__count {
 display: inline;
 }
 /* ── Trigger button styles (for use in any menu) ── */
 /* Desktop globe icon */
 .se-dest-desktop-btn {
 font-size: 24px;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 transition: transform .2s, color .2s;
 position: relative;
 line-height: 1;
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 padding: 0;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover {
 transform: scale(1.15);
 color: #FFCC00;
 }
 /* Tooltip on desktop */
 @media (min-width: 1024px) {
 .se-dest-desktop-btn::after {
 content: "Study Destinations";
 position: absolute;
 bottom: -30px;
 left: 50%;
 transform: translateX(-50%);
 background: #007BFF;
 color: #fff;
 padding: 4px 8px;
 font-size: 12px;
 border-radius: 5px;
 opacity: 0;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .2s;
 white-space: nowrap;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover::after {
 opacity: 1;
 }
 }
 /* Mobile pill button */
 .se-dest-btn {
 background: #0b3770 !important;
 color: #fff !important;
 }
 .se-dest-btn:hover {
 background: #1e66f5 !important;

<h1 class="title-h1 eac-page-title">Conference on the Future of Europe : the future is in your hands</h1>
<span><span>sandoel</span></span>
<span><time datetime="2021-12-07T08:55:30+01:00" title="Tuesday, December 7, 2021 - 08:55">Tue, 12/07/2021 - 08:55</time>
</span>
<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<p>Follow on Twitter at&nbsp;</p>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__RECTORS_Q1.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>
                    </div>
                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The institution has a clear plan to implement the strategy</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The strategy and policy should include explicit allocation of responsibilities for its efficient implementation to individuals at all levels of the institution, from senior management to the heads of departments, schools and faculties, to academic and administrative staff. This will ensure acceptance and accountability for the strategy. The internationalisation strategy and policy should outline a specific implementation plan that sets out explicitly the financial and human resources available.&nbsp; For example, it is recommended to set up an International Relations Office (IRO) to implement mobility and other international projects.</p><p>As with any other activity, the institutional implementation of the internationalisation strategy is dependent on the people behind the activities. It is highly important for an institution to have staff with the right set of skills and knowledge driving the internationalisation agenda and liaising with international students and staff members. Therefore understanding the development needs of the staff and supporting their professional development should be a high priority for the institution. Such development should focus on both staff engaged in international activities as well as the supporting staff, ensuring the most efficient implementation of international activities and cooperative projects across the institution. For example, trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, project management, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries.                         <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad. The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits. Therefore, it is essential to conduct mobility based on an agreed and signed Learning Agreement. The Learning Agreement should be agreed and signed by all parties (the student, the sending institution and the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise) before the start of the mobility. It is not compulsory to circulate papers with original signatures; scanned copies of signatures or digital signatures may be accepted, depending on the national legislation.</p><p>The EU official templates for Learning Agreements for studies and traineeships are available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm&nbsp;&nbsp;</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Including allocation of responsibility to an academic who has the authority to approve, amend and recognise the Learning Agreements on behalf of the responsible academic body</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The formal procedures for recognising student mobility should clearly and unambiguously set out the responsibilities of an appointed academic, who has the authority, on behalf of the appropriate academic body, to:</p><ul><li>Approve the Learning Agreements,</li><li>Exceptionally amend the Learning Agreements, and</li><li>Recognise the successfully completed activities, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams.</li></ul>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Ensuring that the mobile participant, sending and receiving HEI/organisation/enterprise (i.e. all three parties) sign the Learning Agreement before the start of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad. The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits. Therefore, it is essential to conduct mobility based on an agreed and signed Learning Agreement. The Learning Agreement should be agreed and signed by all parties (the student, the sending institution and the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise) before the start of the mobility. It is not compulsory to circulate papers with original signatures; scanned copies of signatures or digital signatures may be accepted, depending on the national legislation.</p><p>The EU official templates for Learning Agreements for studies and traineeships are available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm&nbsp;&nbsp;</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Including allocation of responsibility to an academic who has the authority to approve, amend and recognise the Learning Agreements on behalf of the responsible academic body</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The formal procedures for recognising student mobility should clearly and unambiguously set out the responsibilities of an appointed academic, who has the authority, on behalf of the appropriate academic body, to:</p><ul><li>Approve the Learning Agreements,</li><li>Exceptionally amend the Learning Agreements, and</li><li>Recognise the successfully completed activities, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams.</li></ul>                      </div>

                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Ensuring that the mobile participant, sending and receiving institution/organisation/enterprise (i.e. all three parties) sign the mobility agreement before the start of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>To ensure effective staff mobility, it has to be based on a signed mobility agreement. The mobility agreement has to acceptable and signed by all parties in advance. There are four key elements set out by the mobility agreement, which are intended to increase the relevance and potential impact of the mobility. These are:</p><ul><li>The overall objectives and academic rationale of the mobility,</li><li>The institutional requirements or strategy, and the mobility's added value in the context of modernisation and internationalisation,</li><li>The activities or teaching programme content to be undertaken by the staff member, and,</li><li>The expected outcomes and impact of the mobility on the professional development of the staff member at both institutions.</li></ul><p>For this to work effectively, there needs to be dialogue and discussion between the three parties prior to the signing of the mobility agreement having agreed the common goals which are acceptable.&nbsp;</p>                      </div>

        <div class="eche-report-section-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-report-full-question-wrapper">

                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q10.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question"> During the mobility, your institution fosters the integration of the incoming mobile participants</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The institution appoints responsible person(s) to deal with practical issues (e.g. social, health, and/or psychological problems)</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution should ensure there are named, visible persons who are responsible for the practical issues associated with integrating mobile students. This visibility should be ensured through introduction to this function during the Welcome / Orientation period and be detailed on the website so all mobile students can easily access this support, throughout their stay.&nbsp;</p><p>Non-academic mentoring and support arrangements should already be outlined in the Course Catalogue of the receiving HEI, in the section on general information for students, with relevant contact persons in the respective areas. Academic advisors should have close contact with the practical services which are available to incoming participants as they are often the first line of contact to the incoming student. Further information sessions should be arranged for all staff who work with incoming students to ensure they are adequately signposted on to the appropriate services they require.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It appoints responsible person(s) to deal with academic issues (course timetables, student attendance, coursework, relationship with academic staff, etc.)</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is important that the receiving institution appoints specific named academic advisors who are responsible for dealing with problems related to academic issues (course timetables, student attendance, coursework, relationship with academic staff, etc.) of incoming students.&nbsp; Information on mentoring for thesis writing for incoming students is particularly important and clear mentoring arrangements should be agreed upon between the student, sending and receiving institutions and organised before the mobility.</p><p>For traineeships, a mentor, different from the supervisor, should be nominated to support and encourage the mobile student while in the receiving organisation. The mentor should also provide information on the culture of the enterprise and informal codes and conducts, of the receiving organisation. The contact details of both the supervisor and the mentor should be specified in the Learning Agreement.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It provides preparatory language courses in the local language at the beginning of incoming mobility periods</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Receiving HEI's should provide adequate linguistic support, tailored to individual needs of the mobile participants. These courses may be offered, for example, as intensive courses during the orientation period or as semester or annual courses (in groups, as individual tuition or as subject-specific courses). It is considered good practice to allocate credits to these language classes and describe outcomes according to the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR): <a href="https://europass.cedefop.europa.eu/en/resources/european-language-levels-cefr">https://europass.cedefop.europa.eu/en/resources/european-language-levels-cefr</a>. This does not negate the sending institution's responsibility to ensure that their outgoing mobile participants have reached the recommended language levels (for example the existing OLS - online linguistic support).</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It organises activities to integrate them in the receiving institution and the local community, e.g. with the support of student organisations, Erasmus+ Student and Alumni Association etc.</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>As well as academic and practical support from the institution, incoming students need to feel fully integrated into the student community, something which is best done by their fellow students / peers. Local student association(s), such as Erasmus Student Network (ESN) and the other associations’ member of the ESAA - Erasmus+ Student and Alumni Association (<a href="http://esaa-eu.org/">http://esaa-eu.org/</a>), play an important role in supporting incoming students. Incoming students need to feel welcomed and included in the student organisations. To help this process, the student organisations need to be aware of their role in supporting this integration and have access to the right resources, information, guidance and incentives. As institutions often have many types of student organisations, cooperation between them is encouraged through meetings together, social activities and buddy programmes. A key aspect of these activities is to make sure they are for all students so incoming students are integrated with the local students and hence the culture. Student organisations include for example, ESN (Erasmus Student Network) or ESAA - Erasmus+ Student and Alumni Association (<a href="http://esaa-eu.org/">http://esaa-eu.org/</a>). ESAA runs a buddy system to encourage integration of incoming students with their peers inside the institution and share good practice with other member associations around Europe.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It provides opportunities for incoming mobile participants to share their culture and experiences with their peers inside and with the local community</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Incoming mobile students also bring new perspectives to the institution, the local students and the culture which is part of the internationalisation of the receiving institution. This is a significant opportunity to benefit from the experiences that international students bring. To capitalise on these experiences, the institution and its student organisations should put in place opportunities for incoming students to showcase their talent and perspectives through access to existing local initiatives (e.g. school teaching programmes, community projects) and setting up new initiatives to celebrate the different cultures (e.g. theatre performances, food and cultural weeks etc.). Local associations can support the integration of incoming students with the local community, through existing initiatives such as the Social Erasmus and Erasmus in School projects (<a href="http://socialerasmus.esn.org">http://socialerasmus.esn.org</a>).&nbsp;</p><p>Some incoming students may even have been involved in the management or governance of their sending institutions and recognising this opportunity and involving incoming students in similar functions in the receiving institution such as in the student union (elected representative) or working groups dedicated to the voice of the international student.&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>                      </div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q11.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question"> At the end of the mobility, your institution has formal procedures for recognising student mobility (good practices linked to recognition at the end of the mobility, e.g. in the use of Transcripts of Records and Grade Distribution Tables)</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Transcripts of Records are issued in a timely manner (normally 5 weeks) to both incoming and outgoing students</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is highly important in the recognition framework to provide Transcripts of Records in a timely manner, immediately following the mobility period. After the mobility, the receiving institution should send a Transcript of Records to the student and to the sending institution within a period stipulated in the Inter-Institutional Agreement (normally within five weeks after publication/proclamation of the student’s results at the receiving institution). It can be provided electronically or through any other means accessible to the student and the sending institution. The Transcript of Records from the receiving institution should refer to the educational components agreed upon in the Learning Agreement. Grade distribution information should be included as well, either as a web link or an annex.</p><p>Following the receipt of the Transcript of Records from the receiving institution, the sending institution should automatically transfer and recognise the student’s academic outcomes successfully completed at the receiving institution, as agreed in the Learning Agreement, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams. The Sending Institution will provide a Transcript of Records to the student or record the results in a database or any other means accessible to the student, normally within five weeks after having received the transcript of the receiving institution. The EU official template for the Learning Agreement for studies (including the Transcript of Records) is available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">All credits gained by students during a period of study abroad that were specified in the final version of the Learning Agreement are automatically transferred by your institution and count towards the students' final degree, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The sending institution should ensure that all the credits earned by the mobile student during the mobility period are recognised and counted towards the final degree, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams. The period of study abroad must be clear in the student's records and documents issued to the student (Diploma Supplement or equivalent). This is a golden rule of recognition of credit mobility within the framework of inter-institutional agreements. All the credits towards the student's degree that are earned during the mobility period and which were originally agreed on in the Learning Agreement (or a revised version to it) should be recognised by the sending HEI without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams. Learning Agreements are binding for all the parties and require that, on successful completion of the mobility period, the sending HEI recognises credits earned by the student and documents these credits in the student records, so they can be identified in a transparent way.</p><p>Upon receipt of the Transcript of Records or Training Certificates, the sending HEI should:<br>a) certify the mobile student has fulfilled all requirements stipulated in the Learning Agreement;<br>b) ensure recognition of the mobility period abroad within the time-scale and according to the conditions stipulated in the institutional recognition framework.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Transcripts of Records of incoming students include a description of or a link to the national grading system</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The Transcript of Records from the receiving institution should include grade distribution information, either as a web link or an annex. The local grading scale should be clearly explained, with a statistical distribution of local grades, to provide transparency and understanding of grading practices at the host institution. Where applicable, use should be made of a Grade Distribution Table for the programme of study, according to the ECTS Users’ Guide (<a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/ects/users-guide/index.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/ects/users-guide/index.htm</a>).</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Transcripts of Records of outgoing students provide details of the courses taken abroad</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The Transcript of Records should ensure a transparent recognition of the study period abroad, providing details of the courses the students undertook while studying abroad, including:</p><ul><li>Component code (if any)</li><li>Component title at the Receiving Institution&nbsp; (as indicated in the course catalogue)</li><li>If the component was successfully completed by the student?</li><li>Number of ECTS credits (or equivalent)</li><li>Grades received at the Receiving Institution</li></ul><p>The EU official template for the Learning Agreement (including the Transcript of Records) is available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm&nbsp;</a>&nbsp;</p>                      </div>

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question"> Your institution issues a Diploma Supplement</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>

                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
